author: Alkarim Billawala / alkarim.billawala.ca
weeks: Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders

questions.stem: A second-year medical student is preparing a wellness talk and wants to quote the Statistics Canada figures. She has one line for lifetime prevalence of mood or anxiety disorders among Canadians. Which figure belongs on it?
questions.explain: Why: the pre-week reading quotes Statistics Canada twice — 1 in 3 Canadians will meet criteria for any mental health or substance use disorder, and within that 1 in 5 (21.3%) for a mood or anxiety disorder. Not the others: one in three is the broader any-disorder figure; one in eight is the WHO worldwide figure quoted in Week 40 for any mental disorder; one in ten is not a figure given anywhere this week.

questions.stem: A third-year resident describes feeling emotionally drained after every call shift, increasingly detached and cynical toward patients, and convinced that nothing she does at work makes a difference. Which combination defines the syndrome she is describing?
options: Emotional exhaustion, depersonalization and a low sense of personal accomplishment
questions.explain: Why: burnout is a syndrome of three dimensions after Maslach — emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a low sense of personal accomplishment — developing in response to enduring work-related stress. Not the others: low mood, anhedonia and insomnia are depressive symptoms; absenteeism and errors are consequences of burnout, not its definition; fatigue and poor concentration are non-specific.

questions.stem: Two residents are assessed in the same week. The first feels cynical, exhausted and ineffective on the wards but reports feeling like herself again within days of starting a two-week vacation. The second has felt low and joyless for six weeks, including throughout a recent holiday, and has stopped seeing friends. How should the two be classified?
options: The first has burnout; the second has depression
The first has depression; the second has burnout
questions.explain: Why: the single discriminator is context: burnout's negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are associated with work and improve away from it; depression's are pervasive and persistent across settings. Symptoms that lift on holiday point to burnout; symptoms that persist through a holiday point to depression. Not the others: the two presentations differ exactly on the feature that separates them.

questions.stem: A hospital wellness committee is told that medical students must simply be a more vulnerable group than their peers, which is why their rates of depression are higher. Which finding most directly contradicts this explanation?
options: 27% of medical students report depression or depressive symptoms
Students accepted to medical school have lower rates of depression and burnout than similar-aged peers before training starts
Only 15.7% of depressed medical students seek treatment
questions.explain: Why: the pre-training data foreclose a selection effect: matriculants start with lower rates of depression and burnout than age-matched peers, and stress during medical school then raises the risk. The excess distress is therefore attributable to training, not to who enters medicine. Not the others: the 27%, 15.7% and 38% figures describe prevalence and help-seeking during or after training; none speaks to baseline vulnerability.

guide.s: lower rates of depression and burnout

questions.stem: A question asks for the proportion of Canadian residents who screened positive for depression in the 2018 CMA National Physician Health Survey. What is the figure?
questions.explain: Why: the CMA survey figures are 38% burnout, 48% positive depression screen, and 15% suicidal ideation in the past year. Not the others: 27% is the medical-student depression prevalence from Rotenstein 2016; 38% is the Canadian residents' burnout figure; 15% is their past-year suicidal ideation.

questions.stem: A clerk who screened positive for depression on a wellness survey explains why he has not sought care: he worries the diagnosis could reach his program director, affect his residency match, and lead to mandatory monitoring by the licensing body. What single construct underlies the barriers he describes?
questions.explain: Why: six barriers are named — lack of time, cost, confidentiality concerns, potential career implications, exposure to unwanted interventions, and more unwanted licensing or supervision oversight — and draws them all down into one word, stigma. The clerk names three of the four professional-consequence barriers. Not the others: lack of time and cost are practical barriers on the same list but are not what he describes, and access to psychiatrists is not one of the six.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old nurse has avoided elevators for years, taking the stairs even to the fourteenth floor, and once endured a single elevator ride 'shaking and certain it would drop'. She has now declined a supervisory position because the new unit is only reachable by elevator. Which DSM-5 criterion does the declined position most directly satisfy?
options: A: marked fear about a specific object or situation
C: the situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear
E: the fear has lasted six months or more
F: clinically significant distress or impairment in occupational function
questions.explain: Why: turning down the position is occupational impairment, criterion F — the element that converts a tolerable dislike into a disorder, exactly as Stuart's declined promotion does. Not the others: the fear of elevators is A, the stair-climbing and the endured ride are C, and the years of history are E; each is met, but the question asks which criterion the declined position satisfies.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old refuses to attend birthday parties because a costumed mascot might be present, screaming and hiding when one appears at a shopping centre. Which specifier applies?
questions.explain: Why: the five specifiers are animal, natural environment, blood-injection-injury, situational and other, and costumed characters are the example under other, alongside choking, vomiting and loud noises. Not the others: situational covers airplanes, elevators and enclosed spaces; animal covers insects, spiders and dogs; natural environment covers heights, storms and water.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a phobia of needles that has led him to skip vaccinations and blood tests asks what treatment has the best evidence. Which is it?
options: A short course of lorazepam before each procedure
An SSRI titrated over several months
Cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure
questions.explain: Why: CBT is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia, delivered as systematic desensitization up a fear hierarchy, and that there is little evidence to support medication in most cases. Not the others: no drug is named for specific phobia; benzodiazepines, SSRIs and beta blockers all belong to other disorders' treatment slides this week.

questions.stem: A patient with a spider phobia has just become comfortable looking at a live spider in a jar, which she had rated 5 out of 10. In the example hierarchy, which exposure comes next?
options: Touch the jar containing the spider
Stand two feet from a live spider
questions.explain: Why: the hierarchy runs picture 1/10 → rubber spider 3/10 → live spider in a jar 5/10 → touch the jar 8/10 → stand two feet away 9/10 → touch a live spider 10/10, and exposure moves up one level once the current level is tolerated. Not the others: the rubber spider is below her current level; standing two feet away and touching the spider are two and three steps further up.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman avoids crowded malls, buses and cinemas because she fears she could not get out or get help if she became unwell, and now leaves home only with her husband. She has no fear of any single object. Which diagnosis on the specific phobia differential best fits?
questions.explain: Why: fear of being unable to escape or get help across multiple situation types, with dependence on a companion, is agoraphobia, the first item on the differential. Not the others: a situational specific phobia is fear of one circumscribed situation, not a cluster of them; social anxiety disorder is fear of negative evaluation; panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks not tied to a cue, and none are described.

guide.s: unable to escape or get help

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student has stopped attending tutorials and eating in the cafeteria. She describes intense worry that others will notice her hands trembling or her face flushing and think she is 'pathetic'. She has no fear of the classroom itself and no unexpected attacks. Which feature makes social anxiety disorder the best diagnosis rather than specific phobia or agoraphobia?
options: The avoidance has lasted more than six months
The fear is of being negatively evaluated, including for the visible anxiety itself
The symptoms are out of proportion to the actual threat
She has stopped eating in public
questions.explain: Why: criterion B — fear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated — is the core of social anxiety disorder and the discriminator from specific phobia (fear of the object or situation itself) and agoraphobia (fear of being unable to escape or get help). Not the others: duration and disproportion are shared by all three anxiety disorders; avoiding eating in public is an example of avoidance, not the discriminating fear.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old sales manager has severe anxiety only when giving quarterly presentations to the board; he socializes comfortably, dines out, and has no other feared situations. He asks for a first-line medication. Which is it?
options: Propranolol taken as needed before presentations
questions.explain: Why: fear restricted to speaking or performing in public is the performance-only specifier, and the treatment flowchart routes it to propranolol PRN, taken before the performance. Not the others: the daily SSRIs, venlafaxine XR and pregabalin are the first-line options on the generalized branch, for patients whose fear extends across social situations.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports racing heart, breathlessness and chest tightness that arrive without warning, including while asleep and while alone at home; between attacks she worries constantly about the next one. She is comfortable in social settings. Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?
options: Social anxiety disorder with panic attacks
questions.explain: Why: recurrent unexpected panic attacks — occurring during sleep and when alone, with no social cue — plus worry about further attacks is panic disorder. Not the others: social anxiety with panic attacks requires the attacks to be cued by social situations, as Lindsay's are before presentations; a situational phobia needs one circumscribed situation; GAD is worry about multiple everyday matters, not discrete attacks.

questions.stem: A parent asks at what age social anxiety disorder most often begins. What is the median age of onset?
questions.explain: Why: the median age of onset is 13, with 75% beginning between 7 and 15. Not the others: 7 is the lower bound of that range; 30 is the median onset of GAD, the contrast the week's quizzes draw; 18 is not a figure that applies.

questions.stem: A resident is asked which SSRI appears on the first-line list for generalized social anxiety disorder but not on the GAD first-line list in this week's modules. Which is it?
questions.explain: Why: the social anxiety flowchart names escitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine and paroxetine; the GAD list names escitalopram, paroxetine and sertraline. Fluvoxamine is the one that appears only in the social anxiety list. Not the others: escitalopram and sertraline are first line for both disorders; fluoxetine appears in neither list and features only as Lindsay's past antidepressant.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with Parkinson's disease avoids restaurants because his tremor makes eating in front of others difficult, and he is embarrassed when it is noticed. His avoidance is limited to meals out and is proportionate to the visibility of his tremor. According to criterion J, how should this be classified?
options: Not social anxiety disorder, because the fear is related and proportionate to a visible medical condition
questions.explain: Why: criterion J states that when another medical condition such as Parkinson's disease, obesity or disfigurement is present, the fear must be clearly unrelated or excessive to count. Fear that is related and proportionate to a visible tremor does not meet the criterion. Not the others: neither specifier applies when the diagnosis itself is not met, and there is no phobic object.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old teacher has worried most days for eight months about her finances, her students' outcomes and her health, and says she cannot switch the worry off. She reports restlessness and muscle tension but sleeps well, concentrates adequately, is not irritable and is not unusually tired. Does she meet the criteria for GAD?
options: Yes: worry for more than six months is sufficient on its own
Yes: two of the six associated symptoms with uncontrollable worry meets the threshold
No: at least three of the six associated symptoms are required
No: the worry must be about a single domain
questions.explain: Why: the third criterion requires three or more of six associated symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, concentration or mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance). She has two — restlessness and muscle tension — so the count is not met despite eight months of uncontrollable worry. Not the others: duration and uncontrollability are necessary but not sufficient; GAD is worry about a number of events, so multiple domains fit rather than exclude.

questions.stem: Which statement about the epidemiology of GAD is correct?
options: Lifetime prevalence is about 3%, and it usually begins in childhood
Lifetime prevalence is about 9%, with a median age of onset of 30 and a 2:1 female predominance
Lifetime prevalence is about 20%, with equal sex distribution
It is the most common anxiety disorder and begins at a median age of 13
questions.explain: Why: GAD has 9% lifetime prevalence, median onset 30 (later than the other anxiety disorders, very unlikely before adolescence), and females twice as likely, 2:1. Not the others: 3% and 20% are distractors; median onset 13 is social anxiety disorder; specific phobia, not GAD, is the most common anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with six months of anxiety, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor and a 5 kg weight loss despite a good appetite. Before diagnosing GAD, which item on the differential should be addressed first?
options: Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition, such as hyperthyroidism
questions.explain: Why: the differential leads with anxiety disorder due to another medical condition and names hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma; heat intolerance, tremor and weight loss with a preserved appetite are the classic thyroid picture. Not the others: substance-induced anxiety is second on the list but nothing in the stem suggests caffeine or medication; social anxiety and OCD have no supporting features here.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed GAD prefers to start with psychotherapy. Which pair is recommended most?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
questions.explain: Why: CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy are the two therapies to recommend most. Not the others: exposure, relaxation, biofeedback, imagery and psychoeducation are all on the treatment list but are not the top two; psychodynamic psychotherapy is the one option that appears nowhere on the list.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with GAD, atrial fibrillation on a beta blocker, a documented rash to paroxetine and a good past response to sertraline for depression is to start medication. Given the first-line list and his history, which agent is the most appropriate choice?
questions.explain: Why: the first-line agents are the SSRIs escitalopram, paroxetine and sertraline, the SNRIs venlafaxine and duloxetine, and pregabalin; the paroxetine rash removes that option, and a prior response to sertraline makes it the natural choice. Not the others: paroxetine is contraindicated by the allergy; a benzodiazepine and an antipsychotic are the distractors for the drug class with the most evidence, which is an antidepressant.

questions.stem: A patient with GAD drinks four 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee daily and asks whether that is excessive. Roughly how does his daily caffeine intake compare with the moderate range?
options: About 240 mg, within the moderate range
About 400 mg, just above the moderate range
About 540 mg, roughly double the moderate ceiling
About 800 mg, roughly triple the moderate ceiling
questions.explain: Why: brewed coffee carries 135 mg per 8-ounce cup and a moderate range of 200–300 mg per day; four cups is about 540 mg, roughly double the ceiling, which is why reducing caffeinated and high-sugar drinks is advised. Not the others: 240 mg would be under two cups; 400 mg and 800 mg do not follow from those values.

questions.stem: Which single feature distinguishes GAD from both specific phobia and social anxiety disorder as this week's modules present them?
options: A required count of three of six associated symptoms
The need to rule out medical conditions and substances
The use of an SSRI as first-line treatment
questions.explain: Why: GAD is the only one of the three with a symptom count — three of six; specific phobia (A–G) and social anxiety disorder (A–J) require every criterion. Not the others: the six-month duration is shared by all three; ruling out organic and substance causes appears in all three differentials; SSRIs are first line in both GAD and social anxiety disorder, and no drug is supported in specific phobia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old accountant describes intrusive images of his apartment burning down. He re-checks the stove and every outlet in a fixed sequence before leaving, which takes about 20 minutes each morning; he finds the images senseless and is embarrassed by the checking. He is never late and describes only mild frustration. Which element of the OCD criteria is not clearly met?
options: B: severity, since the rituals occupy under an hour a day and cause only mild distress without impairment
Insight specifier, since he recognizes the thoughts as senseless
questions.explain: Why: criterion B requires marked distress, more than one hour a day, or significant interference with functioning; twenty minutes with mild frustration and no impairment meets none of the three limbs. Not the others: the intrusive fire images are obsessions and the sequenced checking is a compulsion performed to prevent a feared event, so criterion A is met; recognizing the thoughts as senseless describes good insight, a specifier rather than a failed criterion.

guide.s: occupy more than one hour a day

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman's home is filled to the ceilings with newspapers she cannot discard 'because one might contain a warning I will need to keep my family safe'. She also counts light switches in sets of four until the set feels complete. Which diagnosis applies?
questions.explain: Why: the override rule: when hoarding is driven by typical OCD obsessions such as harm prevention or incompleteness — keeping papers that might prevent harm, completing a set — OCD is diagnosed instead of hoarding disorder. Not the others: hoarding disorder is exclusively about difficulty discarding and accumulation without such obsessions; OCPD has no intrusions or rituals; there is no evidence of a fixed delusion without obsessional structure.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man spends hours nightly at online poker, enjoys the excitement, and says he would only stop because of his mounting debts. His wife describes the behaviour as 'compulsive'. What distinguishes this from an OCD compulsion?
options: It occupies more than an hour a day
He derives pleasure from the activity and resists it only because of its consequences
It is performed in response to an obsession
It is a stereotyped movement rather than a behaviour
questions.explain: Why: gambling, paraphilias and substance use are separated from OCD compulsions on one feature: the person derives pleasure from the activity and wishes to resist it only because of its deleterious consequences; OCD compulsions are performed to reduce discomfort, not for pleasure. Not the others: the time spent does not decide the category; there is no obsession driving the poker; a stereotyped movement is a repetitive non-functional motor behaviour such as rocking.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with OCD is started on sertraline. At week 8 she reports no benefit and asks whether the drug has failed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Stop sertraline and switch to clomipramine as first line
Continue and increase the dose: response often takes 6–12 weeks and an adequate trial is 12–15 weeks
Stop the medication abruptly and begin CBT instead
questions.explain: Why: the principles are to start low and aim high, to be patient because response often takes 6–12 weeks, and that an adequate trial requires 12–15 weeks; eight weeks at an unoptimized dose is not a failed trial. Not the others: clomipramine is a second-line agent, not first line; there is no augmentation pathway; medication is discontinued very slowly, never abruptly, and CBT can be added rather than substituted.

questions.stem: A patient with OCD asks whether taking an SSRI together with CBT would work better than either alone. Which statement is correct?
options: The combination is superior to both CBT alone and medication alone
The combination is superior to medication alone but not to CBT alone
Medication alone is superior to CBT alone
CBT adds nothing once an SSRI is started
questions.explain: Why: the algorithm's notes state that CBT is equivalent or superior to pharmacotherapy and that the combination of CBT and medication is superior to medication alone, but not to CBT alone. Not the others: each reverses one half of that statement; relapse rates are also higher with medication unless behavioural strategies are combined.

questions.stem: A therapist builds a contamination hierarchy with a patient whose items run from sorting dirty laundry (25/100) to touching a public toilet seat (80/100). Which statement about the exposure process is correct?
options: Exposure begins with the most distressing item so that habituation generalizes downward
Exposure proceeds systematically from the least distressing item upward while rituals and avoidance are prevented
Exposure is paired with performing the ritual afterward to limit distress
The hierarchy must begin at 100 to be valid
questions.explain: Why: ERP defines the triggers, ranks discomfort, builds a hierarchy with the most distressing item at the top, and then exposes the patient systematically while preventing both rituals and avoidance; treatment starts at the bottom of the hierarchy. Not the others: starting at the top is flooding, not systematic desensitization; performing the ritual afterward is the compulsion cycle that maintains the disorder; the example hierarchy tops out at 80, so a ceiling of 100 is not required.

questions.stem: Two anxiety-over-time graphs are shown: in one, each anxiety peak is followed by a near-vertical drop to baseline and every peak is the same height; in the other, each successive peak is lower and shorter. Which pairing of graph to process is correct?
options: First graph: habituation with exposure; second graph: the compulsion cycle
First graph: the compulsion cycle; second graph: habituation with repeated exposure and response prevention
Both graphs show the compulsion cycle at different stages
Both graphs show habituation, with and without medication
questions.explain: Why: performing a compulsion produces an abrupt drop to baseline and peaks that stay the same height, the highly reinforcing cycle that maintains OCD; repeated exposure with response prevention produces peaks that are progressively lower and shorter as the patient learns the feared outcome does not occur and anxiety subsides on its own — habituation. Not the others: the shapes are the defining difference between the two processes, so they cannot both be one process.

questions.stem: Six weeks after a serious highway collision, a 44-year-old bus driver has nightly nightmares of the crash, refuses to drive on highways, feels persistently numb and detached from his family, and is irritable with poor sleep. He has stopped working. Which statement about his diagnosis is correct?
options: Acute stress disorder, because symptoms began within a month of the event
PTSD: he meets the intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal thresholds and the disturbance has lasted over one month
Adjustment disorder, because the stressor was an accident rather than violence
GAD, because irritability and sleep disturbance dominate
questions.explain: Why: the criteria require at least one intrusion (nightmares), one avoidance (highways), two negative cognition or mood symptoms (persistent negative state, detachment), two arousal symptoms (irritability, sleep), a duration over one month, and impairment; six weeks past a collision with serious injury threatened satisfies all of it. Not the others: acute stress disorder is confined to the first 30 days; a collision threatening death or serious injury is a criterion-A trauma; GAD is generalized worry, not trauma-cued intrusions.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old paramedic with no single defining incident develops intrusive images, avoidance of certain call types and hypervigilance after years of attending fatal collisions. Does her exposure satisfy the trauma criterion?
options: No, because she was never personally in danger
No, because criterion A requires witnessing the death of a family member
Yes, because repeated exposure through occupation is one of the four routes
Yes, but only if she also learned that a loved one was harmed
questions.explain: Why: there are four routes to exposure — direct, witnessing, learning that a traumatic event happened to a loved one, and repeated exposure through occupation — so indirect and cumulative occupational exposure qualifies. Not the others: personal danger is only one route; witnessing a family member's death is not required; the loved-one route is an alternative, not an additional condition.

questions.stem: Ten days after witnessing a fatal stabbing, a 25-year-old has flashbacks, avoids the street where it happened and startles easily. What is the correct diagnosis at this point and the expected course?
options: PTSD; most patients remain symptomatic for years
Acute stress disorder; most patients recover, and a subset who remain symptomatic past 30 days are diagnosed with PTSD
Adjustment disorder; symptoms resolve within three months
No diagnosis; symptoms within a month of trauma are normal
questions.explain: Why: acute stress disorder is PTSD-type symptoms with functional impairment in the first 30 days after a highly traumatic event; most patients recover, and a subset with symptoms beyond 30 days are diagnosed with PTSD; time of onset is the distinguishing axis. Not the others: PTSD requires more than one month; adjustment disorder is a different diagnosis; symptomatic impairment within a month is a disorder, not normal.

questions.stem: Which set of figures matches the epidemiology of PTSD?
options: Lifetime prevalence 2–3%, mean onset 19.5, more common in males
Lifetime prevalence 6–9%, onset in the mid-to-late twenties, twice as common in females
Lifetime prevalence 9%, onset in adolescence, equal sex distribution
Lifetime prevalence 20%, onset after 40, more common in males
questions.explain: Why: lifetime prevalence is 6–9%, onset typically in the mid-to-late twenties (25–30), and twice as common in females. Not the others: 2–3% and 19.5 are OCD's numbers; the remaining sets are invented figures.

questions.stem: A patient with PTSD asks for the single most effective psychotherapy. A second patient is offered a choice limited to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, EMDR, psychodynamic psychotherapy, interpersonal therapy and relaxation therapy. What are the two answers?
options: Most effective: EMDR; from the limited list: trauma-focused CBT
Most effective: trauma-focused CBT; from the limited list: EMDR
Most effective: DBT; from the limited list: relaxation therapy
Most effective: cognitive processing therapy; from the limited list: interpersonal therapy
questions.explain: Why: trauma-focused CBT is the most effective modality and the mainstay, and EMDR is the answer for Annie when trauma-focused CBT is not among the options, EMDR being the only trauma-processing therapy on that list. Not the others: DBT is listed only as a therapy aimed at self-harm in BPD; cognitive processing therapy is a valid modality but not the most effective.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with PTSD is to start medication. Which option is first line, and which is wrong?
options: First line: venlafaxine XR; wrong: a benzodiazepine
questions.explain: Why: the first-line agents are the SSRIs fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline and the SNRI venlafaxine XR, and an antidepressant is chosen over benzodiazepine, ECT and antipsychotic. Not the others: each pairs a wrong class as first line with a first-line agent as wrong.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man develops nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance after being beaten unconscious during a robbery; he also reports headaches, slowed thinking and memory lapses. Which item on the medical differential must be considered alongside PTSD?
questions.explain: Why: the medical differential is traumatic brain injury, if physical trauma occurred, and neurological damage; being beaten unconscious with headaches, slowed thinking and memory lapses is exactly that scenario, and the two can coexist. Not the others: hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the organic mimics of anxiety; conversion disorder is on the psychiatric list, not the medical one.

questions.stem: A public-health student states that suicide rates in Canada are highest among 15-to-24-year-olds because suicide is the second leading cause of death in that group. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Suicide is not a leading cause of death in that age group
The highest suicide rates are in people aged 40–59; the second-place ranking at 15–24 reflects how few other causes of death there are at that age
Suicide rates are highest over age 65
The ranking applies to attempts, not deaths
questions.explain: Why: these are two separate facts: suicide is the second leading cause of death at ages 15–24, and the highest rates are at ages 40–59. A high ranking in the young is a ranking effect, not the highest rate. Not the others: the second-place ranking is correct as stated; no over-65 figure is given; the ranking is about deaths.

questions.stem: Which statement about sex differences in suicide is correct?
options: Males attempt more often and die more often
Females attempt three to four times more often, but males are more likely to die by suicide
Females attempt and die more often
questions.explain: Why: females are 3–4 times more likely to attempt suicide, while males are more likely to die by it. Not the others: each reverses or erases one half of that paradox. No mechanism is given for it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old divorced man with chronic back pain and heavy alcohol use is admitted after a serious overdose, his second attempt. Which of his features is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide across all age groups?
questions.explain: Why: a history of previous attempts is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide for all age groups; always ask about prior attempts. Not the others: pain, substance use and lack of a spouse are all SAD PERSONS risk factors present here, but previous attempts is the strongest.

questions.stem: A clerk hesitates to ask a depressed patient about suicidal thoughts, worried that raising the topic could plant the idea. What should the clerk do?
options: Avoid the topic unless the patient raises it first
Ask indirectly, for example 'you're not thinking of doing anything silly?'
Ask directly and calmly, using a normalizing statement first, because asking does not increase risk
Ask only if a family member is present
questions.explain: Why: the claim that asking increases risk is false: bringing up the topic does not increase risk and that the clinician's own discomfort must not get in the way. Patients do not necessarily volunteer these thoughts, so the approach is frank, calm, normalizing and ends in a direct question. Not the others: avoidance and oblique phrasing are the errors to avoid.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman says she has thought about 'taking all my pills'. Which sequence of questions is the first assessment step?
options: Ask about her childhood, then her family history, then her supports
Clarify whether the thoughts are passive or active, ask which pills and whether she has access to them, then ask whether she thinks she might actually do it
Ask about hope and reasons for living before anything else
Screen for depression with a symptom checklist
questions.explain: Why: step one, assess current plan and intent, separates ideation (passive versus active), then the plan and its feasibility with available means ("Which pills would you take?" "Do you have access to these pills?"), then intent and whether she has started to act. Not the others: protective factors are step four, asked after rapport; developmental history and depression screening are not part of the four-step sequence.

questions.stem: After assessing plan, intent, intensity and risk factors, a resident asks a suicidal patient, 'What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?' Which step of the approach is this, and which protective factor can the interview itself create?
options: Step 2, intensity; access to lethal means
Step 4, protective factors; a strong therapeutic alliance
questions.explain: Why: the question is one of the three scripted step four questions for eliciting hope and ambivalence, and the protective factors listed are children, spouse or family, pets, religious beliefs, intact self-esteem, and a strong therapeutic alliance, the one factor the clinician creates in the encounter. Not the others: access to lethal means is a risk factor; the other pairings mis-assign the step.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man develops persistent low mood, loss of interest and poor energy beginning three days after a left middle cerebral artery stroke, before he has learned the extent of his deficits. Which diagnosis is supported?
options: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
questions.explain: Why: post-stroke mood change with onset days after the event is a direct pathophysiological consequence, post-stroke depression as independent of the psychological effects of acquired disability; the time course tracks the event. Not the others: an adjustment reaction would follow awareness of the disability; a primary depressive disorder is excluded by criterion C when the medical cause is evident; there is no fluctuating inattention to suggest delirium.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman becomes tearful, hopeless and withdrawn beginning three weeks after being told she has a thyroid cancer that imaging suggests has been present for over a year. Which statement is correct?
options: This is a depressive disorder due to another medical condition because the symptoms began after a medical diagnosis
This is most likely a psychological reaction to the diagnosis, because the tumour predated the mood change and the symptoms track the news rather than the pathophysiology
This is a medication-induced depressive disorder
questions.explain: Why: the testicular-cancer scenario makes exactly this point: the cancer was present for some time before the diagnosis, so mood symptoms beginning after the diagnosis most likely represent a psychological reaction to being diagnosed, not a direct pathophysiological consequence. Not the others: timing from the diagnosis is the trap; there is no inattention or medication to implicate.

questions.stem: Which statement about the DSM-5 criteria for disorders due to another medical condition is correct?
options: Each disorder has its own version of all five criteria
Only criterion A differs between the depressive, bipolar and anxiety forms; criteria B to E are the same
A two-week duration and five of nine symptoms are required for the depressive form
Symptoms occurring only during delirium still qualify
questions.explain: Why: the symptoms under criterion A depend on the specific disorder while criteria B–E remain the same: pathophysiological evidence, not better explained by another disorder, not exclusively during delirium, and distress, impairment, hospitalization or psychotic features. Not the others: the disorder-specific criterion A variants carry no symptom counts or durations; symptoms confined to delirium are excluded by criterion D.

guide.s: Criterion A is the only disorder-specific criterion

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV develops persistent depressed mood two weeks after starting a new antiretroviral regimen; his viral load is well controlled and he has no history of drug use. Which label fits best?
options: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
questions.explain: Why: in HIV, three biological pathways carry three different labels: virus on the CNS → due to another medical condition; antiretroviral effect on the CNS → medication-induced; comorbid drug use → substance-induced. Onset after a new antiretroviral with controlled disease and no drug use points to the medication. Not the others: each names a different pathway than the one described.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with no psychiatric history develops new, recurrent, untriggered panic attacks. Which of the three diagnostic factors does her presentation most directly raise?
options: Atypical features: onset outside the typical risk period
questions.explain: Why: the three factors are time course, atypical features and a plausible pathophysiological mechanism, and its own example of an atypical feature is onset of panic disorder symptoms at age 70, outside the typical risk period and therefore a red flag for a medical cause. Not the others: nothing in the stem yet describes a medical condition's course or mechanism.

questions.stem: Which condition appears among the causes of both depressive and manic symptoms?
questions.explain: Why: four conditions appear in both the depressive and manic columns: stroke, traumatic brain injury, Cushing's disease and HIV infection. Not the others: Parkinson's disease is listed only under depressive symptoms; multiple sclerosis only under manic; hyperthyroidism only under anxiety.

questions.stem: A student argues that Nazi physicians must have abandoned their medical ethics entirely in order to take part in genocide. What is wrong with this view?
options: Most Nazi physicians were coerced and acted against their beliefs
They reinterpreted their duty to preserve life through dehumanization, seeing genocide as a 'therapeutic imperative' for society
Only a small minority of German doctors joined the Nazi party
Their ethics were suspended by law during wartime
questions.explain: Why: Nazi doctors did not think genocide contravened their commitment to life; their racism and dehumanization let them see it as helping society, a "therapeutic imperative", exemplified by Fritz Klein's gangrenous-appendix metaphor. Not the others: the German Medical Association documented support without coercion, and more than half of German doctors were early party members; wartime law is not the explanation.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the origin of modern research ethics ?
options: Tuskegee study → Nuremberg Code → Declaration of Helsinki
Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg (1946) → Nuremberg Code → Declaration of Helsinki
Declaration of Helsinki → Nuremberg Code → Belmont Report
Belmont Report → Nuremberg Code → Doctors' Trial
questions.explain: Why: the Doctors' Trial of 1946, in which 20 of 23 defendants were physicians, led to the Nuremberg Code, the first generally accepted code for research on human subjects (ten conditions including informed consent), which heavily informed the Declaration of Helsinki. Not the others: Tuskegee is the American chain that produced the Belmont Report of 1979, a separate lineage.

questions.stem: On a ward round a resident refers to a patient as 'the cirrhotic in bed 4' and remarks that 'he did this to himself'. Which lesson does this illustrate?
options: Dehumanizing discourse: discussing patients as their problems and blaming them for their conditions
questions.explain: Why: dehumanizing discourse in medicine includes discussing patients as their problems ("the heart failure in room 32") and blaming patients for their conditions, such as people who drink or use drugs, so that they receive less sympathy. Not the others: the remark is neither about inherited trauma, nor about resisting authority, nor about research.

questions.stem: Which detail of the Tuskegee syphilis study most directly shows that the harm continued after a cure was available?
options: The men were told they had 'bad blood'
Penicillin became the standard treatment by 1947 but was withheld until the study ended in 1972
The men were recruited through a free healthcare initiative
questions.explain: Why: penicillin had become the standard treatment for syphilis by 1947, yet the team withheld it, withheld information, and blocked access to treatment elsewhere until a whistleblower ended the study in 1972. Not the others: the deception, the start date and the recruitment method describe the design, not the continuation past a cure.

questions.stem: Which figure describes the disproportionate sterilization of Indigenous and Métis people in Alberta between 1969 and 1972. Which is it?
options: More than 25% of those sterilized while only 2.5% of the population
questions.explain: Why: from 1969 to 1972 Indigenous and Métis people accounted for more than 25% of sterilized patients but only 2.5% of the population, a ten-fold overrepresentation, under Alberta's Sexual Sterilization Act (1928–1972), which sterilized over 2,800 women in total. Not the others: 2,800 is the total across all women, not all Indigenous; 70% is the tuberculosis mortality figure from residential schools.

questions.stem: A clerk is told to perform an educational pelvic examination on an anaesthetized patient who was never told about it, and a senior resident says 'everyone does this'. Which response is correct?
options: Proceed, because a widespread practice is by definition acceptable
Proceed, because the exam does not compromise her surgical care
Decline: prevalence does not create consent, and the obligation to resist unethical practice holds even at personal cost
Proceed, but tell the patient afterwards
questions.explain: Why: prevalence does not change the ethics; "just following orders" is unacceptable and that students are obligated to resist unethical practice even in the face of personal consequences. Explicit consent had not been obtained. Not the others: each accepts the appeal to common practice or to lack of physical harm, which is rejected.

guide.s: explicit consent had not been obtained

questions.stem: A resident lists venlafaxine XR as a first-line agent for four disorders covered this week. For which of the following is it second line rather than first line?
questions.explain: Why: in OCD venlafaxine XR sits with clomipramine as second line behind five first-line SSRIs. Not the others: venlafaxine XR is first line in social anxiety disorder, GAD and PTSD.

questions.stem: Which pairing of drug and the only disorder on whose first-line list it appears this week is correct?
questions.explain: Why: duloxetine is named for GAD only. Not the others: fluvoxamine is on the social anxiety and OCD lists, never GAD; pregabalin is social anxiety and GAD, not OCD; propranolol PRN is for performance-only social anxiety, not the generalized form.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman avoids buses, cinemas and queues because she fears she could not get out if she panicked; she is comfortable giving presentations. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explain: Why: fear of two or more of public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, crowds or queues, and being out alone, driven by the thought that escape would be difficult, is agoraphobia. Not the others: she has no fear of evaluation; the fear spans several situation types rather than one object; there is no generalized worry.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man reports four months of 'racing thoughts' about money and his health, lies awake making lists, is exhausted by day, is irritable and tense, and denies feeling special or doing anything out of character. Which feature most reliably steers away from a manic or hypomanic episode?
options: Daytime exhaustion despite poor sleep, rather than reduced need for sleep with preserved energy
questions.explain: Why: in mania sleep is reduced but energy is preserved; worry-driven insomnia leaves the person tired. With no grandiosity and no uncharacteristic behaviour, the picture is GAD. Not the others: four months does not exclude bipolar disorder; irritability occurs in both; situational fast speech is not pressured speech.

questions.stem: A patient with OCD reports that hand-washing gives instant relief but the urge returns just as strong. Their therapist shows two graphs. Which description matches the curve for exposure with response prevention?
options: An abrupt drop to baseline with the same peak every time
Progressively lower peaks that come down sooner, settling on a common low plateau
A steadily rising baseline across sessions
No change in peak but a longer time to recover
questions.explain: Why: exposure without the ritual produces habituation: each successive peak is lower and resolves sooner, because the feared consequence does not occur. Not the others: the abrupt drop with an unchanged peak is the compulsion curve, which maintains the disorder through negative reinforcement.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders the typical age of onset from earliest to latest?
options: GAD, OCD, social anxiety disorder, PTSD
Social anxiety disorder, OCD, PTSD, GAD
OCD, social anxiety disorder, GAD, PTSD
PTSD, GAD, OCD, social anxiety disorder
questions.explain: Why: social anxiety disorder has a median onset of 13, OCD a mean of 19.5, PTSD mid-to-late twenties, and GAD a median of 30, the latest of the anxiety disorders. Not the others: each misplaces at least one disorder.

guide.s: Social anxiety starts in early adolescence

questions.stem: A student recalls that a lifetime prevalence of about 9% was quoted for two disorders this week and that 1 to 3% belongs to a third. Which set is correct?
options: 9%: social anxiety disorder and PTSD; 2–3%: GAD
questions.explain: Why: GAD 9% and PTSD 9% (quiz band 6–9%) share the figure; OCD is 2–3%, and 1–3% is the planted distractor on the PTSD item. Not the others: no lifetime percentage is given for social anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has had five days of elevated mood, sleeping three hours without fatigue, talking rapidly and starting several projects; she is still attending classes and completing her work, and there are no psychotic features. Which is the best characterization?
questions.explain: Why: at least four days of elevated mood with increased energy and no marked functional impairment, no psychosis and no hospitalization is a hypomanic episode. Not the others: mania requires a week or marked impairment; cyclothymia requires two years of subthreshold swings; preserved energy on three hours of sleep is the opposite of GAD's fatigue.

questions.stem: A patient starting lithium asks how the dose will be chosen and what to expect. Which answer is correct?
options: A weight-based dose, with liver enzymes checked monthly
A dose titrated to trough serum levels, with a fine tremor as a common expected effect
A standard loading dose, with osteoporosis screening
A dose set by hepatic function, with vitiligo as a common effect
questions.explain: Why: lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is titrated to serum levels; it is renally cleared, so hepatic function is irrelevant; a fine tremor is a common counselling point, and a coarse tremor signals toxicity. Not the others: weight-based dosing, loading protocols, osteoporosis and vitiligo are not part of lithium initiation; fatty liver belongs to valproate.

questions.stem: A patient reports two weeks of poor sleep, low energy, poor concentration, weight loss and guilt, but denies low mood and still enjoys her usual activities. Why do these five symptoms not satisfy the criteria for a major depressive episode?
options: Because at least one of depressed mood or anhedonia must be present
Because the duration must be four weeks
Because weight loss is not a criterion
questions.explain: Why: the rule is at least five of nine, one of which must be depressed mood or anhedonia; five non-core symptoms do not qualify. Not the others: five is the count; two weeks is the duration; weight change is a criterion.

questions.stem: A patient with social anxiety says, 'I froze once in a meeting, so I always make a fool of myself and I'm a complete failure.' Which two distortions are illustrated, in order?
questions.explain: Why: turning one event into an always rule is overgeneralization; attaching a global negative identity, "a complete failure", is labeling. Not the others: nothing positive is explained away and no future catastrophe is predicted.

questions.stem: Which statement about how medication and psychotherapy compare is correct?
options: In specific phobia, SSRIs and CBT are equally effective
In GAD, pharmacological and psychological treatments have equivalent efficacy
In OCD, medication alone is superior to CBT alone
In PTSD, benzodiazepines are the first-line drug
questions.explain: Why: in GAD medication and therapy have equivalent efficacy, and CBT plus an SSRI is the most effective combination. Not the others: specific phobia has little evidence for any medication; in OCD CBT is equal or superior, and CBT plus medication beats medication alone but not CBT alone; in PTSD the first line is an antidepressant and the benzodiazepine option is wrong.

guide.s: CBT plus medication beats medication alone

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman meets full criteria for a major depressive episode three weeks after being told she has metastatic breast cancer. Her TSH and CBC are normal and she takes no new medications. How is the episode best classified?
options: Major depressive disorder, likely triggered by the diagnosis
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
Adjustment disorder, because a stressor is present
questions.explain: Why: a catastrophic diagnosis that triggers a depressive episode is ordinary major depressive disorder; "secondary to a general medical condition" is reserved for an illness that biologically produces the syndrome, such as hypothyroidism or anaemia. Not the others: her labs exclude a physiological cause; full criteria for an episode take precedence over adjustment disorder; she has had no chemotherapy or new drug.

questions.stem: In a fifteen-minute family-practice visit, a 34-year-old man says he has "had a rough couple of weeks." Which two questions, if both answered no, allow the physician to set aside a diagnosis of depression without going through the full criteria?
options: How has your mood been over the last couple of weeks, and can you still enjoy the things that usually bring you pleasure
Have you had trouble sleeping, and has your appetite changed
Have you had thoughts of harming yourself, and have you lost weight
Are you more tired than usual, and is your concentration worse
questions.explain: Why: the episode requires at least one of depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure; if both are absent the patient cannot meet criteria by definition, so the remaining seven symptoms need not be canvassed. Not the others: sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and suicidal thoughts are among the nine, but none is a gate symptom; a patient can have all of them without the diagnosis if mood and pleasure are intact.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with a new depressive episode takes six medications for hypertension, atrial fibrillation and epilepsy. She recovered on fluoxetine in her twenties. Her daughter did well on venlafaxine last year. Which factor most strongly favours restarting fluoxetine over the alternatives?
options: Her own past response to fluoxetine
Fluoxetine's superior efficacy in the 2018 network meta-analysis
Fluoxetine's minimal cytochrome P450 interaction burden
questions.explain: Why: among a dozen first-line agents that the 2018 Cipriani analysis could not separate on efficacy, the deciding factors are past personal success, interactions, tolerability, discontinuation issues, family response and cost, and a documented remission on a drug is the strongest of these. Not the others: family response is weak evidence (though it helps adherence); no first-line agent is superior in the 2018 data; fluoxetine is not a low-interaction choice in polypharmacy, which would argue against it if it were the only consideration.

questions.stem: A student asks how a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor increases the serotonin signal reaching the postsynaptic neuron. Which statement is correct?
options: It blocks the presynaptic transporter that reabsorbs serotonin from the cleft
It blocks monoamine oxidase so that serotonin is not broken down
It increases the amount of serotonin released from presynaptic vesicles
It acts as a direct agonist at postsynaptic serotonin receptors
questions.explain: Why: the 5-HT reuptake transporter is the vacuum that clears serotonin back into the presynaptic neuron; blocking it leaves more serotonin in the cleft and increases postsynaptic activity. Not the others: blocking monoamine oxidase is the mechanism of MAOIs; SSRIs neither increase release nor act as receptor agonists. The downstream cause of the antidepressant effect, and its delay, remain unexplained.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man started sertraline four days ago and reports feeling noticeably better. His sister, on the same drug for anxiety, says nothing changed for her until the second week and improvement continued for over a month. Which statement best reconciles the two experiences?
options: Early improvement is largely placebo; active drug separates from placebo at about two weeks and reaches its full effect by about six
The drug acts within a day and any delay reflects poor adherence
Improvement before four weeks is impossible with an SSRI
Anxiety responds faster than depression, explaining the difference
questions.explain: Why: in the placebo-controlled sertraline trial both arms improved from day one; the curves separated at about two weeks and the drug arm continued to a plateau near six weeks. Feeling better at day four is real but mostly placebo and the effect of having a plan. Not the others: the synaptic effect is immediate but the clinical effect is delayed regardless of adherence; the old dogma that nothing happens before two to four weeks is wrong; anxiety responds more slowly than depression, and OCD slower still.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man's depression has responded to venlafaxine, and the dose has been raised twice. Which monitoring step is specific to his drug class rather than to SSRIs generally?
questions.explain: Why: at higher doses the serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors can raise blood pressure; that is the side effect SNRIs have that SSRIs do not. Sweating rises with both classes (19% vs 4% placebo even on sertraline). Not the others: weight gain is not a class effect of either group in meta-analyses; sexual dysfunction and gastrointestinal upset occur with both classes.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department shaking, unable to work or manage her children, and sleepless for three days with severe anxiety and low mood. There is no substance use history. Along with starting an SSRI and referring for therapy, which prescription is most appropriate?
options: Clonazepam 0.125 to 0.5 mg twice daily for a few weeks, withdrawn as the antidepressant takes effect
Lorazepam 1 mg sublingually as needed with unlimited refills
No benzodiazepine, because they are addictive in all circumstances
Diazepam nightly for a year alongside the antidepressant
questions.explain: Why: the antidepressant has perhaps a 50 to 60% chance of working and may take six weeks; a long-acting benzodiazepine at low dose as a bridge turns down the acute distress and is tapered as the SSRI works. Not the others: an open-ended as-needed short-acting agent is the pattern that produces dependence; refusing on principle leaves a patient falling apart for weeks; a year of nightly benzodiazepine is long-term use, which is not their role.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man with no psychiatric history presents with a first major depressive episode. His daughter mentions he recently left the stove on twice. Compared with a 77-year-old whose depression first appeared at 30 and has recurred, which statement is correct?
options: His prognosis is worse, with a more chronic course, higher relapse and medical comorbidity, and the episode may be a prodrome of dementia, so cognitive testing and collateral are warranted
His prognosis is better because he has had no prior episodes
Antidepressants are contraindicated after 75 and ECT is first line
First-onset late-life depression is diagnostic of dementia and should be managed as such
questions.explain: Why: late-onset late-life depression differs from recurrent early-onset depression in being highly comorbid with neurocognitive disorder and carrying a worse prognosis: a more chronic course, higher relapse, more medical comorbidity and cognitive impairment, sometimes as the prodrome to dementia. It is a flag for cognitive testing, perhaps imaging, and family collateral. Not the others: no prior episodes is not protective here; medication and psychotherapy remain the algorithm, with ECT used more often when the elderly "crash"; the association is a flag, not a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with moderate depression is told by her family doctor that psychotherapy and medication are equally effective for her. She asks why, in her experience, everyone she knows was given a prescription instead. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Access: about 95% of Canadians with mood or anxiety disorders are offered medication while about 20% receive psychotherapy, and public CBT wait-lists run 6 to 12 months
Medication is more effective than CBT for moderate depression
Psychotherapy is contraindicated when medication is available
Psychologists' services are covered by OHIP but their wait-lists are longer
questions.explain: Why: the 2014 national survey found 95% offered medication and 20% receiving a psychological intervention; the gap is a system problem, with hospital CBT clinics wait-listed 6 to 12 months and private psychologists charging about $250 a session outside OHIP. Not the others: for mild-to-moderate illness the two are equal; psychotherapy is a first-line option; psychologists are not OHIP-covered, physicians' psychotherapy is.

guide.t: 1 · Why most patients never get it

questions.stem: A patient asks how cognitive behavioural therapy differs from the psychoanalysis her grandmother had. Which set of features is characteristic of CBT?
options: Here-and-now focus, an active therapist, session agendas, symptom measurement, homework and the aim of making the patient their own therapist
Free association, a neutral therapist and interpretation of childhood material over years
Weekly sessions without goals so that themes can emerge
A focus on the therapeutic relationship as the main instrument of change
questions.explain: Why: Beck's CBT is structured, manualized and reproducible: goal-setting, an agenda for every session, measurement (PHQ-9, GAD-7), feedback, homework, and a therapist who teaches strategies so the patient becomes their own therapist, all in the present. Not the others: free association, neutrality and interpretation describe the older psychodynamic approach, which worked but could not be trialled; CBT is goal-driven; the relationship matters but is not CBT's defining instrument.

questions.stem: After a mediocre quiz result a 23-year-old student says, "I'll fail the final, lose my place in the program and never work in medicine." A classmate with the same result says, "I'll review the topics I missed." Which cognitive distortion best describes the first student's thinking?
questions.explain: Why: a chain that leaps from a quiz to expulsion to a ruined career is catastrophizing: jumping to the worst conclusion in a single bound, the anxious mind seeing the dangerous outcome rather than the likely one. Not the others: disqualifying the positive discounts good results ("he gave me 80% out of pity"); emotional reasoning treats a feeling as proof ("if it feels hopeless it is"); mind reading assumes others' judgements ("I can tell she thinks I'm weird").

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with moderate depression sleeps until noon, stays in pyjamas, scrolls his phone, ignores friends' messages and lies awake at night berating himself. His physician is prescribing an SSRI. Which additional intervention is appropriate at the same visit?
options: Behavioural activation: an activity log, then a daily plan of physical activity, social contact, an intellectual activity and self-care
Interoceptive exposure to induce the sensations he fears
A course of flooding to his most feared situation
Nothing until the antidepressant has worked for six weeks
questions.explain: Why: inactivity and withdrawal are depression's behavioural pitfalls, and behavioural activation (log the day, then schedule movement, social engagement, intellectual activity and self-care, plus the things that used to bring pleasure) has evidence and belongs in every medication visit for the patient who can still get out of bed. Not the others: interoceptive exposure and flooding are anxiety treatments; there is no reason to wait for the drug before activating behaviour.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with social anxiety leaves every party within ten minutes when her heart starts pounding and feels immediate relief. Her world has narrowed to her apartment and her job. Which statement best explains why her therapist asks her to stay at the next party until the anxiety falls?
options: Anxiety peaks and then subsides on its own if she remains; with repeated exposures the peak lowers and falls sooner, which is habituation, whereas leaving teaches the brain the party was dangerous
Staying proves to the other guests that she is not anxious
Anxiety rises indefinitely unless the situation is left, so she must learn to tolerate a permanently high level
Leaving early is harmless as long as she returns the next week
questions.explain: Why: avoidance gives instant relief and thereby teaches the brain that the situation was dangerous, so the next exposure is worse and the world shrinks; staying lets anxiety peak and fall (it does not go to infinity), and habituation lowers the peak with each repetition. Not the others: the learning is the patient's own, not the guests'; anxiety is time-limited; each avoidance strengthens the cycle.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with panic disorder is terrified of a racing heart. In sessions he runs on the spot without distress because "the doctor could save me," but he will not practise at home and is not improving. Which next step is most consistent with the principles of exposure therapy?
options: Negotiate a home-based exposure he considers safe enough, such as climbing a stairwell until his heart pounds, and progress up a hierarchy from there
Stop interoceptive exposure because it has failed and rely on an SSRI alone
Move directly to flooding by withdrawing all reassurance in session
Prescribe a benzodiazepine to take before each practice
questions.explain: Why: exposure works through repeated practice, and learning that happens only in a hospital office with a rescuer present does not generalize; the answer is a graded, negotiated home exposure (the stairwell) and then the next rung of the hierarchy. Not the others: the exposure has not been given a fair trial; flooding works but is hard to tolerate and consent to; a benzodiazepine before practice is a safety behaviour that blocks the learning.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a first major depressive episode agrees to start sertraline. Which starting regimen best reflects the approach taught, and why?
options: 25 mg daily for one week, then 50 mg, to improve tolerability and adherence; the therapeutic clock starts at 50 mg
50 mg daily from day one, since that is the lowest therapeutic dose
100 mg daily to shorten the time to response
25 mg as needed on bad days
questions.explain: Why: sertraline's range is 50 to 200 mg, but starting at the therapeutic dose risks early nausea, wooziness or anxiety that ends the trial after one tablet; half the lowest dose for a week lets the body adjust, and the two-to-four-week reassessment clock starts at 50 mg. Not the others: 50 mg from day one is acceptable but loses more trials to intolerance; higher starting doses add side effects without speeding response; the drug is taken every day, not as needed.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man started sertraline six weeks ago and has been on 50 mg for five of them. His PHQ-9 has fallen by a third, he tolerates the drug well, but he still has low energy and poor concentration. What is the next step?
options: Continue 50 mg and reassess in another month
questions.explain: Why: a partial response at a low dose calls for dose optimization: increase and wait, continuing up to the maximum of 200 mg before anything is added. Not the others: adding (combination or augmentation) is reserved for residual symptoms at the maximum dose; switching discards a drug that is working; waiting on 50 mg after five weeks is the mistake the second in-lecture question illustrates.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has been in full remission on citalopram for eleven months after her third lifetime depressive episode. She asks whether she can stop. Which advice reflects the guidance taught?
options: Because this is her third episode, the chance of a fourth exceeds 90%, and staying on the medication long term, possibly for life, is recommended
She may stop now, since a year is the standard duration after any episode
She must stop, because antidepressants lose effect after a year
She should switch to a different antidepressant to prevent tolerance
questions.explain: Why: after a first episode remission is held 6 to 12 months; after two episodes (70% recur) two years; after three or more (over 90%) the recommendation is to consider staying on for life. Not the others: one year applies to an uncomplicated first episode; antidepressants produce no tolerance; switching is for non-response, not maintenance.

questions.topic: Titration · What counts as a failed trial
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man says he has "failed everything": fluoxetine (two days, nausea), venlafaxine (never filled after reading about side effects) and sertraline (two doses, a friend's warning). Which conclusion is correct?
options: None of these is an adequate trial, so the algorithm restarts at step one with a first-line agent, started low
He has failed three first-line agents and needs augmentation
He should proceed directly to ECT
He should be switched to an MAOI after a washout
questions.explain: Why: an adequate trial is four weeks at a therapeutic dose; two days, two doses or an unfilled prescription are not failed trials, and the correct move is to go back to step one. Not the others: augmentation follows a partial response at the maximum dose; ECT is for severe or truly resistant illness; MAOIs are essentially never used here.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman on sertraline 200 mg for eight weeks is about 60% better but still ruminates, sleeps poorly and wakes some mornings not wanting to be alive. Her physician decides to add a second agent. Which pairing correctly labels the options?
options: Augmentation: a low-dose atypical antipsychotic, T3 or lithium; combination: mirtazapine or bupropion
Augmentation: switching to venlafaxine; combination: adding CBT
Augmentation: increasing sertraline to 300 mg; combination: adding a hypnotic
questions.explain: Why: at the maximum dose with residual symptoms the gains are kept and something is added: augmentation means a non-antidepressant (T3, an atypical antipsychotic at about a tenth of the schizophrenia dose, lithium, a stimulant, a hypnotic, a benzodiazepine, buspirone); combination means an antidepressant with a different mechanism, mirtazapine or bupropion. Not the others: a second SSRI is neither; switching is not adding; 300 mg is above the standard range and CBT is an augmentation of a different kind.

questions.stem: Three weeks after complicated pancreatic surgery, a 48-year-old man is intermittently drowsy, cannot spell WORLD backwards, knows only why he is in hospital, and describes a green dog outside the window; his temperature was 39 overnight and he is worse in the evenings. Which feature is the core criterion that defines his syndrome?
options: A disturbance in attention and awareness of acute onset that fluctuates during the day
questions.explain: Why: DSM-5 delirium is defined by criterion A, a disturbance in attention and awareness, with criterion B, acute onset and fluctuation, plus an additional cognitive disturbance and a physiological cause. Inattention (WORLD backwards), reduced orientation and evening worsening tied to fever are the defining picture. Not the others: hallucinations and disorientation are the "additional cognitive disturbance" of criterion C, not the core; fever is the cause, not the criterion.

questions.stem: Six months after an ICU admission for sepsis and ventilation, a 49-year-old man has nightmares of the unit, avoids the hospital district, startles at alarms, feels detached and cannot remember parts of the stay. Which psychotherapy was presented for his condition, and what is its central technique?
options: Prolonged exposure therapy, whose core is imaginal exposure: deliberately and repeatedly revisiting the memory until it loses its charge
Dialectical behaviour therapy, whose core is distress-tolerance skills
Psychodynamic therapy, whose core is interpretation of transference
Supportive counselling, whose core is avoiding reminders of the trauma
questions.explain: Why: his symptoms map onto PTSD criteria B to E for more than a month after a criterion-A trauma, and the treatment shown was prolonged exposure (Foa, Hembree and Rothbaum) with imaginal exposure, because avoidance is what maintains PTSD. Not the others: DBT targets emotional dysregulation; psychodynamic therapy is not the trauma-focused treatment presented; avoiding reminders is the pathology, not the therapy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old university student has had eight abrupt episodes over five months of pounding heart, breathlessness, tingling hands and a conviction she is dying, each peaking within minutes and settling within twenty. She now refuses to run and skips lectures in case one strikes. Two emergency visits found normal ECGs and bloodwork. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Social anxiety disorder with panic attacks
questions.explain: Why: recurrent, unexpected attacks peaking within minutes with four or more symptoms, followed by more than a month of maladaptive behaviour change (avoiding exercise and lectures) and no medical or substance explanation, is panic disorder; avoidance of exertion is the classic change because it reproduces the feared sensations. Not the others: her attacks are not cued by scrutiny; there is no pervasive worry about many domains; the avoidance and worry make this a disorder, not isolated attacks.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man's panic attacks occur only when he must speak in meetings or eat in front of colleagues, driven by the fear of embarrassing himself. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
options: Social anxiety disorder with panic attacks
Generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks
questions.explain: Why: what brings the attack on names the disorder: attacks cued by fear of scrutiny or embarrassment are social anxiety disorder, and the attacks become a specifier rather than disappearing. Not the others: panic disorder requires unexpected attacks; agoraphobia is fear of situations where escape is difficult; GAD with panic attacks would need pervasive worry across many domains as the trigger.

guide.s: What brings the attack on names the disorder

questions.stem: During a panic attack a 19-year-old woman notices tingling in her fingers and toes and that her vision goes spotty. Which physiological mechanisms best explain these two symptoms?
options: Vasoconstriction of small peripheral vessels, and pupillary dilation
Vasodilation of all vessels, and pupillary constriction
questions.explain: Why: sympathetic activation dilates vessels in the large muscle groups but constricts the small peripheral vessels, which is why the fingers tingle, and dilates the pupils to admit light, which blurs or spots vision. Not the others: the response bronchodilates and dilates pupils; peristalsis slowing produces nausea, not paresthesias; there is no retinal ischaemia.

guide.s: constriction in the small peripheral vessels

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man with panic disorder was given lorazepam in the emergency department and now takes it most days because it works within minutes. He is a student and an athlete who drinks socially. Which is the strongest reason to move him to definitive treatment rather than continue?
options: Daily use produces tolerance and physical dependence within weeks, with a withdrawal that resembles alcohol withdrawal, and the drug acts as a safety behaviour that blocks the learning CBT depends on
Lorazepam is ineffective against panic symptoms
Benzodiazepines are first line only for generalized anxiety disorder
Lorazepam has a long half-life and accumulates dangerously
questions.explain: Why: benzodiazepines are first line for none of the core anxiety disorders; daily use brings tolerance and dependence within weeks, rebound anxiety, sedation and additive effects with alcohol, and taking the pill teaches him that the pill, not his own tolerance, ended the attack. Not the others: lorazepam works acutely, which is the problem; benzodiazepines are not first line for GAD either; lorazepam is short-acting, which increases dependence risk relative to diazepam.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with panic disorder and no comorbidity asks what the treatments with the best evidence are. Which combination is correct?
options: An SSRI such as sertraline or the SNRI venlafaxine, and CBT that includes interoceptive exposure
A benzodiazepine taken daily and supportive counselling
A tricyclic antidepressant and psychodynamic therapy
Propranolol as needed and mindfulness alone
questions.explain: Why: first-line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, citalopram) or venlafaxine, dosed toward the top of the range and given four to six weeks or more; first-line psychotherapy is CBT with graded exposure and, specifically for panic, interoceptive exposure to the feared sensations. Not the others: benzodiazepines are not first line; tricyclics work but are not preferred; propranolol is for performance anxiety and mindfulness is not an acute treatment.

questions.stem: Three months after her mother's death a 45-year-old woman is tearful and eats less. Which single finding, if present, most strongly shifts the picture from grief toward a major depressive episode?
options: Low mood present all day, most days, with no moments of enjoyment at all
Crying when reminded of her mother
Poor sleep on the anniversary of the death
Feeling sad on difficult days but lifting at other times
questions.explain: Why: the discriminating questions are whether there are any moments of enjoyment and whether the low mood is all day, most days; grief has bad days and lifts between them, whereas depression is pervasive and anhedonic. Not the others: tears at reminders, disturbed sleep around an anniversary and fluctuating sadness are the expected shape of grief.

questions.topic: Depression · The screen before the antidepressant
questions.stem: A family physician is about to start an SSRI for a 20-year-old man with a first major depressive episode. His labs are normal. His father was once hospitalized for "a mood problem." Which step is essential before the prescription is written?
options: Screen him and a family informant for any past manic or hypomanic episode, because an antidepressant alone can precipitate mania in bipolar disorder
Order a urine drug screen, since substance use must be excluded by testing
Refer for CBT first, because psychotherapy must precede medication
Start a mood stabilizer prophylactically because of the family history
questions.explain: Why: every depressed patient is screened for a personal and family history of mania or hypomania before an antidepressant, with collateral from someone who saw the patient during any suspicious period, because antidepressant monotherapy in undiagnosed bipolar disorder can precipitate mania. Not the others: urine drug screens are not routine outside psychosis with an unreliable historian; medication and CBT are both first line; a mood stabilizer is not started on family history alone.

questions.stem: For nine days a 24-year-old woman has been irritable rather than euphoric, sleeping two hours yet full of energy, starting three business ventures, talking rapidly and spending her savings on equipment. How many associated symptoms does her episode require to meet the manic-episode criterion, and why?
options: Four, because her mood disturbance is irritable only
Three, the standard requirement regardless of mood quality
Two, because the episode exceeds one week
Five, as for a major depressive episode
questions.explain: Why: a manic episode needs elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy or goal-directed activity for at least a week, plus three or more associated symptoms, or four if the mood is only irritable. She has decreased need for sleep, increased activity, talkativeness and indiscretion, so she meets it. Not the others: three applies when the mood is elevated; duration does not lower the count; five of nine is the depressive threshold.

guide.s: four if the mood is only irritable

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man has had one prior major depressive episode. Over four days he has become grandiose, sleepless and convinced he is receiving messages from God, and he is admitted to hospital. His symptoms have not yet lasted a week. Which diagnosis is correct, and why?
