options: Bipolar I disorder, because psychosis and hospitalization make the episode manic regardless of the one-week duration
Bipolar II disorder, because the episode is under a week and he has a prior depressive episode
Cyclothymic disorder, pending a longer history
Major depressive disorder with a hypomanic switch
questions.explain: Why: two hierarchy rules: a full manic episode makes the diagnosis bipolar I for good, and severity overrides duration, so an episode with psychosis or requiring hospitalization counts as mania even before a week has passed. Not the others: hypomania by definition has no psychosis and no hospitalization, so bipolar II is excluded; cyclothymia is a chronic subthreshold pattern; a psychotic manic episode is not "MDD with a switch".

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man became manic three weeks after his sertraline dose was raised. His mother stopped the drug immediately. Four weeks later he remains grandiose, sleepless and psychotic. How is the episode best classified?
options: A manic episode of bipolar I disorder, because the symptoms persisted and worsened for weeks after the antidepressant was stopped
A substance/medication-induced manic episode, because an antidepressant preceded it
Schizophrenia, because psychosis has lasted more than a month
questions.explain: Why: had he presented while still on sertraline the label would have been a medication-induced manic episode; symptoms that persist and worsen for three to four weeks off the drug declare a primary bipolar disorder, and he is now bipolar I. Not the others: the medication label does not survive weeks of drug-free mania; psychosis within a discrete mood episode with return to baseline between episodes is bipolar, not schizophrenia; he is oriented and not fluctuating.

questions.topic: Bipolar · Differential of a first mania
questions.stem: A 19-year-old is brought in with three days of pressured speech, no sleep, grandiosity and agitation after a weekend away. He denies drug use but is an unreliable historian. Which investigation is specifically justified here that would not be routine in an outpatient depression assessment?
options: A urine drug screen, because psychosis in an unreliable historian is the accepted indication
A CT head, which is routine in all first mood episodes
An EEG, because mania is usually epileptic
No investigations, since the diagnosis is clinical
questions.explain: Why: urine drug screens are not routine in outpatient or emergency psychiatric practice; the exception is psychosis in someone who cannot give a reliable history, and cocaine or methamphetamine intoxication can look exactly like mania. Not the others: imaging is reserved for focal signs or atypical features; seizure disorders can mimic mania but an EEG is not routine; the medical differential (hyperthyroidism, substances, CNS lesion) still needs bloodwork and a screen.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted with acute mania and psychotic features. The team plans lithium for the long term. Which statement about the first days of treatment reflects usual practice?
options: An atypical antipsychotic is usually started first because it works faster, with the mood stabilizer added jointly or once she settles; the antipsychotic may later be tapered while the mood stabilizer continues long term
Lithium alone is started, since antipsychotics are reserved for schizophrenia
Valproate is preferred in a woman of her age because it is the safest long-term agent
An SSRI is added to prevent the post-manic depression
questions.explain: Why: atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) and mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) are both first line, and very unwell patients start on the faster antipsychotic with the mood stabilizer added and kept long term to prevent both manic and depressive episodes. Not the others: antipsychotics treat mania; valproate is not started in anyone of childbearing age; an antidepressant risks precipitating mania.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man on lithium for six months plays basketball outdoors through a heat wave and has started ibuprofen for a knee injury. He arrives confused, vomiting, ataxic and with a coarse tremor. Which is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Send him to hospital for a serum lithium level now, since delirium, coarse tremor, ataxia and sudden vomiting on lithium indicate toxicity
Reassure him that these are common lithium side effects and review in a month
Increase fluids at home and recheck the level at the scheduled three-month visit
Switch the ibuprofen to naproxen and continue lithium
questions.explain: Why: dehydration and sweating plus an NSAID both raise lithium levels, and confusion or delirium, coarse tremor, ataxia and sudden nausea or vomiting are toxicity until proved otherwise: the level (toxic generally above 1.5 mmol/L) is checked in hospital. Not the others: fine tremor, thirst and nausea are the common effects; coarse tremor and confusion are not; NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors and ARBs all reduce clearance, so another NSAID does not help.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is discharged on lithium 300 mg in the morning and 600 mg at bedtime, started five days ago. When should his first serum level be drawn, and how?
options: Now, at about five days after starting, as a trough drawn 12 hours after the evening dose and before the morning dose; then five days after each dose change
In three months, drawn at any time of day
Only if he develops symptoms of toxicity
One hour after the morning dose, weekly
questions.explain: Why: steady state takes about five days, so the level is drawn five days after starting and five days after every dose change, always as a 12-hour trough (for Jon, 12 hours after the 600 mg bedtime dose); thereafter every three months, then every six months once stable, with renal and thyroid function and calcium every six months. Not the others: waiting three months or for symptoms misses early toxicity; a post-dose peak is uninterpretable.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, well for two years on valproate, wants to conceive. Which counselling is correct?
options: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and should not be continued; she needs ongoing mood stabilization because pregnancy and the postpartum are high-risk periods, and alternatives include lamotrigine, an atypical antipsychotic, or lithium with close level monitoring and counselling about Ebstein's anomaly
All mood stabilizers must be stopped before conception and restarted after delivery
Valproate may be continued because it has the best-established safety record in pregnancy
Lithium is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding is encouraged on it
questions.explain: Why: valproate carries a 5 to 9% risk of neural tube defects and about 11% of other malformations and is not used in anyone who could become pregnant; the risk of a mood episode in pregnancy and especially postpartum is high, so she must stay stabilized: lamotrigine (safe, no levels), an atypical antipsychotic, or lithium, which is not contraindicated but carries a 1 in 1,000 Ebstein's risk versus 1 in 20,000 baseline, needs frequent level adjustment, and is generally incompatible with breastfeeding. Not the others: stopping everything invites relapse; valproate is the most teratogenic; lithium is permitted with counselling.

cards.prompt: What proportion of Canadians will meet criteria for a mood or anxiety disorder in their lifetime, and for any mental health or substance use disorder?
cards.answer: Mood or anxiety disorder: 1 in 5 (about 21.3%). Any mental health or substance use disorder: 1 in 3.

cards.text: Burnout is a syndrome of {{emotional exhaustion}}, {{depersonalization}} and a low sense of {{personal accomplishment}}, developing in response to enduring work-related stress.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are risk factors for burnout?
What proportion of healthcare trainees and professionals report burnout?
What is the discriminator between burnout and depression?
cards.answer: Burnout's negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are tied to work and improve away from work; depression's are pervasive and persistent across contexts and time.

cards.prompt: Place the wellness-to-illness continuum in order from its starting point to its endpoint.
items: Stress
Burnout
Depression
Suicidality

cards.prompt: Match each figure to the population and measure it describes.

US residents with depression or depressive symptoms
Canadian residents with a positive depression screen
Depressed medical students who sought treatment

cards.prompt: Match each source to what it studied.
pairs: Depression and depressive symptoms among resident physicians
Depression and suicidal ideation among medical students
Burnout, depression screen and suicidal ideation in Canadian residents
Background review for the anxiety self-learning modules

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among the six barriers to medical trainees seeking mental health treatment?
options: More unwanted licensing or supervision oversight

guide.s: lower rates of depression and burnout

cards.prompt: Compared with similar-aged peers, students accepted to medical school have which pattern of depression and burnout before training begins?
Which of the following are system-level consequences of burnout?

guide.s: most common mental health disorder in women

cards.prompt: Where does specific phobia rank among mental disorders in women and in men?
cards.answer: Most common mental health disorder in women; second most common in men, behind substance-related disorders.

cards.text: In specific phobia the phobic object {{almost always}} provokes immediate fear, is actively avoided or {{endured with intense fear}}, and the fear typically lasts {{six months}} or more.

cards.prompt: Match each feared stimulus to its DSM-5 specifier.
Which specifiers are the most common specific phobias?
What is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia, and what is the evidence for medication?
cards.answer: CBT with exposure (systematic desensitization). Little evidence supports medication in most cases; no drug is named.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of systematic desensitization in order.
items: Rank fears on a hierarchy from 1 to 10, with 10 the most feared
Start graded exposure at the lowest level, paired with relaxation techniques
Once desensitized at that level, move up to the next level

cards.prompt: Order the spider-phobia exposure hierarchy from least to most feared.
items: Look at a picture of a spider
Hold a rubber spider
Look at a live spider in a jar
Touch the jar containing the spider
Stand two feet from a live spider
Touch a live spider

cards.prompt: A fear driven by anticipated negative evaluation by others points to which diagnosis rather than specific phobia?
In Stuart's case, what specifier applies, and which feature of his history makes the fear a disorder rather than a dislike?
cards.answer: Situational (airplanes). Occupational impairment: he is considering declining a promotion because of the fear.

cards.text: Social anxiety disorder is the {{second}} most common anxiety disorder, with a median age of onset of {{13}} and 75% beginning between ages {{7 and 15}}.

cards.prompt: What is the core fear in social anxiety disorder (criterion B)?
cards.answer: Fear of acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms, that will be negatively evaluated by others.

cards.prompt: Which disorders does criterion I name as ones that must not better explain the presentation?
Which medical conditions does criterion J give as examples, and what must be true of the fear for the diagnosis to stand?
cards.answer: Parkinson's disease, obesity, and disfigurement from burns or injury. The fear must be clearly unrelated to the condition or excessive.

cards.prompt: When does the performance-only specifier apply, and what does it change about treatment?
cards.answer: When the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public. Treatment becomes propranolol as needed rather than a daily SSRI, venlafaxine XR or pregabalin.

cards.prompt: Match each first-line agent for social anxiety disorder to its class.
Which SSRIs are named on the social anxiety disorder first-line flowchart?
Which two entries on the social anxiety differential appear on neither the specific phobia nor the GAD differential, and which non-disorder opens the list?
cards.answer: Selective mutism and avoidant personality disorder. The list opens with normative shyness.

cards.prompt: Which of these are examples of avoidance in social anxiety disorder?
What are the two named components of CBT for social anxiety disorder, and why is CBT the gold-standard non-pharmacological treatment rather than simply the gold standard?
cards.answer: Cognitive techniques (restructuring and challenging maladaptive thoughts) and behavioural techniques (exposures). Because, unlike specific phobia, social anxiety disorder also has a first-line drug list.

cards.text: GAD requires excessive worry more days than not for at least {{six months}} about a number of events, which the person finds {{difficult to control}}, with {{three}} or more of six associated symptoms.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among the six associated symptoms of GAD?
Give GAD's lifetime prevalence, median age of onset, sex ratio, and rate of comorbid major depressive disorder.
cards.answer: 9% lifetime; median onset 30 (latest of the anxiety disorders, rarely before adolescence); females 2:1; comorbid MDD in up to 50%.

cards.prompt: Match each excluded diagnosis to the reason for excluding it in Peter's case.
pairs: No recurrent unexpected panic attacks; worry is generalized
A pervasive personality pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control

cards.prompt: Which two medical conditions are named as causes of anxiety to rule out, and which substance is its worked example?
cards.answer: Pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism. Caffeine.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among the psychological treatments for GAD?
Which two therapies are recommended most for GAD, and what is the purpose of psychoeducation?
cards.answer: CBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. Psychoeducation aims to prevent avoidance of anxiety triggers.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for GAD?
Which drug class has the most evidence for treating GAD?
Which four SSRI side effects are listed for GAD?
cards.answer: GI symptoms, headaches, weight gain and sexual dysfunction (all of the above).

cards.prompt: Match each drink to its caffeine content per serving.
Compare the median ages of onset of social anxiety disorder and GAD.
cards.answer: Social anxiety disorder: median 13, 75% between 7 and 15. GAD: median 30, very unlikely before adolescence, the latest-onset anxiety disorder.

guide.s: occupy more than one hour a day

cards.text: OCD criterion B requires marked distress, symptoms occupying more than {{one hour}} a day, or significant interference with {{functioning}}.

cards.prompt: Give OCD's lifetime prevalence, mean age of onset, and the rate in first-degree relatives.
cards.answer: Lifetime prevalence 2–3%; mean onset 19.5 years (earlier peak in males); about 10% of first-degree relatives affected. It is the WHO's tenth leading cause of disability and runs a chronic course.

cards.prompt: Match each obsessive thought to its corresponding rituals.
pairs: Ordering, arranging, placing objects just so

cards.prompt: What are the OCD specifiers in DSM-5?
cards.answer: Insight: with good or fair insight, with poor insight, or with absent insight/delusional beliefs. And tic-related, if there is a current or past tic disorder.

cards.prompt: Match each related disorder to its discriminating feature.
pairs: Obsessions and compulsions limited to physical appearance
Exclusively difficulty discarding and excessive accumulation
Hair pulling in the absence of obsessions
Enduring perfectionism and rigid control without intrusions

cards.prompt: How is a complex tic distinguished from a compulsion?
cards.answer: Compulsions are usually preceded by obsessions; tics are often preceded by premonitory sensory urges. Tics are less complex and not aimed at neutralizing obsessions; both diagnoses may be given.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for OCD?
Which two agents are the popular second-line options for OCD?
cards.answer: Clomipramine (a tricyclic) and venlafaxine XR (an SNRI).

cards.text: In OCD the treatment goal is {{improvement}} rather than remission; doses start low and aim {{high}}; response often takes {{6–12}} weeks; an adequate trial requires {{12–15}} weeks; treatment continues for at least {{one year}}.

cards.prompt: Put the steps of exposure and response prevention in order.
items: Define a range of obsessional triggers
Rank the degree of discomfort with each trigger
Build a hierarchy with the most distressing trigger at the top
Expose the patient systematically to each trigger while preventing rituals and avoidance

cards.prompt: Which of the following are components of CBT for OCD?
Which is a distinctive advantage of medication over CBT for OCD?

cards.text: PTSD requires at least {{one}} intrusion symptom, {{one}} avoidance symptom, {{two}} negative cognition or mood symptoms and {{two}} arousal symptoms, lasting more than {{one month}}.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are routes of trauma exposure?
options: Learning it happened to a loved one

cards.prompt: Which of the following are intrusion symptoms in the PTSD criteria?
Which of the following are arousal and reactivity symptoms in the PTSD criteria?
Give PTSD's lifetime prevalence, sex ratio, typical onset, most common trauma source and effect on suicide risk.
cards.answer: Lifetime prevalence 9% (quiz band 6–9%); twice as common in females; onset mid-to-late twenties (25–30); sexual or relationship violence is the most common trauma; suicide risk increased two- to three-fold.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are PTSD risk factors?
What single axis distinguishes acute stress disorder from PTSD, and what is the expected course of acute stress disorder?
cards.answer: Time: acute stress disorder is symptoms within the first 30 days; PTSD is a disturbance lasting over one month. Most patients with acute stress disorder recover; a subset persist and are diagnosed with PTSD.

cards.prompt: Match each therapy to its description.
pairs: Psychoeducation, relaxation, cognitive processing, trauma narrative, mastery of reminders
Rhythmic movements or sounds while processing trauma memories
Gradual confrontation of trauma memories, feelings and situations

cards.prompt: Which therapy is most effective for PTSD, and which is the answer for Annie when trauma-focused CBT is not offered?
cards.answer: Most effective and mainstay: trauma-focused CBT. For Annie from a list without TF-CBT: EMDR, the only trauma-processing therapy offered.

cards.prompt: Which agents are first line for PTSD?
How is venlafaxine XR positioned in the PTSD and OCD modules respectively?
options: First line in PTSD, second line in OCD
Second line in PTSD, first line in OCD

cards.text: In 2013 there were over {{4,000}} suicides in Canada; suicide was the {{ninth}} leading cause of death overall and the {{second}} leading cause at ages 15 to 24, with the highest rates at ages {{40 to 59}}.

cards.prompt: State the sex difference in suicide attempts and deaths.
cards.answer: Females are three to four times more likely to attempt suicide; males are more likely to die by suicide.

cards.prompt: Match each letter of SAD PERSONS to its item.

cards.text: SAD PERSONS: Sex (male), Age (under 20 or over {{45}}), Depression, Previous attempts, {{Ethanol}} or substance use, Rational thinking loss, {{Social supports}} lacking, Organized plan, No spouse, Sickness or pain.

cards.prompt: Match each risk factor to its category.
Which single risk factor is one of the most powerful predictors of suicide for all age groups?
cards.answer: A history of previous suicide attempts. Always ask about prior attempts.

cards.prompt: Does asking a patient about suicide increase their risk?
options: Yes, it can plant the idea
No; the real barrier is the clinician's own discomfort
Only if asked more than once

cards.prompt: Put the four suicide-assessment steps in order.
items: Assess current suicidal plan and intent
Assess the intensity of the suicidal thinking
Assess risk factors (SAD PERSONS)
Assess reasons for living and protective factors

cards.prompt: Distinguish passive from active suicidal thoughts.
cards.answer: Passive: a wish to be dead or never to wake up. Active: a specific plan, such as jumping from a height, hanging, or overdosing.

cards.prompt: Which of the following belong to the assessment of the intensity of suicidal thinking?
options: Arrangements such as a note or a will

cards.prompt: Which of the following are protective factors against suicide?
What defines a mental disorder due to another medical condition, and what does the definition explicitly exclude?
cards.answer: Psychiatric symptoms that are a direct pathophysiological consequence of a medical condition and improve when it is treated. It excludes psychosocial reactions to having the illness.

cards.prompt: Which of the following are among criteria B to E for a disorder due to another medical condition?
options: Evidence from history, examination or laboratory findings of a direct pathophysiological consequence
Not better explained by another mental disorder
Symptoms present for at least two weeks
Does not occur exclusively during a delirium
At least five of nine symptoms

cards.prompt: Criterion E is satisfied by any one of which three things?
cards.answer: Clinically significant distress or impairment; hospitalization necessitated to prevent harm to self or others; or the presence of psychotic features.

cards.prompt: Match each disorder due to another medical condition to its criterion A.
pairs: Prominent, persistent depressed mood or markedly diminished interest predominating
Prominent, persistent elevated, expansive or irritable mood and increased activity or energy predominating
Panic attacks or anxiety predominant in the clinical picture

cards.prompt: Match each scenario to whether it is a direct pathophysiological consequence.
pairs: Panic attacks remitting after pheochromocytoma excision
Low mood two days after an MCA stroke
No: psychological reaction to a symptom
Hopelessness four weeks after a cancer diagnosis
No: reaction to the diagnosis; the tumour predated it

cards.prompt: Match each competing explanation to the criterion that excludes it.
pairs: C: not better explained by another mental disorder
B fails: no direct pathophysiological consequence
B: the cause is the drug, so medication-induced

cards.prompt: How is delirium defined, and how does it relate to the diagnosis?
cards.answer: Rapid-onset, fluctuating changes in attention and orientation in the acutely ill. Symptoms occurring only during delirium are not a disorder due to another medical condition.

cards.prompt: Match each pathway to depression in HIV/AIDS with the diagnosis it produces.
pairs: Effect of the virus on the CNS
Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
Effect of antiretrovirals on the CNS

cards.text: Diagnosing a disorder due to another medical condition rests on {{time course}} (onset, exacerbation or remission with the condition), {{atypical features}} such as onset of panic at age 70, and a known or plausible {{pathophysiological mechanism}}.

cards.prompt: Which conditions induce anxiety symptoms?
Which two medications are named as inducing psychiatric symptoms?
cards.answer: Prednisone and antiretrovirals.

cards.prompt: What did the Nazi doctor Fritz Klein say when asked how he reconciled his oath with killing, and what is the lesson?
cards.answer: That out of respect for human life he would remove a gangrenous appendix, and 'the Jew is the gangrenous appendix in the body of mankind'. The oath was reinterpreted through a medical metaphor, not abandoned.

cards.text: During the Holocaust {{11 million}} civilian non-combatants were murdered, including {{6 million}} Jews, {{250,000}} people with disabilities and {{200,000}} Roma.

cards.prompt: What proportion of German doctors joined the Nazi party early, and what was the character of their support?
cards.answer: More than half were early joining members; the German Medical Association documented support for the Nazi agenda without coercion.

cards.prompt: Order the escalation that physicians led.
items: Sterilization of hundreds of thousands with 'hereditary diseases'
Systematic euthanasia of disabled children and the mentally ill
Industrialized genocide in extermination camps

cards.prompt: Which roles did physicians play in the death camps?
options: Selecting who was sent to the gas chambers and who to labour camps

cards.prompt: What is the Nuremberg Code, how many conditions does it set, and which three are named?
cards.answer: The first generally accepted code governing research on human subjects, produced after the 1946 Doctors' Trial (20 of 23 defendants physicians). Ten conditions, among them informed consent, avoiding unnecessary mental or physical harm, and the right to withdraw consent at any time.

cards.prompt: Match each milestone to its year.
pairs: Tuskegee study ends after a whistleblower
Alberta Sexual Sterilization Act in force

cards.prompt: What was Syndrome K?
cards.answer: A fictional diagnosis invented by Dr. Adriano Ossicini at Fatebenefratelli Hospital in Rome in 1943 to mark healthy Jews who needed hiding; the 'patients' coughed to simulate TB during Nazi inspections, and dozens were saved.

cards.prompt: Which two features does the medical profession share with the Nazi regime, making physicians vulnerable to 'following orders'?
cards.answer: A culture of conformity and deference to hierarchy, and an ethical imperative to help that can be redirected.

cards.prompt: Where was intergenerational trauma first recognized, and how can it manifest in descendants?
cards.answer: In Holocaust survivors and their descendants; children and grandchildren of genocide survivors can show complex PTSD. It is now recognized in descendants of other genocides, of enslaved people, and of Indigenous Peoples.

cards.text: The Tuskegee study ran from {{1932}} to 1972, enrolled {{600}} Black men in Alabama who were told they had '{{bad blood}}', and withheld penicillin although it was standard by {{1947}}.

cards.prompt: What was the tuberculosis mortality at some residential schools, and what was the physicians' role?
cards.answer: Up to 70% of children died of TB alone at some schools in the early 1900s. Doctors did not intervene to prevent children with TB from being forcibly removed into those schools; later, physicians ran nutrition experiments on hundreds of children from six schools.

cards.prompt: What survey data exist on educational pelvic examinations under anaesthesia?
cards.answer: In 2003, 90% of 400 Philadelphia medical students surveyed had performed one; at the University of Oklahoma a large majority had, but only about a quarter of patients had consented.

cards.prompt: Match each anti-dehumanization strategy to its named construct.
pairs: Make patients more identifiable and increase personal responsibility
Give patients a more active role in decisions
Increase moral concern and individualize patients

cards.prompt: Match each disorder or episode to its duration threshold.
pairs: Specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, GAD

cards.prompt: Match each disorder to its symptom count.
pairs: 3 symptoms, 4 if mood is only irritable

cards.prompt: Match each drug to where it sits this week.
pairs: First line in social anxiety and OCD, not GAD
First line in social anxiety and GAD
First line SAD, GAD, PTSD; second line OCD

cards.prompt: Which SSRIs are on the first-line list for PTSD?
Which disorder this week has no first-line drug, and what is its treatment?
cards.answer: Specific phobia: little evidence supports medication in most cases. CBT with systematic desensitization is the gold standard: rank fears 1 to 10, start at 1/10, pair graded exposure with relaxation, advance once desensitized.

cards.prompt: Match each therapy to the disorder it is named for.
Contrast the anxiety curve after a compulsion with the curve across repeated exposures with response prevention.
cards.answer: Compulsion: abrupt drop straight back to baseline with the peak unchanged next time (negative reinforcement; disorder maintained). Exposure with response prevention: progressively lower peaks that resolve sooner, settling onto one low plateau (habituation).

cards.prompt: Match each statement to its cognitive distortion.
pairs: 'He only invited me to be nice'
'The presentation will be a total disaster'

cards.prompt: In this course, what are the three features of the cognitive triad?
Match each figure to its disorder.
Which situations belong to the DSM-5 agoraphobia list?
options: Standing in line or being in a crowd

cards.prompt: Which three absent features separate worry-driven 'racing thoughts' from a manic episode?
cards.answer: No decreased need for sleep with preserved energy (the patient is tired), no grandiosity, and no uncharacteristic or impulsive behaviour.

cards.text: Lithium is dosed by titration to {{serum levels}}, is cleared by the {{kidney}}, causes a {{fine}} tremor as a common effect while a {{coarse}} tremor signals toxicity, and fatty liver belongs to {{valproate}}.

cards.prompt: What is the best lifestyle counselling to prevent a recurrent manic episode, and why?
cards.answer: Maintain a regular sleep cycle: sleep loss is both a prodromal sign and a precipitant of mania.

cards.prompt: Match each depression risk factor to its domain.
Match each formative-quiz question to its answer.
pairs: Anxiety falling across induced panic exposures

cards.prompt: Which four self-learning modules are not tested by any of the fifteen quiz questions?
cards.answer: OCD and related disorders, PTSD, suicide risk assessment, and mental disorders due to another medical condition.

cards.prompt: A major depressive episode can be the presentation of which of the following?
options: A depressive disorder due to another medical condition

cards.text: Major depressive disorder is counted as the {{third}} leading cause of disability worldwide, with an estimated lifetime risk of about {{20}}%.

cards.prompt: Which two questions screen for a major depressive episode, and what does a negative answer to both mean?
cards.answer: How has your mood been over the last couple of weeks? Can you still enjoy the things that usually bring you pleasure? Both negative means the patient cannot meet criteria, because one of depressed mood or anhedonia is required.

cards.text: In children and adolescents the mood criterion of a major depressive episode can be {{irritable}} rather than sad, and failure to make expected {{weight}} gain counts for the weight criterion.

cards.prompt: Order the assessment steps from first to last.
items: Establish the diagnosis
Rule out medical conditions (hyperthyroidism, seizure disorder, asthma)
Consider comorbidity including substance use
Consider the special population (child, geriatric, pregnancy)
Stratify severity
Lay out the options and let the patient choose

cards.prompt: Give the three reasons SSRIs and SNRIs are first line for depression.
cards.answer: A long evidence base; generally very good tolerability; effectiveness for the common comorbidity (anxiety and trauma disorders as well as depression).

cards.prompt: What did the 2009 and 2018 Cipriani meta-analyses each show about choosing an antidepressant?
cards.answer: 2009: on efficacy versus acceptability, escitalopram and sertraline stood out. 2018, with far more data: every antidepressant beats placebo and none is clearly best, so the choice rests on history, interactions, tolerability, discontinuation, family response and cost.

cards.prompt: Which factors were taught as the basis for choosing among first-line antidepressants?
options: Family history of a successful trial
Superior efficacy of the newest agent

cards.prompt: Match the mechanism to the drug class that blocks it.
pairs: Not understood; the delay lives here

cards.text: Drug and placebo curves separate at about {{two}} weeks; the full antidepressant effect takes up to {{six}} weeks; OCD can take {{10 to 12}} weeks.

cards.prompt: What is the nocebo effect and why does it matter when prescribing an antidepressant?
cards.answer: The placebo effect in reverse: a patient warned heavily of side effects and danger experiences more of them. Consent must be honest, but over-emphasis can scare the patient off or manufacture a failed trial.

cards.prompt: Match the side effect to its management or teaching point.
pairs: Take on a full stomach; settles in 1–2 weeks
SNRIs at higher dose; check at each visit
Persists while on the drug; ask so patients do not stop silently
Stay the course; too early to judge

cards.prompt: Do SSRIs and SNRIs cause weight gain, and which antidepressants are the exceptions?
cards.answer: Not as a class in meta-analyses, so it need not be consented for; paroxetine (more anticholinergic) and mirtazapine are the exceptions.

cards.text: In the sertraline-versus-placebo GAD trial the adverse events that separated most clearly were nausea ({{28}}% vs 13%) and sweating ({{19}}% vs 4%).
As a bridge while an SSRI starts: clonazepam {{0.125–0.5}} mg PO twice daily. For rare panic attacks or a specific phobia: lorazepam {{1}} mg sublingually as needed.

cards.prompt: Why are benzodiazepines habit-forming when antidepressants are not?
cards.answer: Addictiveness tracks how fast a substance is felt. A benzodiazepine calms within minutes and the brain links the pill to the feeling; an antidepressant is not felt at all and makes a non-depressed person no happier.

cards.prompt: Which cautions apply to benzodiazepines in older patients?
Which features are shared by the treatment of depression in the very young and the very old?
options: Start low, go slow, and keep going
Longer drug trials before calling failure

cards.text: Late-life depression is onset after {{60}}; late late-life depression begins after {{75}}. The distinction that matters is early-adult-onset depression recurring in late life versus {{first onset}} late in life.

cards.prompt: Why does a first depressive episode at 75 carry a worse prognosis than a recurrence at 75?
cards.answer: First-onset late-life depression is highly comorbid with neurocognitive disorder: a more chronic course, higher relapse, more medical comorbidity and cognitive impairment, sometimes the prodrome to dementia. It prompts cognitive testing, perhaps an MRI, and family collateral.

cards.prompt: What are first- and second-line treatments for adolescent depression, and what is the regulatory status of antidepressants under 18 in Canada?
cards.answer: First line CBT or interpersonal therapy; second line an SSRI, with fluoxetine carrying the most evidence. Health Canada has approved no antidepressant under 18, so all such prescribing is off label.

cards.prompt: What did the 2004 black-box warning say, what happened after it, and what is the current position?
cards.answer: Antidepressants increased suicidal thinking and behaviour versus placebo in short-term studies of patients under 24. Prescribing fell sharply, untreated depression worsened and completed suicides rose. Current position: the risk of untreated depression is far greater; SSRIs may be appropriate with careful monitoring, weekly for the first month.

cards.prompt: Match the step of stepped care to its focus.
pairs: Recognition and assessment by the GP
Mild depression: watchful waiting, self-help, exercise
Moderate or severe depression: medication, psychological intervention, social support
Treatment-resistant, recurrent, atypical or psychotic depression
Risk to life or severe self-neglect: inpatient care, ECT

cards.prompt: Order the steps of an ECT treatment.
items: Anaesthetist gives a general anaesthetic
Anaesthetist gives a muscle relaxant
Psychiatrist attaches EEG monitors
Psychiatrist pushes the button
Seizure of about 30 seconds
About 30 minutes in recovery, then ward or home

cards.text: ECT is the gold standard for {{psychotic}} depression, given {{three}} times a week with significant improvement usually by {{six}} sessions; cognitive testing at {{six months}} shows baseline function.
rTMS is given for about {{30}} minutes a session, {{five}} days a week for {{four to six}} weeks, with side effects limited to local irritation and no anaesthetic.

cards.prompt: Match the deep brain stimulation target to its indication.

guide.t: 1 · Why most patients never get it

cards.text: In the 2014 Canadian survey, {{95}}% of people with a mood or anxiety disorder were offered medication and {{20}}% received a psychological intervention; hospital CBT wait-lists run {{6 to 12}} months.

guide.t: 1 · Why most patients never get it

cards.prompt: Which psychotherapy providers are covered by OHIP, and what does a psychologist typically charge?
cards.answer: A physician's psychotherapy (family doctor or psychiatrist) is covered. Psychologists are not, at about $250 a session; social workers and registered psychotherapists charge roughly $150 to $250.

cards.text: CBT was developed in the {{1970s}} by the psychologist {{Aaron Beck}} as a structured, manualized treatment, originally a {{16}}-session manual.

cards.prompt: Which features distinguished CBT from earlier psychotherapy?
options: Teaching the patient to be their own therapist

cards.prompt: Match the scale to what it measures.
In the CBT triangle, which element is the target and which are the levers?
cards.answer: Feelings are the outcome the therapy wants to change; thoughts (the cognitive part) and behaviour (the behavioural part) are the levers that reach them. A situation produces thoughts, and thoughts, behaviour and feelings influence one another.

cards.prompt: Match the example to the distortion.
pairs: "I can tell she thinks I'm weird"
"If I feel like it's hopeless it must be true"

cards.prompt: Order the seven columns of the Mind Over Mood thought record.
items: Situation
Moods, rated 0–100
Automatic thoughts, hot thought circled
Evidence for the hot thought
Evidence against the hot thought
Alternative or balanced thoughts, rated for belief
Moods now, re-rated

cards.prompt: A panic patient, just after an induced attack, rates his chance of dying at 50%. What is the reframe?
cards.answer: His heart rate has risen thousands of times without killing him; every time, the anxious brain insists death is near. What makes this time different?

cards.prompt: Match the disorder to its behavioural pitfall.
Which items make up the daily action plan in behavioural activation?
Who is behavioural activation for, and who is it not for?
cards.answer: For the depressed patient in between, who can still get out of bed, and it belongs in every medication visit. Not for the patient who cannot get out of bed, has lost 10 pounds, is psychotic or is actively suicidal.

cards.text: If a person stays in the feared situation, anxiety peaks and then falls as the body {{habituates}}; with each repeated exposure the peak is {{lower}} and the fall {{faster}}. Avoidance makes the world {{smaller}}.

cards.prompt: What turns panic attacks into panic disorder?
cards.answer: Attacks alone are no diagnosis. Panic disorder is the attacks plus the behaviour that grows around them: worry about the next attack and avoidance of the subway, open spaces, anywhere without a safe place.

cards.prompt: Which methods were taught for interoceptive exposure in panic disorder?
options: Hyperventilating for 20 seconds to a minute

cards.text: Hyperventilation causes fogginess and tunnel vision by blowing off {{carbon dioxide}} and dilating vessels, a normal physiological response that frightens the unprepared.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between a fear hierarchy and flooding, and do both work?
cards.answer: A hierarchy starts exposure at the bottom rung and climbs; flooding starts at the top. Both work, but flooding is hard to tolerate and hard to consent to, and a graded approach reaches the same place more tolerably.

guide.s: not an acute treatment for distress

cards.prompt: Which statement about mindfulness in mood disorders is correct?
options: It is not an acute treatment for distress but is in guidelines for relapse prevention in depression
It is the first-line treatment for a panic attack in progress
It replaces exposure therapy in anxiety disorders
It requires the patient to stop thinking

cards.prompt: What did the two-year follow-up of remitted depressed patients show for CBT versus clinical management?
cards.answer: About three quarters of the CBT group remained in remission at two years versus about one in five with clinical management: a patient who keeps using the skills is protected after therapy ends.

cards.prompt: Match the feature to the treatment it belongs to.
pairs: Long acting, can be very effective
Motivation and hard work, difficult to access

cards.text: For mild-to-moderate depression, one half to {{two thirds}} of patients get better with either CBT or medication; the two are {{equal}}.

cards.prompt: Name features that make a patient a poor candidate for CBT regardless of diagnosis.
cards.answer: A single parent working two jobs with no time, English not a first language, limited literacy, a flat refusal to do exposure work, or no access to an affordable or timely course.

cards.prompt: Why is "suicidality" as a referral reason compared to "fatigue"?
cards.answer: Both are symptoms with many causes. A depressive episode is treated as depression; an acute break-up gets support and safety planning, possibly admission, but not an antidepressant or CBT for a depression that is not there.

cards.text: Sertraline's effective range is {{50}} to {{200}} mg once daily; the usual start is {{25}} mg for a week, and the reassessment clock starts at 50 mg.

cards.prompt: Why cut sertraline's lowest dose in half for the first week?
cards.answer: Starting at 50 mg risks nausea, wooziness or anxiety after the first tablet and a trial abandoned after one or two doses; a week at 25 mg lets the body adjust and improves tolerability and adherence.

cards.text: On a rating scale, a {{25}}% reduction in score is a response and a score below the scale's {{cutoff}} is remission.

cards.prompt: Match the outcome at two to four weeks to its action.
pairs: Stay on the medication 6 to 12 months or longer
Switch: within class, then a different class
Optimize the dose up to the maximum

cards.text: After two depressive episodes there is a {{70}}% chance of a third; after three, more than {{90}}%. Two episodes means about {{two}} years of treatment; more than two means consider treatment for life.

guide.s: four weeks at a therapeutic dose

cards.prompt: What is an adequate antidepressant trial, and what is not?
cards.answer: Four weeks at a therapeutic dose. Two days of a drug stopped for nausea, a prescription never filled, or two doses abandoned on a friend's advice are not failed trials; the algorithm restarts at step one.

cards.prompt: Order the trials for a patient with no improvement on sertraline.
items: Trial 1: sertraline, started low and titrated
Trial 2: switch within class, e.g. escitalopram
Trial 3: switch to a different class, e.g. an SNRI

cards.prompt: What is psychiatry's rule about polypharmacy in depression, in contrast to pain or oncology?
cards.answer: One drug, maxed out, see what is left, then add. A patient arriving on five low-dose agents is cleared back to one drug at the right dose.

cards.prompt: Which are augmentation agents, that is, non-antidepressants added at the maximum antidepressant dose?
options: An atypical antipsychotic at low dose

cards.prompt: Which two antidepressants were named for combination, and why those?
cards.answer: Mirtazapine and bupropion, because each works through a different mechanism from serotonin reuptake inhibition (bupropion is a noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake inhibitor).

guide.s: a tenth of the schizophrenia dose

cards.text: An atypical antipsychotic used to augment an antidepressant is given at about a {{tenth}} of the schizophrenia dose, and the pharmacy leaflet's word "antipsychotic" needs a stigma conversation.

guide.s: None of these treatments is curative

cards.prompt: Why is an antidepressant started alongside ECT?
cards.answer: No psychiatric treatment is curative; ECT ends the episode quickly, but the antidepressant is needed to hold remission afterwards. Depression is managed chronically, like blood pressure.

guide.s: Washout is needed only after an MAOI

cards.prompt: Between which antidepressant switches is a washout period required?
options: Between an SSRI and an SNRI

cards.prompt: What happens when an SSRI is stopped abruptly, and how dangerous is it?
cards.answer: A discontinuation reaction: flaring anxiety, stomach upset, broken sleep and odd neurological sensations. Unpleasant but not dangerous like alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal; taper slowly and monitor for recurrence.

cards.prompt: A patient stable on venlafaxine for twenty years relapses. What is the first move, and why not switch?
cards.answer: Increase the dose, then add if needed; antidepressants do not produce tolerance, so relapse is not a reason to abandon a drug that has worked.

cards.text: {{40 to 60}}% of patients benefit from the first SSRI trial: about two thirds in clean populations, nearer a coin toss where substance use and personality pathology are common.

cards.prompt: Before calling a depression treatment-resistant, which should be revisited?
options: A missed diagnosis of bipolar, personality or neurocognitive disorder

cards.prompt: A patient on sertraline 50 mg for five weeks is partly better; the same patient at week ten is still depressed. What is the answer both times?
cards.answer: Increase the dose. At five weeks: not add (50 mg is low), not switch (there are gains), not wait. At ten weeks: still increase; optimization should have happened sooner, and adding or switching remains premature.

cards.prompt: Order the events of Adam's 2015 course.
items: Referral for a pancreatic lesion (May)
Whipple procedure (June 16)
Anastomotic leak, sepsis, ventilation, delirium, fistula, GI bleed
Haemoglobin nadir near 55 g/L in mid-July with rebound
Discharge from hospital (August 11)
Post-ICU PTSD and prolonged exposure therapy

cards.prompt: Which are DSM-5 criteria for delirium?
options: A disturbance in attention and awareness
Onset over hours to days with fluctuation during the day
An additional disturbance in cognition such as disorientation or perception
Evidence of a direct physiological cause
Persistence for at least one month

cards.prompt: What did Adam's consult note record on July 10, 2015?
cards.answer: Fluctuating consciousness when not sedated, inattention, disorientation and disorganization; visual and auditory hallucinations (a green dog outside the window, conversations with dead relatives); symptoms tracking his fever; inattentive, unable to spell WORLD backwards, oriented only to purpose, drowsy; temperature 39.0 overnight, heart rate about 130.

cards.prompt: Match the PTSD criterion to its content.
pairs: Exposure to trauma, direct or indirect
Intrusion: memories, dreams, dissociative reactions, distress at cues
Persistent avoidance of memories and reminders
Negative alterations in cognition and mood
Altered arousal and reactivity: startle, hypervigilance, sleep
Duration of B to E more than one month

cards.text: The core technique of prolonged exposure therapy for PTSD is {{imaginal}} exposure: returning to the memory deliberately and repeatedly, because {{avoidance}} is what keeps PTSD alive.
A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort peaking within {{minutes}}, with {{four}} or more symptoms; five hours of anxiety is a state of anxiety, not a panic attack.

cards.prompt: Match the symptom to its group.
State the criteria for panic disorder.
cards.answer: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks; after at least one, a month or more of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour; not attributable to a substance or medical condition; not better explained by another disorder.

cards.prompt: Match the trigger of panic attacks to the diagnosis.
pairs: Fear of embarrassment or being judged
Social anxiety disorder with panic attacks
One attack under real stress, no preoccupation or avoidance

cards.prompt: Give the four screening questions for panic disorder.
cards.answer: Do you have episodes of anxiety that go from zero to 100 in minutes? What symptoms do you get? Do they always follow a stressful situation or sometimes come out of the blue? Have you changed your routines because of them? Also ask about nocturnal attacks.

cards.prompt: Match the sympathetic effect to the panic symptom.

cards.text: The {{locus coeruleus}} is the brainstem origin of most noradrenergic pathways, projecting to the spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, hypothalamus and {{amygdala}} and activating the HPA axis.

cards.prompt: What physiological fact reassures a patient that a panic attack will end?
cards.answer: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are eventually destroyed and the parasympathetic system restores equilibrium, so anxiety cannot last forever; the same fact underpins interoceptive exposure.

cards.text: Short half-life benzodiazepines such as {{lorazepam}} and alprazolam carry more tolerance and dependence risk than long-acting {{diazepam}}; all act at {{GABA-A}} receptors.

cards.prompt: Which are accepted roles for a benzodiazepine in panic disorder?
options: A small as-needed supply for severe attacks that other strategies have failed, under a contract
A few-week bridge at antidepressant initiation

cards.prompt: What does benzodiazepine withdrawal look like?
cards.answer: Like alcohol withdrawal: anxiety, agitation, insomnia, nausea, tremor, rarely seizures; rebound anxiety appears as each dose wears off.

guide.s: higher end of the dose range

cards.text: Anxiety indications need the higher end of the SSRI range: sertraline up to {{200}} mg or more for anxiety and OCD versus 100 to 200 for depression, and {{four to six}} weeks or longer at a therapeutic dose.

cards.prompt: What is interoceptive exposure and what are two examples?
cards.answer: Deliberately inducing panic sensations so the patient learns they can be tolerated: hyperventilating into a paper bag, spinning in a swivel chair.

cards.prompt: How does severity guide the choice between medication and CBT?
cards.answer: Mild to moderate: comparable efficacy, the patient may choose either or both. Severe: medication first, because exposure therapy is impossible when symptoms are overwhelming.

guide.s: side effects can be used to advantage

cards.prompt: Match the comorbidity to the antidepressant whose side-effect profile suits it.
How is depression with active alcohol use disorder sequenced now?
cards.answer: Treated in tandem: start the antidepressant, use motivational interviewing for the alcohol, defer intensive psychotherapy until there is some stability. The old rule of treating the alcohol first is gone.

cards.text: A major depressive episode needs {{five}} of nine symptoms nearly every day for {{two}} weeks, with at least one of depressed mood or {{anhedonia}}; sleep, appetite and concentration changes alone never qualify.

cards.prompt: Distinguish passive from active suicidal ideation with the phrases taught.
cards.answer: Passive: "what's the point, life's not worth living." Active: "I'm having thoughts of overdosing on my medication."

cards.prompt: Which are part of the minimum work-up before attributing a depressive syndrome to primary depression?
options: Routine urine drug screen in every outpatient

cards.prompt: Which conditions were named as producing or precipitating depressive syndromes?
options: Anaemia and iron or B12 deficiency

cards.prompt: What is required to call a depressive syndrome substance-induced, and which substances were named?
cards.answer: A substance whose intoxication or withdrawal plausibly produces the syndrome, in the right time relationship: alcohol, cocaine withdrawal (markedly dysphoric), steroids.

guide.s: Bipolar depression is the harder problem

cards.prompt: Why is missing bipolar disorder in a depressed patient so consequential?
cards.answer: Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania; most of the time a bipolar patient spends unwell is spent depressed; and bipolar depressions respond poorly. Screen personal and family history, with collateral, before any antidepressant.

cards.prompt: Which are common SSRI side effects?
options: Early activation in the first two weeks
Stevens-Johnson syndrome as a common effect

cards.prompt: Why is SSRI sexual dysfunction the most bothersome side effect, and how is it managed?
cards.answer: It persists rather than settling and grows with dose, while anxiety needs higher doses. Manage with the lowest effective dose, a switch, or added bupropion; mirtazapine carries less risk.

cards.prompt: Match the serious effect to its context.
pairs: Platelet effects in the already predisposed; not a reason to stop before surgery
Hyperreflexia, clonus, autonomic instability, altered mental status; Hunter criteria; tramadol raises risk

cards.text: After a first depressive episode, continue the antidepressant {{6 to 12}} months after remission; after a second or later episode, {{2 to 5}} years or indefinitely; taper slowly at a calm time.

cards.prompt: Which are first-line psychotherapies for an acute major depressive episode?
Name the focus areas of interpersonal therapy.
cards.answer: Grief or major loss; a major life or role transition; interpersonal disputes; interpersonal sensitivity or deficits.

cards.prompt: Which are first-line options for bipolar depression?
Why is lamotrigine often chosen for young women with bipolar II?
cards.answer: Better tolerated, no lithium-style blood-level monitoring, and safe in pregnancy without teratogenic risk.

cards.prompt: Expand DIG FAST and state the manic-episode thresholds.
cards.answer: Distractibility, Indiscretion (painful-consequence activities), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep need decreased, Talkativeness. Mood change (elevated or irritable) plus increased energy for at least one week (any duration if hospitalized), with three or more of these, four if the mood is only irritable.

cards.prompt: What scale of behaviour counts as the 'indiscretion' criterion of mania?
cards.answer: Spending tens of thousands, not buying an unaffordable dress; also hypersexuality and out-of-character substance use.

guide.s: energized on two or three hours

cards.text: The manic sleep criterion is decreased {{need}} for sleep: energized on {{two or three}} hours as if after a full night, not insomnia with fatigue.

cards.prompt: Jon's speech was louder and faster. Was it pressured?
cards.answer: No. It remained interruptible; pressured speech is fast and hard to break into.

cards.text: Hypomania is the manic picture for at least {{four}} days without marked impairment, {{hospitalization}} or {{psychosis}}; bipolar II needs a hypomanic and a depressive episode with no history of mania.

cards.prompt: Which statements are correct?
options: A full manic episode makes the diagnosis bipolar I permanently
Psychosis or hospitalization makes an episode manic even under one week
Bipolar I requires at least one depressive episode
A patient with a manic episode can later be reclassified as bipolar II

guide.s: return to baseline between discrete mood episodes

cards.prompt: What longitudinal feature separates bipolar disorder from schizophrenia?
cards.answer: Bipolar patients return to baseline between discrete mood episodes; schizophrenia usually leaves residual psychosis even on treatment. Schizoaffective disorder is a psychotic illness with a mood disorder present most of the time.

guide.s: differential of a first manic presentation

cards.prompt: Which belong on the differential of a first manic presentation?
options: Major depressive disorder, once mania has declared itself

cards.text: ADHD is excluded from a first manic presentation by its childhood onset before age {{12}} and chronic course; manic distractibility sits inside a discrete episode.
A child of a parent with bipolar disorder has about a {{tenfold}} increase in risk, more if both parents are affected; heritability is quoted at {{40}}% (CBL) and 60 to 80% in published estimates.

cards.prompt: Which were named as the most heritable psychiatric conditions?
Match the agent to its class in acute mania.
Order the usual pharmacological course of a severe manic episode.
items: Start an atypical antipsychotic for speed
Add a mood stabilizer jointly or once the patient settles
Taper the antipsychotic when better, if possible
Continue the mood stabilizer long term to prevent mania and depression

cards.prompt: What is the main long-term liability of atypical antipsychotics, and what is being studied to offset it?
cards.answer: They are metabolically promoting: appetite, weight (60 pounds in a month has been seen on olanzapine), glucose and cholesterol. Metformin and GLP-1 agonists started alongside them are under study.

cards.text: {{Valproate}} is not started in anyone of childbearing age: neural tube defects in {{5 to 9}}% and other malformations in about {{11}}%.

cards.prompt: Which are uses of lithium?
options: Augmentation in resistant, highly suicidal unipolar depression

cards.prompt: What is distinctive about lithium's effect on suicide?
cards.answer: It is one of two psychiatric drugs believed to have genuine anti-suicidal properties, which is why it is also used to augment antidepressants in hard-to-treat, suicidal depression.

cards.text: Lithium targets about {{0.8 to 1.2}} mmol/L in acute mania and about 0.6 to 1.0 for maintenance; toxicity is generally above {{1.5}}; the level, not the dose, is the target.

cards.prompt: Which features on lithium should trigger an urgent level in hospital?
Which raise lithium levels?
Which are common, non-toxic lithium effects?

cards.text: Lithium's fine tremor is sometimes treated with low-dose {{propranolol}}; a coarse tremor suggests toxicity.

cards.prompt: Match the organ to lithium's effect on it.
pairs: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; chronic kidney disease, rarely end-stage

cards.prompt: Order the lithium monitoring steps in time.
items: Baseline renal function, electrolytes with calcium, TSH, CBC, ECG where indicated
12-hour trough level 5 days after starting
Level 5 days after every dose change
Level every 3 months once established
Level every 6 months when stable, with renal and thyroid function and calcium

cards.prompt: Jon takes lithium 300 mg in the morning and 600 mg at bedtime. When is his level drawn?
cards.answer: Twelve hours after the 600 mg bedtime dose, before the morning dose, five days after starting and after each change; his sleep and behaviour normalized within two weeks.

cards.text: First-trimester lithium carries about a {{1 in 1,000}} risk of Ebstein's anomaly versus 1 in {{20,000}} baseline; it is surgically correctable, and lithium is {{not}} contraindicated in pregnancy.

cards.prompt: What is the usual advice for a woman with bipolar disorder stabilized on lithium who plans pregnancy?
cards.answer: Continue it, because pregnancy and especially the postpartum are high-risk periods and lithium is what got her well; monitor and adjust levels frequently as fluid volumes shift; breastfeeding is generally not recommended, which leads some to switch to an atypical antipsychotic and accept relapse risk.

cards.prompt: Which were part of Jon's discharge teaching for bipolar disorder?
options: Learn personal warning signs and enlist family
Stop lithium once well for a month

cards.prompt: A patient on sertraline 25 mg for three weeks has no change; later at 200 mg for three weeks is still significantly depressed after some gain. What is done at each point?
cards.answer: 25 mg is sub-therapeutic: titrate as tolerated (100 to 200 mg for depression). At 200 mg with a partial response, augment: bupropion, a low-dose atypical antipsychotic, or psychotherapy.

cards.prompt: A patient on sertraline 100 mg for four weeks has had no benefit at all. What next, and does class matter?
cards.answer: Switch. Switching to a different class offers no advantage over switching within class; choose by side-effect profile, for instance bupropion for the fatigued patient.

guides.title: Week 41 · 1 Wellness in Medicine & the Burden of Mood and Anxiety Disorders
guides.html:
Pre-week · PW01 · PW02

Wellness in Medicine & the Burden of Mood and Anxiety Disorders

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How common mood and anxiety disorders are, why physicians are at higher risk, and what burnout is, costs, and hides behind.

How common mood and anxiety disorders are

Two Statistics Canada figures frame the week. One in three Canadians will meet criteria for a mental health or substance use disorder in their lifetime. Within that, one in five (about 21.3%) will meet criteria for a mood or anxiety disorder. The two numbers nest: the first is any disorder, the second is mood or anxiety specifically.

Mood and anxiety disorders carry a major impact on morbidity and mortality, and unrecognized they impair recovery from any other medical condition — the argument for every specialty, not only psychiatry. Teaching of these topics at UofT began in 2013; the strand on physicians' own mental health was added at students' request, on the premise that health care providers are more at risk than the rest of the population across medical school, residency and staff practice.

The pre-week package sets ten objectives in three blocks: one on the medical profession itself; a bipolar block of five (clinical features by DSM-5 criteria → differential diagnosis → psychosocial impact → biopsychosocial treatment → pharmacology); and an anxiety block of four on the same ladder, with clinical features covering anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD together. Both pharmacology objectives ask for mechanism of action and common or serious side effects, not drug names alone.

The assigned pre-week items
Four items, in order: the Wellness in Medicine module (below); two video lectures by Dr. Jason Quinn on bipolar and related disorders — Diagnosis and Psychosocial Impact and Treatment; and the background review for the anxiety modules, Craske and Stein, Anxiety, Lancet 2016. The optional guidelines (Katzman 2014 on anxiety, PTSD and OCD; CANMAT/ISBD 2018 on bipolar disorder; ISBD 2009 on safety monitoring; CANMAT 2016 on depression) are explicitly excluded from the Mastery Exercise.

The evidence base is two JAMA meta-analyses — Mata et al. 2015 on depression and depressive symptoms in resident physicians, and Rotenstein et al. 2016 on medical students, which also measured suicidal ideation — plus Canadian data from the CMA. The reflective hook is Michelle's story and the ways the medical system creates barriers to trainees and physicians seeking help.

Burnout: the definition

Burnout is a syndrome of three dimensions, after Maslach:

  1. Emotional exhaustion
  2. Depersonalization
  3. Low sense of personal accomplishment

It develops in response to enduring work-related stress and leads to decreased effectiveness at work. The definition is anchored to work, which is what later separates it from depression.

When it happens

Five risk factors, all occupational: high workload, low sense of control, low autonomy, seemingly endless or meaningless work, and work–life imbalance. All five are common features of medical training, and the resulting prevalence is 24–54% of healthcare trainees and professionals reporting burnout. No individual-level predisposing factors are given; the risk lives in the structure of the work.

What burnout costs

Individual consequencesSystem consequences
Loss of empathyPoor quality care
AbsenteeismPatient dissatisfaction
QuittingIncreased medical errors
Relationship problemsIncreased malpractice litigation
Family problemsIncreased hospital-associated infections
Health problemsIncreased patient mortality

The two columns are independent lists, not matched pairs. The system column escalates from soft outcomes to hard ones, ending in hospital-associated infections and patient mortality — the consequences of burnout fall on patients as well as on the person burning out.

Burnout and depression

Burnout may precede or precipitate depression, and it is a modifiable risk and aggravating factor for depression. The pathway is drawn as a continuum: stress → burnout → depression → suicidality, with burnout the way-station between ordinary stress and illness. The summary slide states it more strongly: burnout leads to increased risk of depression and suicidality.

BurnoutDepression
Improves away from workNegative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are pervasive and persistent
Negative thoughts, feelings and behaviours are associated with workPresent across contexts and over time
The discriminator is context: a resident who is cynical and depleted on service but well on a two-week holiday has burnout; a resident who is anhedonic on holiday too has depression.

The numbers

The order of the evidence matters. Before training, students accepted to medical school have lower rates of depression and burnout than similar-aged peers. Stress during medical school then raises the risk of both. Because matriculants start better off and end up worse, the excess distress is attributable to training rather than to who chooses medicine.

PopulationMeasureFigure
Healthcare trainees and professionalsReport burnout24–54%
Medical studentsDepression or depressive symptoms27%
General population, 18–25Depression9.3%
General population, 26–49Depression7.2%
Medical studentsRise in depressive symptoms after training begins13.5%
Medical studentsSuicidal ideation, past two weeks to a year11% (past two weeks 7.4%; past year 24.4%)
US residentsDepression or depressive symptoms21–43%
US residentsMedian absolute increase in depressive symptoms within a year of starting residency16%
Canadian residents (CMA national survey, 2018)Burnout38%
Canadian residentsPositive depression screen48%
Canadian residentsSuicidal ideation, past year15%
Medical students screening positive for depressionSought psychiatric or mental health treatment15.7%

Three sets are easily confused: the medical-student figures (27% depression; 11% suicidal ideation), the US resident figures (21–43%; a 16% increase in the first year), and the Canadian resident figures from the CMA survey (38% burnout, 48% depression screen, 15% suicidal ideation). The student depression rate of 27% is roughly three to four times the general-population rates of 9.3% and 7.2%. The past-year suicidal-ideation figure is larger than the pooled headline figure.

The treatment gap and why it exists

Of medical students who screen positive for depression, 15.7% seek psychiatric or mental health treatment — roughly one in six, leaving about 84% untreated. Six barriers explain why, converging on a single construct:

  1. Lack of time
  2. Cost
  3. Confidentiality concerns
  4. Potential career implications
  5. Exposure to unwanted interventions
  6. More unwanted licensing or supervision oversight

The first two are practical; the other four are consequences specific to being a trainee in medicine. All six drain into stigma, with an irony: mental health conditions are heavily stigmatized in the medical profession even though physicians long fought to have them classified as medical diagnoses.

Michelle's story
A trainee's own account, followed by the task of identifying reasons medical trainees may not seek care. The intended answers are the barriers above and the stigma beneath them; there is no single correct response.

Resources named

UofT Medicine Wellness · 10 TED Talks for When You Feel Burnt Out · the Provider Resilience app for burnout · MoodGym, a CBT website for depression · Sleepio, a CBT website for insomnia and depression. Three of the five are self-directed e-health tools, matching the evidence on web-based tools for burnout, depression and suicidality among health professionals.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • One in three is any mental health or substance use disorder; one in five (21.3%) is a mood or anxiety disorder. Reversing them is the common error.
  • Burnout has three dimensions, not two: exhaustion, depersonalization and low accomplishment. Cynicism alone is not the definition.
  • 24–54% is trainees and professionals together; 27% is medical students; 38% is Canadian residents. Each figure belongs to one population.
  • Selection does not explain the excess: entrants are healthier than peers before training starts.
  • Burnout improves away from work; depression does not. A vignette turns on whether symptoms lift on holiday.
  • Mata 2015 = residents; Rotenstein 2016 = students plus suicidal ideation.
  • No treatment for burnout and no protective factors are named; the only recommendations are the resources list.
Modifiable is the load-bearing word. Burnout is presented as a modifiable risk factor for depression, which is the argument for institutional intervention. An option that treats burnout as a fixed personal trait, or as equivalent to depression, is wrong.
One in five Canadians will have a mood or anxiety disorder; physicians are at higher risk at every career stage, and training itself raises it. Burnout is a three-part, work-bound syndrome that improves away from work, sits between stress and depression on a continuum, costs patients as well as clinicians, and goes untreated in most depressed medical students because six barriers converge on stigma.

guides.title: Week 41 · 2 Specific Phobia
guides.html:
SLM01 · Anxiety

Specific Phobia

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Criteria, stimulus specifiers, the differential, and why graded exposure rather than medication is the treatment.

The case: Stuart, 45, afraid of flying

A 45-year-old stockbroker on Bay Street, married with two children, has just been promoted into a role that requires flying from Toronto to Alberta and British Columbia several times a month. He is considering turning the promotion down because of a significant fear of flying. For years he has driven or taken the train to meetings instead — including driving from Toronto to Los Angeles each year for the annual general meeting. No psychiatric or medical history; lorazepam 2 mg as needed for anxiety; no substance use; his mother had severe agoraphobia; he is outgoing with a close network of supports.

The case maps onto the criteria: the feared situation is flying (criterion A); the loudest feature is active avoidance, driving across the continent rather than boarding a plane (C); and occupational impairment — a promotion at risk — is what turns a dislike of flying into a disorder (F). The specifier is situational. Three details are there to mislead: the outgoing personality and strong supports argue against social anxiety disorder; the mother's agoraphobia is family loading, but agoraphobia is itself on the differential; and the as-needed lorazepam is a realistic community prescription that the treatment guidance does not support.

Epidemiology

Specific phobia is the most common mental health disorder in women and the second most common in men, behind substance-related disorders. It is commonly comorbid with other anxiety disorders, mood disorders and substance-related disorders. No prevalence percentage, age of onset or sex ratio is given; those two sentences are the whole epidemiology, and both are repeated in the summary.

DSM-5 criteria

All seven are required.

Criterion
AMarked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation (flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection, seeing blood)
BThe phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety
CThe phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety
DThe fear or anxiety is out of proportion to the actual danger posed and to the sociocultural context
EThe fear, anxiety or avoidance is persistent, typically lasting six months or more
FIt causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of function
GNot better explained by symptoms of another mental disorder

Three details of wording carry exam weight. Criterion B says almost always, not always, so a patient who manages the occasional exposure still meets it. Criterion C allows endurance with intense fear as well as avoidance: the passenger who white-knuckles the flight still qualifies. The only number in the set is the six-month duration, which is the same duration threshold used for social anxiety disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

Specifiers: the phobic stimulus

SpecifierExamples
AnimalInsects, spiders, dogs
Natural environmentHeights, storms, water
Blood-injection-injuryNeedles, invasive medical procedures
SituationalAirplanes, elevators, enclosed spaces
OtherChoking, vomiting, loud noises, costumed characters

The summary names the four most common phobia types as animals, natural environments, blood-injection-injury and situational; other is a valid specifier but is not claimed to be common. The pairing most often tested is the odd one: a fear of clowns is other, not situational.

Differential diagnosis

Nine possibilities, in this order: agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, trauma- and stressor-related disorders, eating disorders, psychotic disorders, and other medical conditions or substances. It gives no discriminators of its own; the organizing question is what exactly is feared, and what makes the fear stop.

DiagnosisWhat drives the fear or avoidance
Specific phobiaOne circumscribed object or situation; immediate fear on exposure
Social anxiety disorderFear of negative evaluation by others
AgoraphobiaFear of being unable to escape or get help, across multiple situation types
Separation anxiety disorderFear of separation from an attachment figure
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected panic attacks not tied to one cue
Obsessive-compulsive disorderAvoidance driven by an obsession
Trauma- and stressor-related disordersAvoidance of trauma reminders
Eating disordersAvoidance of food driven by weight or shape concern
Psychotic disordersAvoidance driven by a delusion

Only the social-anxiety and panic discriminators come from this week's own modules; the rest are standard psychiatry. The final item on the list, ruling out medical conditions and substances, appears in all three anxiety modules.

Treatment

Cognitive behavioural therapy

CBT is the gold-standard treatment for specific phobia. It works by exposure to the feared stimulus, that is, systematic desensitization. The CBT triangle behind it — thoughts, feelings and behaviours joined by bidirectional arrows — is the justification for treating a phobia behaviourally: changing behaviour through exposure changes the thoughts and feelings, rather than the patient being argued out of the belief.

Systematic desensitization

  1. The person ranks their fears on a hierarchy from 1 to 10, with 10 the most feared.
  2. Exposure starts at the lowest level, with graded exposures paired with relaxation techniques.
  3. Once the person is desensitized at that level, exposure moves up to the next; progression is criterion-based, not time-based.
Spider hierarchyFear level
Look at a picture of a spider1/10
Hold a rubber spider3/10
Look at a live spider in a jar5/10
Touch the jar containing the spider8/10
Stand two feet from a live spider9/10
Touch a live spider10/10

The hierarchy climbs along two axes at once, representational to real and distance to contact, and its biggest jump (5 to 8) comes at the first physical contact with the container. Starting at the bottom is what makes this graded exposure rather than flooding.

Medication

There is little evidence to support medication in specific phobia in most cases; no drug is named for it. Specific phobia is the one anxiety disorder in this week's set with no first-line drug, which is the contrast to hold against social anxiety disorder (a full first-line flowchart) and GAD (three drug classes).

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Impairment is the diagnostic hinge. A dislike of flying becomes a disorder when a promotion is at stake.
  • Endured with intense fear counts. Boarding the plane in terror still satisfies criterion C.
  • Six months is the duration, shared with social anxiety disorder and GAD.
  • Clown = other, elevator = situational, needle = blood-injection-injury, storm = natural environment.
  • Most common disorder in women, second in men, with substance-related disorders first in men.
  • CBT with graded exposure is the answer to every treatment question; a medication option, including the patient's own as-needed benzodiazepine, is not supported.
  • A fear of multiple public situations with no escape is agoraphobia; a fear of being judged is social anxiety disorder; neither is a specific phobia even when a single situation dominates the story.
The benzodiazepine in the case is not the recommended treatment. Stuart arrives on lorazepam 2 mg as needed; yet medications have little evidence in specific phobia and CBT is the gold standard. A question asking for the best treatment expects CBT, not continuation or optimization of the benzodiazepine.
Specific phobia is marked, immediate, out-of-proportion fear of one object or situation, avoided or endured, lasting six months or more and causing impairment. It is the commonest mental disorder in women, is specified by stimulus type, and is treated with CBT by graded exposure up a 1-to-10 hierarchy, with no first-line medication.

guides.title: Week 41 · 3 Social Anxiety Disorder
guides.html:
SLM02 · Anxiety

Social Anxiety Disorder

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Fear of negative evaluation: the ten criteria, the performance-only specifier, the differential, and the first-line drug flowchart.

The case: Lindsay, 23, presenting in class

A 23-year-old law student, single, family in Ottawa, has increasing anxiety about presenting in class. Before a presentation she gets tachycardia, shortness of breath, chest pain, chills, a choking sensation and a fear of losing control. She also avoids social gatherings because she fears she will do something embarrassing. History: a depressive episode in high school treated with fluoxetine; hyperthyroidism; an oral contraceptive; one or two shots of whisky before presentations "to calm her nerves" and no other alcohol or substance use; a father described as a worrier; a supportive family; shy throughout school.

The six somatic symptoms are panic-attack symptoms, placed so that the reader must choose between social anxiety disorder with panic attacks and panic disorder. Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks; Lindsay's are cued, arriving before presentations. Her stated fear of doing something embarrassing is the fear of negative evaluation at the core of the diagnosis. Because she avoids social gatherings as well as presentations, the performance-only specifier does not apply, which also decides her drug treatment.
