Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

How well-meaning physicians took part in genocide, the codes that followed, the Canadian and American parallels, and the everyday dehumanization to recognize in oneself.

Why this is taught in medical school

The Holocaust was the largest mass killing in history, and German physicians played a significant role in supporting, rationalizing, planning and carrying out the genocide. Yet 15 to 22% of Canadians have not heard of it. The central claim: Nazi doctors were not monsters who abandoned medicine; they believed they were fulfilling a "therapeutic imperative", helping society as a whole, and their racism and dehumanization of their victims let them see genocide as treatment. Asked how he reconciled his oath with killing, the Nazi doctor Fritz Klein answered that out of respect for human life he would remove a gangrenous appendix from a diseased body, and that "the Jew is the gangrenous appendix in the body of mankind". The medical metaphor did the moral work; the oath was reinterpreted rather than broken. Dismissing such people as inhuman misses the point that well-meaning humans justified and carried out these acts, which is why understanding them is the only protection against justifying unethical behaviour in ourselves.

Background

WhenWhat
1933Hitler democratically elected chancellor; Germany becomes a totalitarian dictatorship. The mechanism was legal and electoral.
1930sNewspapers, entertainment, educational materials and public discourse portray Jews as rats, subhumans, parasites and viruses, blamed for Germany's misfortunes after the First World War: "it's wrong to kill a person, but permissible to exterminate a rat"
1939Expansion into Poland starts the Second World War
1941–1945"The Final Solution": systematic murder of Jews and others deemed undesirable

Nazi antisemitism drew on over 2,000 years of scapegoating, and is distinctive in casting Jews as both "less than" and "more than": subhuman, yet rich, powerful, subversive and pulling the strings of governments and economies. Most racism dehumanizes downward; antisemitism does both at once, which is why conspiracy theory is its native form.

Eleven million civilian non-combatants were murdered, including six million Jews, 250,000 people with disabilities, 200,000 Roma, thousands of Jehovah's Witnesses, gay men, Black people and political opponents, and millions of Eastern European civilians — in industrialized extermination camps such as Auschwitz, where victims were shipped by train into gas chambers, and in mass shootings, where local populations sometimes helped identify and round up Jews.

What physicians did

  • They volunteered. A large share of Nazi academics were doctors; more than half of German doctors were early members of the Nazi party; the German Medical Association documented its members' support without coercion. "We had no choice" is false.
  • They led the escalation. Physicians sterilized hundreds of thousands of people with "hereditary diseases", progressing to systematic euthanasia of disabled children and the mentally ill, and then to industrialized genocide. Disabled and mentally ill people were the first victims, and physicians ran that phase.
  • They ran the camps' killing. Three roles: selecting who went to the gas chamber and who to the labour camp, overseeing the gas chambers, and performing experiments on non-consenting subjects.
  • The experiments: oxygen deprivation, freezing, infection with malaria or typhus, mustard gas, forced ingestion of seawater, induced gangrene in wounds, and experiments on twins including amputations, poisonings and dissections. Most served the war effort.
  • The justification was the common good: purifying and protecting the German people from a group perceived as parasitic. Utilitarian in form, built on a dehumanized premise, and dressed as public health.

Four lessons

1. Research ethics

The Nuremberg Trials of 1946 included the Doctors' Trial, in which 20 of 23 defendants were physicians, and through it the world learned of the experiments. The trials produced the Nuremberg Code, the first generally accepted code governing research on human subjects: ten conditions, among them informed consent, avoiding unnecessary mental or physical harm, and the right to withdraw consent at any time. The Code heavily informed the Declaration of Helsinki, which still governs medical research today.

2. Dehumanizing discourse

The Holocaust did not happen "out of the blue"; it followed a decade of increasingly dehumanizing ways of talking about and treating Jews and other marginalized groups. Dehumanization makes it easier to treat people as undeserving of sympathy or rights, to blame them for their own or the nation's misfortune, and to treat them unfairly or cruelly. The categorization of human races as biologically distinct is not consistent with human genome mapping, and that treating race as biological rather than a social construct has itself been used to justify inequity.

Dehumanizing discourse inside medicine
Discussing patients as their problems ("the heart failure in room 32") · blaming obese patients, smokers and people who use drugs for any problem they develop · treating patients with cognitive issues as less important or less deserving of excellent care · speaking disparagingly of underhoused patients · disparaging language and poor care for racialized patients, as happened to Joyce Echaquan in Quebec. Recognizing such discourse in ourselves comes first.

3. Resisting authority

"I was just following orders" became synonymous with complicity, and since the Holocaust it is unacceptable as an excuse. Physicians may be especially vulnerable, because the profession shares two features with the regime: a culture of conformity and deference to hierarchy, and an ethical imperative to help, which in Nazi Germany became the imperative to "cleanse" society. Having a moral mission is itself a risk when the mission is redirected. Resistance existed: Oskar Schindler saved 1,200 Jews, and in Rome in 1943 doctors at Fatebenefratelli Hospital invented "Syndrome K", a fictional diagnosis created by Dr. Adriano Ossicini to mark healthy Jews who needed hiding; when Nazis inspected, the "patients" coughed to simulate tuberculosis and dozens were saved. Where Klein used a medical frame to justify killing, Ossicini used one to protect life. The normative conclusion: we are obligated to fight unethical practice even in the face of personal consequences.

4. Intergenerational trauma

Intergenerational trauma was first recognized in Holocaust survivors and their descendants. Children and grandchildren of genocide survivors can show complex post-traumatic stress disorder and other effects of their forebears' mistreatment. The phenomenon is now recognized in descendants of other wars and genocides, of enslaved people, and of Indigenous Peoples, including the intergenerational health effects of colonial practices and systemic racism across Turtle Island.

Atrocities by "well-meaning" physicians in North America

CaseWhat happenedThe lesson
Tuskegee syphilis study, 1932–1972The US Public Health Service recruited 600 Black men in rural Alabama to "free healthcare", told them they had "bad blood", gave placebo, and studied the natural history of untreated syphilis. Penicillin was standard by 1947 and was withheld for 25 more years; information was withheld and access to treatment elsewhere blocked. Ended by a whistleblower.Produced the 1979 Belmont Report, the American counterpart of the Nuremberg Code
Residential schools, CanadaThousands of Indigenous children died; at some schools in the early 1900s up to 70% died of tuberculosis alone. Doctors did not intervene to stop forcible removals of children with TB into those conditions. Later, nutrition experiments on hundreds of children from six schools while the remedy, ending imposed starvation, was already known.Silence is participation; the medical establishment proactively carried out a colonizing agenda: fomented smallpox epidemics, experiments in Indian Hospitals, forced sterilization, abductions
Sterilization of Indigenous womenAlberta's Sexual Sterilization Act, 1928–1972: over 2,800 women sterilized as "defective" and "unfit to produce children". From 1969 to 1972, Indigenous and Métis people were over 25% of those sterilized but 2.5% of the population. Justified as an "act of mercy".Altruism as cover for a human rights violation; the same structure as the "therapeutic imperative"
ICE detainees, September 2020Project South reported hysterectomies on detained immigrant women without full informed consent, raised by a nurse; internet translation and fellow detainees were used instead of a medical language line. The allegations are under investigation.Consent fails at the language line; this is contemporary

The two cases

Scenario 1. A second-year student in the emergency department is offered a first-ever suture on a prominent forehead laceration in a 34-year-old woman with features of Down syndrome. Introduced as "the student doctor", the student privately raises concern about the visible site; the physician replies that the patient is "slow-minded, it's not like she's going to care". The threads: dehumanizing language about a patient with a cognitive disability; a title that obscures the learner's status and undermines consent; hierarchy pressing a junior to comply. The discussion questions ask about informed consent, the effect of language on power and treatment, and how active inclusion of patients in decisions protects against dehumanization, whether subtle (infantilization) or overt (neglect, abuse).

Scenario 2. A third-year student on obstetrics and gynaecology is asked by the senior resident to perform an educational pelvic examination on a 41-year-old woman under general anaesthesia for hysterectomy; explicit consent had not been obtained. The resident dismisses the hesitation ("it's something we all have to do", she "doesn't mind"), and a fourth-year clerk obliges. In a 2003 survey of 400 Philadelphia medical students, 90% had performed a pelvic exam on an anaesthetized woman; at the University of Oklahoma most students had, but only about a quarter of patients had consented. The questions ask whether prevalence changes the ethics (it does not), whose responsibility consent is, whether the patient must be told, and how hierarchy sustains the practice.

Actionable steps

Dehumanization is unconscious and rooted in old stereotypes, so there is no single fix. Haque and Waytz offer six strategies:

StrategyConstruct
Make patients more identifiable and increase personal responsibilityIndividuation
Give patients a more active role in decision-makingAgency reorientation
Promote common identity to de-emphasize boundariesPromoting similarity
Highlight characteristics that humanize and distinguish patientsPersonification and humanizing procedure
Increase empathyEmpathetic balance and physician selection
Increase moral concern; personify and individualizeMoral engagement

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Well-meaning, not monstrous. The therapeutic imperative plus a dehumanized premise produces atrocity.
  • Sterilization then euthanasia then genocide; disabled and mentally ill people first; physicians led.
  • 20 of 23 defendants at the Doctors' Trial were physicians; ten Nuremberg conditions; Helsinki descends from Nuremberg; Belmont (1979) descends from Tuskegee.
  • 1932 to 1972, 600 men, penicillin by 1947: withheld treatment, withheld information, blocked access.
  • 70% TB mortality at some residential schools; 2,800 sterilized under Alberta's Act; 25% versus 2.5% in 1969 to 1972.
  • Prevalence is not consent: 90% of students had done it; a quarter of patients had agreed.
  • Intergenerational trauma was first described in Holocaust survivors' descendants and manifests as complex PTSD.
"Just following orders" and "it's what we all do" are the same defence. Hierarchy plus a mission is the risk structure in medicine itself, and the stated obligation is to resist even at personal cost. Silence counts as participation, as the residential-school physicians showed.
Physicians did not abandon medicine to take part in the Holocaust; they redirected it. The protections that followed, the Nuremberg Code and Helsinki, and their North American parallels after Tuskegee, exist because well-meaning doctors dehumanized their patients by degrees, and the same process runs through Canadian residential schools, forced sterilization, and everyday clinical language today.

guides.title: Week 41 · 10 Depression: the Episode, Choosing Treatment, and the Lifespan
guides.html:
Lecture 1 · Grujich

Depression: the Episode, Choosing Treatment, and the Lifespan

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

What a major depressive episode can mean, the two screening questions, why SSRIs and SNRIs come first and how to choose among them, their mechanism, onset and side effects, the benzodiazepine bridge, depression in the old and the young, stepped care, and ECT, rTMS and the newer neurostimulation.

Normal life, the episode, and what the episode can mean

Mood oscillates: Friday lifts it, a rained-out camping weekend drops it, the sun brings it back. A major depressive episode is a cluster of symptoms lasting at least a few weeks that falls below what normal life produces, and much of the work of assessment is deciding what normal is. The episode is a syndrome, not a diagnosis. Major depressive disorder is one or more major depressive episodes, a recurrent illness that begins young, remits and returns, and therefore occupies a large share of a lifetime: it is counted as the third leading cause of disability worldwide, with an estimated lifetime risk of about 20%, the same one-in-five figure as mental illness in general among Canadians.

An episode can beMeaning
Major depressive disorderThe episode itself is the illness. A catastrophic diagnosis of cancer followed by depression is still MDD, "likely triggered by this significant event"
Bipolar disorderThe same episode in a patient whose chart shows a past manic or hypomanic episode; the diagnosis is bipolar, the episode is depressive
Secondary to a general medical conditionThe illness biologically produces the episode: the anaemic, hypothyroid patient with low mood, lost interest, low energy, excess sleep and hopelessness
Secondary to a substance use disorderA depression clearly related to, for instance, chronic methamphetamine use follows an addictions pathway, not a depression pathway

Two screeners, then the whole list

In a busy clinic two questions come first: "How has your mood been over the last couple of weeks?" and "Are you still able to enjoy the things that usually bring you pleasure?" A no to both means the patient cannot have depression by definition and the rest can be skipped; a yes to either opens the full screen. The DSM-5 episode: five or more of nine symptoms in the same two-week period, a change from previous functioning, at least one being depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure; the others are significant weight or appetite change (more than 5% of body weight in a month; in children, failure to gain expected weight), insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation observable by others, fatigue, worthlessness or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional), poor concentration or indecisiveness, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation, plan or attempt. In children and adolescents the mood can be irritable rather than sad. Two further clauses do the discriminating: the symptoms must cause clinically significant distress or functional impairment ("work is not happening for me, relationships are not happening"), and the episode must not be attributable to a substance or another medical condition. All nine symptoms in someone who is still getting by is either a very mild presentation or a hard time, not necessarily a disorder.

Assessment and the treatment map

On referral: establish the diagnosis; rule out medical conditions (hyperthyroidism, seizure disorder, asthma, which can look like a panic attack; blood work, general medical questions, sometimes a sleep study); consider comorbidity including substance use; the special population (child, geriatric, pregnancy); severity; and the patient's choice. The treatment options are therapy, biological treatment, which has bifurcated into medications and neurostimulation, and combination.

Why SSRIs and SNRIs, and how to choose between a dozen first-line drugs

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors are first line because they have a long evidence base, are generally very well tolerated, and are effective for the common comorbidity: anxiety disorders and trauma disorders as well as depression. At higher doses the SNRIs add a noradrenergic effect; otherwise they behave alike.

SSRIsSNRIs
Citalopram (Celexa) · escitalopram (Cipralex) · fluvoxamine (Luvox) · fluoxetine (Prozac) · sertraline (Zoloft) · paroxetine (Paxil); vortioxetine (Trintellix) is listed alongside themVenlafaxine (Effexor) · duloxetine (Cymbalta) · desvenlafaxine (Pristiq)

The Canadian guidelines call about a dozen drugs first line. The 2009 Cipriani meta-analysis of twelve second-generation antidepressants plotted efficacy against acceptability and put escitalopram and sertraline alone in the top-right corner; everyone started prescribing those two. The 2018 Cipriani re-analysis in the Lancet, with far more data including unpublished trials, showed every antidepressant beating placebo (response odds ratios from amitriptyline 2.13 and mirtazapine 1.89 at the top through escitalopram 1.68, sertraline 1.67, fluoxetine 1.52 and citalopram 1.52 to reboxetine 1.37 at the bottom) with no clinically meaningful separation between them. Two messages: antidepressants work, and which one is best is a wash. The choice turns on past success with a drug (restart the fluoxetine that worked at 25), drug–drug interactions (cytochrome P450 burden matters in polypharmacy and the elderly), tolerability (anticholinergic and weight-gain liabilities differ), discontinuation issues (some agents are harder to come off), family history of a successful trial (weak evidence, but it helps adherence), and cost: new drugs cost more and are usually not better.

Mechanism, and why "how long does it take" has two answers

Serotonin is stored in presynaptic vesicles, released into the cleft, binds a family of postsynaptic receptors and produces downstream effects. Two cleaning mechanisms clear it: the 5-HT reuptake transporter, a vacuum that pulls serotonin back into the presynaptic neuron, and monoamine oxidase, which breaks it down. The monoamine hypothesis holds that depression reflects low activation of the serotonin system. SSRIs and SNRIs block the transporter, leaving more serotonin in the cleft and increasing postsynaptic activity; MAOIs irreversibly block monoamine oxidase to the same end. More serotonin in the cleft is measurable within a day; the delay from there to the antidepressant effect is not understood (receptor down-regulation may contribute), and neurostimulation works without the monoamine system, so the hypothesis is one of several.

The placebo curve, and the two-week rule
In a randomized double-blind trial of sertraline versus placebo for generalized anxiety disorder (Brawman-Mintzer 2006, n = 182 vs 188), both groups improved by about two points on the Hamilton anxiety scale in the first week: on day one everyone gets better, sugar pill or drug. The curves separate at about two weeks and the active drug keeps improving to a plateau at about six weeks (a 13.8-point fall versus 10.1 on placebo at week 12). So the old dogma that nothing happens for two to four weeks is wrong in both directions: a patient may feel better right away, largely placebo, and the full biological benefit takes up to six weeks. Depression responds a little faster than anxiety; OCD can take 10 to 12 weeks.

Side effects, and how to talk about them

The nocebo effect is the placebo effect in reverse: a patient warned of big side effects and big danger has more side effects. Consent has to be honest and transparent, but leaning too heavily on risk can scare a patient off or manufacture a failed trial.

SystemEffectsWhat to say
Gastrointestinal (serotonin receptors are more abundant in the gut than the brain)Nausea, reflux, diarrhoea, constipationTake on a full stomach; settles within one to two weeks; persistent vomiting is a failed trial
NeurologicHeadache, dizzinessMild, common on placebo too, resolves in a week or two
PeripheralRaised blood pressure with SNRIs at higher doses; sweatingCheck blood pressure at each visit on an SNRI; night sweats are rarely a deal-breaker
PsychologicalTransient increase in anxiety, sedation or insomnia, emotional bluntingA patient "freaking out" at one week stays the course; it is too early to judge. Tired: take at bedtime. Energized: take in the morning. Once daily either way
SexualDecreased libido; delayed or difficult orgasm; erectile dysfunctionPersists for as long as the drug is taken and can be the reason for silent discontinuation; a sexual history at the first visit opens the conversation

In the sertraline trial the adverse events that separated from placebo were nausea (28% vs 13%), sweating (19% vs 4%), insomnia, diarrhoea, fatigue and sexual effects; dizziness, anxiety and dyspepsia matched placebo. Nothing was dangerous: nuisance effects, not Stevens-Johnson reactions. Weight gain is not a class effect of SSRIs or SNRIs in meta-analyses and does not need to be consented for, although individuals vary and regained appetite after anxiety-related weight loss can look like gain; the exceptions are paroxetine, which is more anticholinergic and is little used now, and mirtazapine, a first-line non-serotonergic antidepressant with its own side-effect profile.

Benzodiazepines: vilified, and useful as a bridge

How addictive a substance is tracks how fast it is felt: oral oxycodone in about 45 minutes, injected instantly; smoked crack instantly. An antidepressant is felt not at all; it is not a happy pill. A benzodiazepine calms within minutes, and the brain quickly learns that this drug produces this feeling. With unlimited as-needed supply, a vulnerability to addiction and no education, dependence follows; prescribed and followed mindfully, benzodiazepines are safe and effective.

RoleDrug and doseCaution
Bridge while an SSRI starts, to treat acute distressClonazepam 0.125–0.5 mg PO twice daily: long-acting (about 6 to 8 hours), not felt quickly, covers a day of generalized anxiety; withdrawn as the antidepressant takes holdAddictive: avoid in substance misuse. In the elderly: falls, cognitive impairment, sedation
Rare panic attacks or a specific phobiaLorazepam 1 mg sublingual as needed: the twice-a-year flyer who needs four tablets before boarding does not need 16 sessions of psychotherapy or a year of antidepressantBenzodiazepines and alcohol act on the same receptors; one or two glasses of wine is about half to one tablet of lorazepam, so they are not mixed, and a history of severe alcohol use disorder argues against prescribing at all

The emergency-department picture: a patient who is "vibrating", cannot work and has not slept for days gets an SSRI with a 50 to 60% chance of working, possibly six weeks away, a concurrent benzodiazepine to turn down the volume, and a therapy referral. Refusing the benzodiazepine on principle is the error.

Depression across the lifespan

The very young and the very old share the same features: fewer studies (the trial subject is an 18-year-old white male), a need for collateral from parents, spouse or children, psychotherapy as first line for milder cases, additional caution with medication, the rule "start low and go slow, and keep going" (slow does not mean stopping short of a full dose), and evidence that longer drug trials are needed before calling failure.

Late-life depression

Onset after 60 defines late-life depression; late late-life depression begins after 75. The distinction that matters is early-adult-onset depression recurring in late life versus first onset late in life. Episodes at 20, 40 and 70 are ordinary recurrence. A first episode at 75 is highly comorbid with neurocognitive disorder and carries a worse prognosis: a more chronic course, higher relapse rate, more medical comorbidity and cognitive impairment, sometimes as the prodrome to dementia. Pharmacologically the elderly have a lower threshold for side effects (pharmacokinetic change), more medical burden, more polypharmacy and interactions, and they "crash" fast when they stop eating and drinking, which is why ECT is used more often and why a frail patient who has not spoken or eaten for days is fast-tracked to it. The algorithm is otherwise unchanged: a psychologically minded, cognitively intact 75-year-old with mild depression can start with therapy. A first-onset diagnosis late in life is a flag for cognitive testing, perhaps an MRI, and family collateral (is dad leaving the stove on? still driving?), not a diagnosis of dementia in itself.

Adolescent depression

First line is CBT or interpersonal therapy; second line is an SSRI, with fluoxetine carrying the most evidence, probably because it has been studied longest. Health Canada has approved no antidepressant under 18, so every such prescription is off label. The 2004 black-box warning reported more suicidal thinking and behaviour on antidepressants than placebo in short-term studies of children, adolescents and young adults under 24; prescribing, which had been rising too fast, dropped sharply, untreated depressions worsened and completed suicides rose. The correction followed: the risk posed by untreated depression in morbidity and mortality "has always been far greater than the very small risk associated with antidepressant treatment" (NEJM 2014), and treatment with SSRIs "may be appropriate with careful monitoring" (Can J Psychiatry 2016), meaning weekly follow-up for the first month for suicidality and adverse events. In practice: weekly visits, an explicit conversation about the warning and the off-label status alongside the statement that the drugs work, an earlier visit for any flare of suicidal thinking, a parent or caregiver involved almost always, and documentation of all of it: "if it's not documented, it didn't happen". For a mild episode, supportive clinical care may suffice: psychoeducation, active empathic listening, and advice on sleep hygiene, eating and exercise.

Severity decides the step

StepWhoFocusWhat they do
1GP, practice nurseRecognitionAssessment
2Primary care teamMild depressionWatchful waiting, guided self-help, computerised CBT, exercise, brief psychological interventions
3Primary care teamModerate or severe depressionMedication, psychological interventions, social support
4Mental-health specialists, crisis teamsTreatment-resistant, recurrent, atypical and psychotic depression; significant riskMedication, complex psychological interventions, combined treatments
5Inpatient care, crisis teamsRisk to life, severe self-neglectMedication, combined treatments, ECT

"Just haven't been myself" in primary care is step 1 or 2, where exercise and behavioural activation (get dressed, show up to class) have evidence. Psychosis, dehydration or an active plan in the emergency department starts at step 4 or 5, up to admission or an involuntary form.

Neurostimulation

Electroconvulsive therapy is "like a colonoscopy": a clean, safe medical procedure. The anaesthetist gives a general anaesthetic (propofol, conscious sedation without intubation) and then a muscle relaxant; the psychiatrist attaches EEG monitors, applies the paddles and pushes the button; the millisecond shock induces a seizure of about 30 seconds seen on the EEG, with a bite guard for the jaw and no convulsive movements because of the paralytic; the patient wakes, spends about 30 minutes in recovery and returns to the ward or home. It is very effective and safe, the gold standard for psychotic depression, the fastest treatment for the frail and severely ill, given three times a week with significant improvement usually by six sessions, and typically 9 to 20 treatments in a course. Side effects are mainly anaesthetic: headache, nausea, muscle soreness, and short-term amnesia whose sources (the depression, the anaesthetic, the seizures) are hard to separate; the weeks around treatment are murky, but cognitive testing six months after ECT shows baseline function.

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation stimulates or inhibits a selected brain region with a magnetic field: no anaesthetic, a tapping on the scalp, about 30 minutes a session, five days a week for four to six weeks, side effects limited to local irritation. Deep brain stimulation places a lead through a burr hole into the target (subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson's disease; Brodmann area 25 and other sites in depression) wired to an implanted pulse generator; experimental for depression. MRI-guided focused ultrasound lesions a single point in the brain without opening the skull.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Cancer then depression = MDD; hypothyroidism producing the syndrome = secondary to a general medical condition.
  • Two screeners: mood and anhedonia; both negative excludes the diagnosis.
  • Escitalopram and sertraline won in 2009; in 2018 everything works and nothing is clearly best. Choose by history, interactions, tolerability, discontinuation, family response, cost.
  • SSRIs decrease reabsorption by the presynaptic neuron; MAOIs decrease breakdown. Neither explains the delay.
  • Separation from placebo at two weeks, full effect at six; OCD 10 to 12.
  • Raised blood pressure is the SNRI-only side effect; weight gain is not a class effect (paroxetine, mirtazapine excepted).
  • Clonazepam 0.125–0.5 mg BID as a bridge; lorazepam 1 mg SL PRN for rare panic or a phobia; alcohol equivalence; the elderly fall.
  • First-onset depression after 75: worse prognosis, think neurocognitive disorder, ECT sooner.
  • Adolescents: CBT or IPT first, fluoxetine second, nothing approved under 18, black box under 24, weekly follow-up for a month.
  • ECT: gold standard for psychotic depression, three per week, improvement by six, side effects mostly anaesthetic, memory at baseline by six months.
A depressive episode is a syndrome whose meaning (MDD, bipolar, medical, substance) decides the pathway. Screen with two questions, treat by severity, and start an SSRI or SNRI knowing that they all work about equally, separate from placebo at two weeks and peak at six, cause gut, sexual and, for SNRIs, blood-pressure effects, and can be bridged with a low-dose benzodiazepine. Go low and slow but all the way in the young and the old, watch first-onset late-life depression as a dementia flag, monitor adolescents weekly, and reach for ECT, the fastest and most effective treatment, when severity or frailty demands it.

guides.title: Week 41 · 11 CBT for Depression and Anxiety: Thoughts, Activation and Exposure
guides.html:
Lecture 2 · Grujich

CBT for Depression and Anxiety: Thoughts, Activation and Exposure

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Why so few patients get psychotherapy, what Beck's CBT changed, the cognitive triangle and the nine distortions, the thought record and reframing, behavioural activation, exposure and habituation including interoceptive exposure for panic, hierarchies versus flooding, mindfulness, and the evidence for CBT against medication.

Why most patients never get it

Medication and psychotherapy are both first-line treatments for mild-to-moderate depression and for the anxiety disorders. In the 2014 Survey on Living with Chronic Diseases in Canada, 95% of people with a mood or anxiety disorder said a doctor had suggested a prescription; 20% had received a psychological intervention in the past 12 months. The gap is the system: a hospital CBT clinic wait-list runs 6 to 12 months, while a family doctor can prescribe an antidepressant the same day. Psychotherapy is treatment provided by talking, practised since Freud; a psychotherapist is anyone with formal training who practises it: MD, PhD psychologist, social worker, registered psychotherapist, occupational therapist, nurse. A psychologist's session costs about $250 and is not covered by OHIP; social workers and psychotherapists charge roughly $150 to $250; a physician's psychotherapy, family doctor or psychiatrist, is OHIP-covered.

What made CBT different

Freud's therapy often worked but could not be trialled: it was esoteric and patient-specific. In the 1970s the psychologist Aaron Beck produced a structured, manualized, reproducible treatment, originally a 16-session manual, that fit the research model and has since been shown to work for depression, panic disorder, the other anxiety disorders, PTSD, eating disorders, ADHD and addictions. Its features: a focus on the here and now rather than childhood; an active therapist who teaches strategies and reviews homework rather than a blank slate offering interpretations; goal-setting that is problem-focused and action-oriented; an agenda for every session; measurement of symptoms with scales such as the PHQ-9 for depression and the GAD-7 for generalized anxiety; feedback after every session; homework; and the aim of teaching the patient to be their own therapist.

The triangle
A situation produces thoughts; thoughts, behaviour and feelings then influence one another in every direction. Feelings are the outcome the therapy wants to change, and the two levers that reach them are the thoughts (the cognitive part) and the behaviour (the behavioural part). Epictetus stated the cognitive premise: people are affected not by events but by the view they take of them. Cervantes stated the behavioural one: good actions ennoble us, and we are the sons and daughters of our deeds.

The cognitive part: distortions and the thought record

Two students fail the same first exam. One thinks "I have failed exams before, 15% of the class also failed, I didn't read the past exams"; mood dips and recovers. The other thinks "I can't believe I failed, I'm so embarrassed, I'm probably the stupidest person in the class, I should never have been accepted, I'm an utter failure"; mood drops and stays down. Made the default pathway, the second stream has a cumulative depressive effect and undermines the studying that would prevent the next failure. Those default pathways are cognitive distortions, and identifying them is the C in CBT.

DistortionExample
Black or white thinking"You're either perfect or a loser"
Catastrophizing"I'm going to fail and be kicked out of med school"; Anxiety Girl, "able to jump to the worst conclusion in a single bound"; the anxious mind sees the dangerous outcome rather than the likely one
Disqualifying the positive"He probably gave me an 80% out of pity"
Emotional reasoning"If I feel like it's hopeless it must be true"
Labeling"I'm so stupid"
Magnification / minimization"His irritated tone tells me that he doesn't like me"
Mind reading"I can tell she thinks I'm weird": the social-anxiety pattern, walking into a room already sure of everyone's judgement
Jumping to conclusions"I didn't do well on the quiz, I'll probably fail the final"
Overgeneralizing"All of my friendships are fake"

The thought record (from Mind Over Mood, Greenberger and Padesky) has seven columns: the situation (who, what, when, where); the moods, one word each, rated 0 to 100 at the time; the automatic thoughts of the seconds in which the mood formed, with the hot thought circled; evidence for the hot thought; evidence against it; alternative or balanced thoughts, each rated for belief; and the moods now, re-rated. The balanced thought is not "I'm happy I failed" but "it sucks that I failed, I didn't study well, I've failed before, I'll do better next time", and the mood falls from 80 to 60. Done daily, several times a day, the exercise rewires the default from the distortion to a rational appraisal. Cognitive reframing in the room does the same work: a man with panic disorder, a former professional soccer player who kept presenting to emergency with a normal ECG and troponins, filmed just after an induced attack, puts his chance of dying at 50% and believes it, and says his mind is stuck and cannot reach the rationale. The reframe: his heart rate has risen thousands of times without killing him, and every time the anxious brain insists death is near; what makes this time different?

The behavioural part: activation

The behavioural pitfalls are avoidance in anxiety and inactivity and withdrawal in depression. The depressed day: dozing until noon, unwashed, in pyjamas, television and doom-scrolling, takeout, friends' messages unanswered, "what a loser, I did nothing all day", then no sleep because of the sleeping in, and the cycle continues. Behavioural activation starts with an activity log, a Monday-to-Sunday grid by the hour, to see how the days are really spent; then an action plan: each day, some physical exercise ("the body likes to move", no prescriptive minutes), social engagement in graded steps (text a friend, order a coffee and speak to the server, walk with a friend, a date), intellectual activity, and self-care (the patient whose grown-out hair roots announce a relapse), plus mindfulness and the things that used to bring pleasure: pick up the guitar even though it brings no joy yet, "fake it till you make it". It is for the patient in between, not the one who cannot get out of bed, has lost 10 pounds or is psychotic or actively suicidal, and it belongs in every medication visit and every primary-care encounter.

The behavioural part: exposure

At a party the anxiety climbs after the trigger, crosses the "uncomfortable" line, and the person leaves. The relief is immediate, and the brain learns that the environment is dangerous and should be avoided; the next party is worse, and the pattern repeats as a sawtooth of rising anxiety, avoidance and relief. The more you avoid, the smaller your world gets: the high-functioning patient who can no longer take the subway, attend meetings, see friends or go to Toastmasters. The alternative is to sit with the discomfort: anxiety rises but not to infinity, peaks, and then falls on its own as the body habituates, and with each repeated exposure the peak is lower and the fall faster. Anxiety decreases with subsequent exposures; that is habituation, and the hot tub is the everyday version: unbearable for a moment, then comfortable.

Panic and interoceptive exposure

Panic attacks alone are no diagnosis; everyone has one at some point. Panic disorder is the attacks plus the behaviour that grows around them: avoiding the subway, open spaces, anywhere without a safe place or a hospital. The attack is a feed-forward loop: a normal odd heartbeat, the brain reads danger, adrenaline drives a sympathetic response, the faster heart and breathing read as more danger, and within seconds or minutes the body is on fire and the brain says you are going to die. The attack is time-limited, on the order of 10 to 20 minutes, even when the person feels anxious all day, and the fear of death is why 20- and 30-year-olds present with chest pain. Treatment has to teach the brain that the sensations are not dangerous, so the sensations are induced on purpose: running on the spot for the patient whose trigger is a fast heart rate; hyperventilating for 20 seconds to a minute (fogginess and tunnel vision from blowing off carbon dioxide and dilating vessels, physiologically normal, frightening if unexpected); lying flat and then doing burpees for orthostatic light-headedness. Homework is what produces learning; once a week in the office is like one Thai lesson a week. The patient who felt safe running in a hospital office was assigned the hospital stairwell "until his heart felt like it would explode", then graduated to the next rung.

Hierarchies, flooding, experiments, mindfulness

Exposure normally climbs a fear ladder from the bottom. Starting at the top, flooding, also works but is hard to tolerate and hard to consent to; the child in floats thrown into the deep end screamed for twenty minutes on day one and was fine by the end of the week, and would probably have got there by the shallow end too. Behavioural experiments write down the prediction ("everyone will judge me"), run the test, and revisit it next session. Mindfulness means letting the brain do what it does, which is think, without treating the thoughts as truth or boarding the train they drive: decentring and observing them with curiosity and without judgement, attention on the feet on the floor and the back against the chair while the hour in the bank queue passes either way. It is not an acute treatment for distress; it is an immunization once the person is coming out of the episode, it is in the guidelines for relapse prevention in depression, and it is a performance skill under pressure.

Does it work, and CBT or medication?

In a two-year follow-up of remitted depressed patients (Fava 1998, 20 per arm), the proportion still in remission stayed far higher after CBT (about three quarters) than after clinical management (about one in five). Stopping a medication carries a risk of relapse; a patient who keeps doing thought records, exposures and activation after the sixteen sessions is protected, not infallibly, but measurably, because the therapist's job was to make them their own therapist.

MedicationsCBT
ProsEasy to take · safe · help with comorbidity (one drug covers depression, PTSD and panic) · readily available; a treatment plan alone makes people feel better tomorrowLong acting · safe · can be very effective
ConsSide effects · limited benefit (relief of impairing symptoms, not happiness) · relapse when stopped; the worst case is a failed trial, with no permanent damageMotivation and hard work · difficult to access

For mild-to-moderate depression one half to two thirds of patients get better with either; they are equal, and the patient may choose medication, CBT or both. Candidacy matters more than the diagnosis: a single mother with two jobs, English not her first language, limited literacy, or a flat refusal to do exposure work is not a CBT candidate however the chart reads; and a good candidate may still face a wait-list or a private fee. Navigation services (Sunnybrook's Family Navigation Project) find what is actually available. Suicidality is a symptom, not a diagnosis, like fatigue: a depressive episode is treated as depression; an acute break-up gets support and safety planning, possibly admission, but neither an antidepressant nor CBT for a depression that does not exist.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • 95% offered medication, 20% received psychotherapy; wait-lists of 6 to 12 months; psychologists are not OHIP-covered.
  • Beck, 1970s, manualized, here and now, active therapist, measurement, homework, own therapist.
  • Thoughts and behaviours are the levers; feelings are the target.
  • Catastrophizing is the anxious distortion (Anxiety Girl); mind reading is the social-anxiety one.
  • Thought record: situation, moods 0–100, automatic thoughts with the hot thought, evidence for, evidence against, balanced thought, moods now.
  • Avoidance is anxiety's pitfall; inactivity and withdrawal are depression's.
  • Habituation: anxiety peaks and falls if you stay; peaks lower with each exposure. Avoidance shrinks the world.
  • Interoceptive exposure for panic: run on the spot, hyperventilate, burpees; the brain must learn the sensations are safe.
  • Hierarchy versus flooding: both work; flooding is harder to tolerate.
  • Mindfulness prevents relapse; it does not treat acute distress.
  • CBT and medication are equal for mild-to-moderate illness; CBT outlasts its course.
CBT is Beck's structured, measured, homework-driven treatment of the here and now. Its cognitive half catches distortions and rewrites the hot thought with a thought record; its behavioural half breaks depression's withdrawal with activation and anxiety's avoidance with graded exposure until habituation does the rest, including deliberately provoked panic sensations. It matches medication in the mild-to-moderate range, protects against relapse after it ends, and is limited by motivation and access rather than by efficacy.

guides.title: Week 41 · 12 Titrating Antidepressants, and Delirium to PTSD after the ICU
guides.html:
Lecture 3 · Grujich

Titrating Antidepressants, and Delirium to PTSD after the ICU

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The sertraline algorithm from 25 mg to 200 mg: reassess at two to four weeks with a scale, hold remission for 6 to 12 months or longer, switch within and then across class, optimize before adding, and augment or combine; adequate trials, discontinuation and washout; the refractory checklist; and Adam's course from a Whipple procedure through delirium to PTSD treated with prolonged exposure.

Start here: sertraline, 25 then 50

Most antidepressant prescriptions come from primary care, so the algorithm belongs to every physician. The usual starting choices are sertraline or escitalopram; what a prescriber gets comfortable with in training tends to stay, and the newer, more expensive agents have not proved better. Sertraline's effective range is 50 to 200 mg once daily (the CPS range; pharmacogenetic outliers may need 25 or 300 to 400 mg, but that is the exception). Starting at 50 mg risks early intolerance: a patient who vomits or feels woozy or anxious after the first tablet will not take a second. So the lowest dose is cut in half: 25 mg for one week, "not a therapeutic dose, but I want your body to get comfortable with it", then 50 mg. Slow titration increases tolerability and adherence. The tablet is taken every day, on a full stomach; it is not an as-needed drug like acetaminophen. The clock starts at 50 mg.

Reassess at two to four weeks, with a scale

Response is judged by interview, mental status examination and measurement-based practice: a validated scale such as the PHQ-9 or the Beck Depression Inventory. A 25% reduction in score is a response; remission is a score below the scale's cutoff. Three outcomes follow.

Outcome at 2–4 weeksActionDetail
Full remissionStay on the medication 6 to 12 monthsUsually "a year, then we come off it". After a severe episode (a serious attempt, a long admission) two years or lifelong are both reasonable. Two episodes carry a 70% chance of a third; three carry more than 90%: two episodes means two years, more than two means consider staying on for life
No improvementSwitchTrial 2 within class (sertraline to escitalopram, start low and go slow, reassess in a month), then trial 3 in a different class (an SNRI or another first-line agent). An adequate trial is four weeks at a therapeutic dose: two days of fluoxetine stopped for nausea, a venlafaxine script never filled, sertraline taken twice are not failed trials, and the algorithm restarts at step one
Some improvementOptimize the doseIncrease (50 to 75 mg and onward) and wait each time; bumping quickly to 200 mg leaves the patient on an unnecessarily high dose with more side effects because the full response is delayed. Continue to the maximum, 200 mg
Add only at the maximum dose with residual symptoms. Residual symptoms means 60% better but still ruminating, still anxious, energy not back, still waking with passive thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Gains are held, not thrown away for an unknown next drug. Psychiatry's rule is the opposite of pain or oncology polypharmacy: one drug, maxed out, see what is left, then add. A patient arriving on five low-dose agents is cleared back to one drug at the right dose.

Add: augmentation, combination, therapy, neurostimulation

StrategyMeaningAgents
AugmentationAdd a non-antidepressantT3 (liothyronine, not thyroxine), an atypical antipsychotic at about a tenth of the schizophrenia dose (the strongest evidence, and a stigma conversation when the pharmacy leaflet says "antipsychotic"), lithium, a stimulant, a hypnotic, a benzodiazepine, buspirone
CombinationAdd an antidepressant with a different mechanismMirtazapine (not a serotonin reuptake mechanism) or bupropion (a noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake inhibitor)
PsychotherapyAugment with CBT"If I get 70% better, maybe CBT will take me to where I want to go"
NeurostimulationConcurrent rTMS; ECT for severe illnessNone of these treatments is curative. ECT pulls a patient out quickly, but an antidepressant is started alongside to hold remission afterwards; depression, anxiety and psychosis are managed like blood pressure, chronically

Duration, discontinuation, switching mechanics

  • The goal is to improve symptoms and function. Once achieved, stay on for 6 to 12 months to reduce relapse; consider two years or longer after multiple or severe episodes; the choice is the patient's, and a patient who feels well and wants to continue may.
  • Antidepressants produce no tolerance. Twenty years on venlafaxine that stops working calls for a dose increase, then an add-on, not reflexive switching.
  • Never stop cold turkey. The discontinuation reaction is not dangerous like alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, but anxiety flares, the stomach hurts, sleep breaks and odd neurological sensations appear; taper slowly and monitor for recurrence.
  • Washout is needed only after an MAOI, which irreversibly blocks monoamine oxidase; starting an SSRI too soon floods the cleft with serotonin and noradrenaline. Between all other antidepressants there is no washout: fluoxetine can stop today and sertraline start tomorrow, though a cross-titration over a week or two is the usual practice.
  • The placebo effect is real and is used: two hours of assessment, a plan, and stated optimism instil hope, which is part of the treatment.

When it is not working: the refractory checklist

40 to 60% of patients benefit from the first SSRI trial (about two thirds in clean populations, nearer a coin toss where substance use and personality pathology are common). Before calling resistance, revisit adherence (patients take pills they can feel, sleeping pills and painkillers, and forget the ones they cannot), medical illness, substance misuse (intoxication and withdrawal mimic mood disorders) and comorbidity. And revisit the diagnosis: the treatment-resistant depression that is really bipolar disorder and needs a mood stabilizer, the personality disorder that needs specific therapy, the neurocognitive disorder whose depression is a by-product.

Two questions, one answer
A patient started on sertraline five weeks ago is on 50 mg, somewhat better, still symptomatic, tolerating it well: increase the dose. Not add (50 mg is a low dose), not switch (there have been gains), not wait (five weeks is long enough). The same patient returns at week ten still depressed: increase again. Ten weeks without optimization was too long, which is why early follow-up is frequent; adding or switching is still premature.

Key messages of the morning

  1. Medications and CBT are first-line options for MDD and anxiety.
  2. In anxiety, benzodiazepines are a bridge or for time-limited focused use, not long-term management.
  3. SSRIs and SNRIs are the commonest first-line choice because they are safe, effective and well tolerated.
  4. SSRIs take two to four weeks to work, and often start sooner.
  5. Know their side effects.
  6. If symptoms remain: increase, switch, combine or augment.
  7. Do not forget ECT and rTMS.

Adam: from a Whipple procedure to delirium to PTSD

A patient followed for years told his own story. Adam, 48, with a parathyroidectomy for an adenoma about twenty years earlier and recurrent kidney stones from hypercalciuria, was referred in May 2015 for a pancreatic lesion. He had a Whipple procedure on June 16, 2015 and was discharged on August 11, 2015; the mountain between the two dates was an anastomotic leak, sepsis, respiratory failure with mechanical ventilation, delirium, a pancreatic fistula and a gastro-duodenal bleed. His haemoglobin fell from about 135 g/L at surgery into the 65 to 85 range through late June and early July, bottomed near 55 in mid-July with an abrupt rebound, and climbed back to normal by the end of July.

The delirium

The consult note of July 10, 2015: since surgery, whenever not sedated, a fluctuating level of consciousness, inattention, disorientation and disorganization, with visual and auditory hallucinations, a green dog outside the window and conversations with dead relatives; worse the day before and better today; symptoms fluctuating with his clinical state, in particular fever; minimal headache, no weakness, paresthesias or visual disturbance. Vitals: afebrile now but 38.0 that morning and 39.0 overnight, heart rate around 130. Mental status: inattentive, unable to spell WORLD backwards, oriented only to purpose, drowsy. Against the DSM-5 criteria, the highlighted parts are the ones that decide it:

CriterionContentAdam
AA disturbance in attention (reduced ability to direct, focus, sustain and shift) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment)Inattentive, cannot spell WORLD backwards, oriented to purpose only
BDevelops over a short period (hours to days), a change from baseline, and tends to fluctuate in severity during the dayPost-operative onset; fluctuating with sedation and fever, worse yesterday
CAn additional disturbance in cognition (memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception)Disorientation; visual and auditory hallucinations
DNot better explained by another neurocognitive disorder; not in the context of severely reduced arousal such as comaNo prior cognitive disorder; rousable
EEvidence that it is a direct physiological consequence of another medical condition, intoxication or withdrawal, a toxin, or multiple aetiologiesSepsis, fever, ventilation, bleeding

What delirium was like is recorded in Adam's own pencil sketches: two embracing skeletal figures; a hospital room seen from the foot of the bed with staff standing round it; a reclining figure among indistinct shapes; three elongated animal-headed figures on cracked ground. They are the patient's record of the hallucinated world, and they were the prompt for the live discussion.

The aftermath: PTSD

"What was your emotional experience post-ICU?" is answered by the PTSD criteria: A exposure to trauma, direct or indirect; B intrusion symptoms (distressing memories, dreams, dissociative reactions, distress at cues); C persistent avoidance of memories and external reminders; D cognitive and mood alterations (inability to remember aspects of the trauma, persistent exaggerated negative beliefs, self-blame, a persistent negative emotional state, loss of interest, detachment, inability to feel positive emotions); E marked alteration in arousal and reactivity (irritability, recklessness, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, poor concentration, sleep disturbance); F duration of B to E more than one month. Critical illness and delirium are traumas, and PTSD follows the ICU. The treatment shown is prolonged exposure therapy (Foa, Hembree and Rothbaum's manual) and its core technique, imaginal exposure: returning to the memory deliberately and repeatedly until it loses its charge, the same logic as every exposure in the CBT hour, because avoidance is what keeps PTSD alive.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Sertraline 50–200 mg; 25 mg for a week first; the clock starts at 50.
  • Two to four weeks with a scale: remission, no improvement, some improvement. Response = 25% reduction; remission = below cutoff.
  • Remission: 6–12 months; two episodes, two years (70% recur); three, consider lifelong (over 90%).
  • No improvement: switch within class, then across class. Some improvement: optimize to 200 before adding.
  • Adequate trial = four weeks at a therapeutic dose.
  • Augment = non-antidepressant (T3, atypical antipsychotic, lithium, stimulant, hypnotic, benzodiazepine, buspirone); combine = mirtazapine or bupropion.
  • No tolerance; no washout except after an MAOI; taper, never stop abruptly.
  • Refractory: adherence, medical illness, substances, comorbidity, missed bipolar or personality or neurocognitive diagnosis; 40–60% respond to the first SSRI.
  • Delirium = attention and awareness + acute and fluctuating + another cognitive deficit + a physiological cause. Fever-linked fluctuation and a green dog are the picture.
  • ICU delirium can be followed by PTSD; the treatment is exposure to the memory.
Titration is a loop: start sertraline at 25 mg for a week, then 50; measure at two to four weeks; remit and hold for 6 to 12 months or longer; no response, switch within class then across; partial response, optimize to the maximum and only then add a non-antidepressant, a different-mechanism antidepressant, therapy or neurostimulation. Adequate means four weeks at a therapeutic dose, there is no tolerance and no washout except after an MAOI, and a treatment that keeps failing is a prompt to recheck adherence, medicine, substances and the diagnosis itself. Adam's course shows delirium's three defining features and the PTSD that can follow an ICU, treated by facing the memory.
