guides.html:
CBL 41 · faculty session

CBL 41, Jon Jacobs I: Panic Disorder and the Depressive Episode

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Jon's first two acts: unexpected panic attacks with avoidance, the physiology under the symptoms, why the benzodiazepine he was given is not a treatment, SSRIs and CBT with interoceptive exposure, how to choose between them, the depressive episode that followed, grief versus depression, the medical and bipolar differential, antidepressant classes, side effects and duration, and the screen that was missed.

The case in four acts

Jon, 20, comes to the emergency department convinced he is having a heart attack: palpitations, dizziness, nausea, numbness, trouble breathing, six months of such episodes with no trigger, and he has stopped going to school and basketball. Chest x-ray, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, liver enzymes, TSH and ECG are normal; he does not smoke, use cannabis or illicit drugs, drinks a beer a couple of nights a month, and takes three large coffees a day. He is discharged with as-needed lorazepam and sent to his family doctor. Act 1: panic disorder.

At follow-up he is sullen and tearful, sleeping more (unable to fall asleep until 3 or 4 a.m., then sleeping into the day), unmotivated, "useless", withdrawn, unable to concentrate, 5 to 10 pounds lighter with no appetite, and sometimes feels life is not worth living, without plan or intent. Act 2: major depressive disorder, current episode, moderate, with comorbid panic disorder. Sertraline 25 mg is started, partly because his mother did well on it, with a CBT referral, and increased to 50 mg after a week.

A month later his mother brings him back, having stopped the sertraline herself: he is agitated and pacing, not sleeping, up all night arranging his clothes by colour, talking about special messages, saving humanity and communicating with God, and has decided to buy a car with no job; the family now discloses that his father has bipolar disorder. On examination he is dishevelled, shirt on backwards, beard unkempt, speech louder and faster but still interruptible, mood "really great", affect elevated and at times irritable, thought process disorganized and tangential, with grandiose and religious delusions, suicidal ideation without a plan (a martyr who must die to save the world), oriented, some insight, judgement impaired; symptoms have persisted and worsened for three to four weeks off the drug. Act 3: bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with psychotic features. His family doctor completes a Form 1 and he is admitted.

The inpatient psychiatrist reviews the options with Jon and his mother and together they choose lithium, titrated to 300 mg in the morning and 600 mg at night; the target is the level, not the dose. Within two weeks his sleep and behaviour normalize. Act 4: maintenance: a chronic illness, long-term medication, warning signs, sleep protection, no shift work, exercise, no recreational substances, regular levels.

Panic attack, panic disorder, and what the trigger tells you

A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes and usually lasts only minutes, with four or more symptoms: cardiac (palpitations, tachycardia, chest pain), respiratory (shortness of breath, a choking sensation), neurological (trembling, dizziness, paresthesias in the hands and feet, blurred vision), autonomic (sweating, chills, hot flushes, nausea), dissociative (depersonalization, derealization) and cognitive (fear of dying, of a heart attack, of losing control or going crazy). Five hours of feeling very anxious is a state of anxiety, not a panic attack, and the content of the worry (five coffees, cocaine two hours ago, a deadline) points to its cause. Panic disorder requires recurrent, unexpected attacks and, after at least one, a month or more of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour, not attributable to a substance or a medical condition (hyperthyroidism produces panic-like symptoms) and not better explained by another disorder. Jon's avoidance of school and basketball is the maladaptive change; avoidance of exercise is classic, because exertion reproduces the feared sensations. Ask also about nocturnal panic attacks. Screening questions: "Do you ever have episodes of anxiety that come on so suddenly that you go from zero to 100 in minutes?"; "What symptoms do you experience?"; "Do they always follow a stressful situation, or sometimes come out of the blue?"; "Have you changed your routines because of them?"

What brings the attack on names the disorder. Out of the blue: panic disorder. Fear of doing or saying something embarrassing, of being judged: social anxiety disorder with panic attacks, the attacks reclassified as a specifier rather than removed. Worry about anything and everything: generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks. An isolated attack under real stress, got through with support and without preoccupation or avoidance, is no disorder at all.

The physiology under the symptoms

A panic attack is a model of sympathetic activation. Epinephrine and norepinephrine, released by sympathetic stimulation of the adrenal medulla, drive the fight-or-flight response; the locus coeruleus, a brainstem nucleus and the origin of most noradrenergic pathways, projects to the spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, hypothalamus and amygdala, alters cognition, raises motivation and activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis with cortisol release. The response is all-or-nothing and peaks fast because threats demand immediate action.

SystemEffectSymptom
CardiovascularHeart rate and contractility up; cardiac output and blood pressure upPalpitations, tachycardia, chest pain
VascularDilation in large muscle groups, constriction in the small peripheral vesselsTingling fingers and toes
RespiratoryRate and bronchodilation up; hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosisBreathlessness, choking sensation, blurred vision, confusion from transiently reduced cerebral blood flow
GastrointestinalPeristalsis slowsNausea, constipation, or an urgent bowel movement
Ocular, skin, metabolicPupils dilate; sweating; glycogenolysisSpotty vision; sweating, chills; energy

The clinical use: the catecholamines are eventually destroyed and the parasympathetic system restores equilibrium, so anxiety cannot last forever. Told to a patient mid-attack, that is honest reassurance, and it is the principle behind interoceptive exposure.

Benzodiazepines, and the first-line treatments for panic disorder

Benzodiazepines act at GABA-A receptors and are still the most widely used anxiolytics, but they are first line for none of the core anxiety disorders, nor for PTSD or OCD. They relieve the attack without touching the misinterpretation and avoidance that maintain the disorder; daily use produces tolerance and, within weeks, physical dependence, with a withdrawal that resembles alcohol withdrawal (anxiety, agitation, insomnia, nausea, tremor, rarely seizures) and rebound anxiety as each dose wears off; they sedate, impair concentration, add to alcohol, and in the elderly cause falls and cognitive change (the dementia evidence is mixed). Short half-life agents (lorazepam, alprazolam) carry more tolerance and dependence risk than long-acting ones (diazepam). Taking the pill also works as a safety behaviour that blocks the learning CBT depends on. Their legitimate roles are narrow: a small as-needed supply for severe attacks that other strategies have failed, under a verbal contract that more than occasional use will not be renewed; or a few-week bridge at antidepressant initiation, because the antidepressant takes weeks and can transiently increase agitation, preferably a long-acting agent, and usually avoidable by starting low and titrating slowly. Every prescription comes with counselling about dependence, rebound and withdrawal.

First-line pharmacotherapy for panic disorder is an SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, citalopram; paroxetine is less used for weight gain and sedation; fluvoxamine mostly for OCD) or the SNRI venlafaxine; "you can never go wrong by starting an SSRI." SSRIs increase serotonin in the cleft and receptor sensitivity. Anxiety indications need the higher end of the dose range (sertraline up to 200 mg or more for anxiety and OCD, versus 100 to 200 for depression), and take four to six weeks at a therapeutic dose, longer for anxiety. First-line psychotherapy is CBT, 12 to 20 weekly sessions: reappraising anxious thoughts, relaxation, graded exposure up a hierarchy (imagine the flight, watch planes take off, board), and for panic interoceptive exposure: hyperventilate into a paper bag, spin in a swivel chair, and learn that the sensations can be tolerated. CBT's effects last longer than medication's because it reaches the behaviour that perpetuates the anxiety; medication alone relapses more.

Choosing between medication and therapy

Severity is the hinge: for mild-to-moderate anxiety or depression the two are comparable and the patient may choose either or both; severe symptoms usually need medication first, because exposure therapy is impossible when symptoms are overwhelming. Then the patient's preference and beliefs (which predict adherence: "I've tried the talk thing" versus "I've always preferred natural approaches"), motivation, comorbidity (an SSRI treats both the depression and the panic; side effects can be used to advantage: mirtazapine for weight loss and insomnia, bupropion for fatigue or sexual dysfunction, duloxetine for neuropathic pain), suicide risk, prior response, family response to a specific drug (a genetic clue and a belief the patient already holds; Jon's mother and sertraline), and active substance use, which makes therapy impractical and is now treated in tandem with the depression rather than first. Treatment factors: onset (four to six weeks, with early activation), durability (CBT gains persist), effort and side-effect burden, and access and cost: a full CBT course is hard to find publicly funded, private therapy is faster but unfunded, drug coverage depends on a family plan or OHIP+, and medication is cheaper, immediate and less work. Anxious patients are often exceptionally sensitive to side effects and somatically preoccupied, so they need more psychoeducation and closer follow-up. Needing medication is not a personal failing.

The depressive episode, grief, and the screen that was missed

A major depressive episode needs five of nine symptoms nearly every day for two weeks, a change from functioning, with at least one of depressed mood or anhedonia: depressed mood; markedly diminished interest or pleasure; significant weight or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia; psychomotor agitation or retardation; fatigue; worthlessness or excessive guilt; poor concentration or indecisiveness; recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, plan or attempt. Sleep, appetite and concentration changes alone never qualify. Suicidality is passive ("what's the point") or active ("I'm having thoughts of overdosing"). Severity: mild with minimal impairment, moderate with clear impairment, severe with marked impairment and possibly mood-congruent psychosis. Jon met criteria comfortably (mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia with a delayed sleep phase, appetite and weight loss, low energy, poor concentration, worthlessness, passive ideation); energy and psychomotor change were never explicitly assessed. Grief is not depression: a dog that died three days ago produces tearfulness, anhedonia and poor sleep as a proportionate response; at three months the questions that discriminate are whether there are any moments of enjoyment and whether the low mood is all day, most days, since grief has bad days and lifts between them.

The differential: bipolar I (at least one manic episode; a depressive episode is not required), bipolar II (a hypomanic episode of at least four days and a depressive episode, no mania, no psychosis), substance-induced depressive disorder (alcohol, cocaine withdrawal, steroids; the physiology must make sense), and depressive disorder due to another medical condition (anaemia, iron or B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism; diabetes, stroke, myocardial infarction, multiple sclerosis and any long debilitation are comorbid or precipitating). Minimum work-up: CBC, B12, TSH. Urine drug screens are not routine in outpatient or emergency practice; the exception is psychosis in an unreliable historian. Before any antidepressant, screen every depressed patient for a personal and family history of mania or hypomania, because antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate mania, and collateral from someone who saw the patient during the episode in question is the only reliable way to find a past hypomania. Bipolar depression is the harder problem: most of the time a patient with bipolar disorder spends unwell is spent depressed, and those depressions respond poorly. Sometimes the illness declares itself anyway: Jon's father's diagnosis surfaced only at the manic presentation.

Antidepressants: agents, side effects, duration

First line for depression: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, citalopram, paroxetine, fluvoxamine) and SNRIs (venlafaxine; duloxetine, which also treats neuropathic pain; desvenlafaxine), plus bupropion (an NDRI, activating, almost no sexual dysfunction, can worsen anxiety), mirtazapine (a NaSSA that increases appetite and sleep, useful in the depressed patient who has lost weight and cannot sleep, unpopular with the young for the same reasons) and vortioxetine. Take it at the same time daily, in the morning with at least 350 kcal of food, at night only if sedating; the effect of SSRIs on sleep is unpredictable and clinicians disagree about it. Side effects: GI upset (the gut is rich in serotonin receptors), headache and dizziness, activation in the first two weeks, sedation or insomnia, emotional blunting, and sexual dysfunction, the most bothersome because it persists and grows with dose (manage with the lowest effective dose, a switch, or added bupropion). Less common but serious: hyponatraemia and SIADH in the elderly (monitor sodium), bleeding through platelet effects in the already predisposed (not enough to stop before surgery), and serotonin syndrome, a medical emergency of hyperreflexia, clonus, autonomic instability, altered mental status and agitation, diagnosed clinically with the Hunter criteria, rare even on several serotonergic agents, riskier with opioids such as tramadol. Duration: after a first episode, 6 to 12 months after remission; after a second or later episode, 2 to 5 years or indefinitely; taper slowly at a calm time in life. Psychotherapy improves the odds of coming off successfully. First-line psychotherapies for depression: CBT (behavioural activation with scheduled pleasurable and mastery activities; the thought record), interpersonal therapy (grief, role transition, interpersonal disputes, interpersonal sensitivity) and behavioural activation itself.

Bipolar depression is treated differently. Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania or hypomania; first-line options are quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium and lamotrigine, with cariprazine and olanzapine-fluoxetine also supported; an antidepressant, if used at all, is combined with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic. Lamotrigine is often chosen for young women with bipolar II: better tolerated, no lithium monitoring, safe in pregnancy. The take-home: screen for bipolar disorder, and if it is there, never an antidepressant alone.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Panic attack: four or more symptoms, peaking in minutes. Panic disorder: recurrent, unexpected, plus a month of worry or avoidance. The trigger names the disorder; socially cued attacks are social anxiety disorder with panic attacks.
  • Fingers tingle from peripheral vasoconstriction; hyperventilation gives respiratory alkalosis; catecholamines run out, so panic ends.
  • Benzodiazepines are first line for nothing; short half-life means more dependence; bridge or severe-attack PRN only.
  • Panic disorder: SSRI or venlafaxine at the top of the range plus CBT with interoceptive exposure.
  • MDE: five of nine, two weeks, mood or anhedonia; grief lifts between bad days.
  • Every depressed patient is screened for mania before an antidepressant; CBC, B12, TSH.
Jon's first two acts run the anxiety-and-depression half of the week in one patient: recurrent unexpected attacks with avoidance make panic disorder, whose treatment is an SSRI or venlafaxine at the top of the range plus CBT with interoceptive exposure rather than the lorazepam he left the emergency department with; the physiology under the symptoms is the psychoeducation; and the depressive episode that followed met criteria but was started on an antidepressant without the one screen that every depressed patient needs, for a personal and family history of mania.

guides.title: Week 41 · 14 CBL 41, Jon Jacobs II: Mania, Bipolar I and Lithium
guides.html:
CBL 41 · faculty session

CBL 41, Jon Jacobs II: Mania, Bipolar I and Lithium

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The manic episode the antidepressant unmasked, DIG FAST and its thresholds, the two hierarchy rules that make Jon bipolar I, the differential of a first mania, genetics, acute treatment with atypical antipsychotics and mood stabilizers, and lithium in full: window, toxicity, interactions, monitoring and pregnancy; closing with the titration and conception scenarios.

Where the case stood

Jon, 20, had six months of unexpected panic attacks, then a major depressive episode treated with sertraline 25 then 50 mg; a month later his mother brought him back off the drug, agitated, sleepless, arranging his clothes by colour all night, talking about saving humanity and communicating with God, planning to buy a car with no job, and the family disclosed that his father has bipolar disorder. The first half of this case is in the previous guide; this half is the manic presentation, the diagnosis, and lithium.

Mania, and why Jon is bipolar I

A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood together with increased goal-directed activity or energy, lasting at least one week (any duration if hospitalization is needed), with three or more associated symptoms (four if the mood is only irritable): Distractibility, Indiscretion (activities with painful consequences: spending tens of thousands, hypersexuality, out-of-character substance use), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas or racing thoughts, Activity increase or psychomotor agitation, Sleep need decreased (energized on two or three hours), Talkativeness or pressured speech. It causes marked impairment, needs hospitalization, or includes psychosis. Jon had elevated and irritable mood, increased goal-directed activity (organizing clothes all night), no sleep, grandiose and religious delusions, impulsive spending, distractibility and a disorganized thought process for about four weeks; his speech was louder and faster but still interruptible, so not quite pressured. Hypomania is the same picture for at least four days without marked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis; bipolar II needs a hypomanic and a depressive episode with no history of mania.

Two hierarchy rules
A full manic episode makes the diagnosis bipolar I for good; such a patient can never be bipolar II. And severity overrides duration: an episode with psychosis or requiring hospitalization counts as bipolar I even if it has not lasted a week. Had Jon presented while still taking sertraline the label would have been a medication-induced manic episode; symptoms persisting and worsening three to four weeks after stopping make it bipolar disorder.

The differential of a first manic presentation: substance or medication induced (the antidepressant; cocaine or methamphetamine intoxication; alcohol withdrawal; the longer symptoms persist off the substance, the more likely a primary illness, and repeated "substance-induced" admissions with symptoms between them point the same way); another medical condition (hyperthyroidism, seizure disorder, CNS lesion); schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, distinguished because bipolar patients return to baseline between discrete mood episodes whereas schizophrenia usually leaves residual psychosis even on treatment, and schizoaffective disorder is a psychotic illness with a mood disorder present most of the time; ADHD, excluded by its childhood onset before 12 and chronic course; anxiety and trauma disorders, which mimic and often coexist. Once the manic episode has declared itself, MDD leaves the differential. Collateral from family on the timeline relative to the antidepressant, any earlier highs, the father's diagnosis and treatment response, and safety (weapons, driving, finances) is essential, and investigations should include CBC, electrolytes with calcium, creatinine, liver enzymes, TSH, a urine drug screen (justified here) and an ECG, several doubling as lithium baselines.

Genetics: having a parent with bipolar disorder raises risk about tenfold, more if both parents are affected; heritability is quoted at 40% (CBL) and 60 to 80% in published estimates; schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, ADHD and autism are the most heritable psychiatric conditions, and a family history of any mood disorder raises the risk of any mood disorder. The practical implication is the screen before the antidepressant, and a relative's good response to a drug is a reason to choose it.

Treating acute mania

Two first-line classes: atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) and mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate), alone or combined. In practice a very unwell patient starts on an atypical antipsychotic because it works faster, with a mood stabilizer added jointly or once things settle; the antipsychotic can often be tapered later, but the mood stabilizer stays long term to prevent both manic and depressive episodes. The choice weighs speed, psychosis, prior personal or family response (a relative who did well on lithium), side effects, comorbidity, childbearing potential and, for lithium specifically, the patient's reliability with pills and blood work. All of these drugs carry heavy side effects and the conversation is hard: the atypicals are metabolically promoting (appetite, weight, glucose, cholesterol; 60 pounds in a month on olanzapine is not unheard of), and metformin or GLP-1 agonists started alongside them are under study; olanzapine that ends an admission may not be the drug that sustains recovery outside it. Valproate is not started in anyone of childbearing age. Medication reduces the likelihood, frequency and intensity of episodes; it does not eliminate them.

Lithium

TopicContent
UsesAcute mania (slower than an atypical), bipolar depression, maintenance; one of two psychiatric drugs with anti-suicidal properties, hence also an augmenting agent in hard-to-treat, highly suicidal unipolar depression
Therapeutic windowNarrow. Targets about 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L in acute mania, lower (about 0.6 to 1.0) for maintenance; toxicity generally above 1.5. The level, not the dose, is the target; a suicide-attempt overdose with a level of 4.0 needed emergency dialysis
ToxicityCoarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, sudden nausea and vomiting, confusion or delirium, seizures, renal failure, death. Any of delirium, marked tremor, ataxia, confusion or sudden vomiting on lithium means a level in hospital
Precipitants and interactionsDehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea, salt restriction, summer sweating (a basketball player's counselling point); NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs reduce clearance
Common effectsFine tremor (propranolol helps), polyuria and polydipsia, nausea and diarrhoea, weight gain, acne, alopecia, metallic taste, cognitive dulling; "a medicine that can be hard to tolerate"
Organ risksHypothyroidism (commonest; treated with levothyroxine), goitre, autoimmune thyroiditis, rarely hyperthyroidism; hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic kidney disease, usually reversible on stopping, rarely progressing to end-stage renal disease
MonitoringBaseline renal function, electrolytes with calcium, TSH, CBC, ECG where indicated; a 12-hour trough level 5 days after starting and 5 days after every dose change, then every 3 months, then every 6 months when stable; renal and thyroid function and calcium every 6 months; weight, lipids and glucose because of weight gain
PregnancyNot contraindicated. Pregnancy and especially the postpartum are high-risk periods, so a woman stabilized on lithium is usually advised to continue; counsel a 1 in 1,000 risk of Ebstein's anomaly with first-trimester exposure versus 1 in 20,000 baseline, surgically correctable; levels need frequent adjustment as fluid volumes shift; breastfeeding is generally not recommended, which is one reason some women switch to an atypical antipsychotic and accept the relapse risk. Valproate is contraindicated (neural tube defects 5 to 9%, other malformations 11%); carbamazepine also raises neural tube risk; lamotrigine is safe and often chosen for young women; the atypical antipsychotics were described as having a better pregnancy safety profile without teratogenicity and as compatible with breastfeeding, at the cost of metabolic risk. Mount Sinai runs a five-day postpartum program for high-risk women, with daily psychiatric review and overnight feeding support to protect sleep

Closing scenarios

  • A 28-year-old on sertraline 25 mg for three weeks with no change: 25 mg is sub-therapeutic (100 to 200 mg treats depression; anxiety and OCD need the top of the range); increase as tolerated with psychoeducation, since the full effect takes four to six weeks at a therapeutic dose and early response is a good prognostic sign. Sleep improves at 50 mg but symptoms persist: keep titrating; mood and anxiety lift first, cognition, sleep, fatigue and appetite lag. Still significantly depressed after three weeks at 200 mg: a partial response, already optimized, so augment with bupropion, a low-dose atypical antipsychotic, or psychotherapy.
  • A 30-year-old on sertraline 100 mg for four weeks with no benefit at all: switch; switching to a different class offers no advantage over switching within the class, so choose by side-effect profile (bupropion for the fatigued patient).
  • A 29-year-old with bipolar disorder trying to conceive: the risk of a mood episode in pregnancy and postpartum is high, so she needs mood stabilization; continue what works; valproate is out; lithium carries the Ebstein's risk and needs close levels; lamotrigine and the atypicals are the safer alternatives.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Mania: mood plus energy, one week, three of DIG FAST (four if only irritable); a manic episode is bipolar I forever; psychosis or hospitalization makes it bipolar I regardless of duration; bipolar I needs no depressive episode.
  • Louder and faster but interruptible is not pressured speech.
  • Mania three to four weeks off the antidepressant is bipolar disorder, not medication-induced.
  • Acute mania: antipsychotic first for speed, mood stabilizer for the long term; valproate never in childbearing age.
  • Lithium: level in 5 days and after every change, 12-hour trough; 0.8 to 1.2 acute, toxic above 1.5; NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, dehydration; thyroid, calcium, creatinine; Ebstein's 1 in 1,000; no breastfeeding.
  • Sub-therapeutic dose: titrate. Partial response at maximum: augment. No response: switch, within or across class alike.
The antidepressant unmasked a manic episode with psychosis, which the hierarchy rules make bipolar I for life whatever its duration, and which persisting for weeks off the drug is no longer medication-induced. Acute mania is treated with an atypical antipsychotic for speed and a mood stabilizer for the long term, never valproate in someone who could become pregnant. Lithium, chosen with Jon and his mother, has a narrow window (0.8 to 1.2 acute, toxic above 1.5), a five-day trough after every change, thyroid, calcium and kidney monitoring, a short list of drugs and states that raise its level, and a pregnancy conversation about Ebstein's anomaly and breastfeeding. Sub-therapeutic doses are titrated, partial responses at the maximum are augmented, and non-responses are switched.

guides.html:
Across SLM01–07 · WFQ

Integrated Review: Anxiety & Related Disorders, and the Weekly Formative Quiz

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The seven disorders side by side, the drug and therapy maps, the numbers ladder, the pairwise discriminators, the mood and lithium rules the formative quiz reaches for, and all fifteen quiz items walked through.

The week on one page

Seven disorders share one architecture: a core fear or intrusion, a duration threshold, an avoidance or neutralizing behaviour, and a treatment built on exposure. The differences are what the exam tests.

DisorderCoreThresholdBehaviourFirst-line psychotherapyFirst-line drugs
Specific phobiaA specific object or situationAll of A–G; ≥6 monthsAvoidance or endurance with intense fearCBT with systematic desensitization (graded exposure + relaxation)None: little evidence for medication
Social anxiety disorderNegative evaluation by othersAll of A–J; ≥6 monthsAvoidance of social or performance situationsCBT: cognitive restructuring + exposuresSSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine), venlafaxine XR, pregabalin; performance only: propranolol PRN
Generalized anxiety disorderUncontrollable worry about a number of events≥3 of 6 associated symptoms; more days than not for ≥6 monthsWorry, tension, avoidance of triggersCBT and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy; therapy equals medicationSSRIs (escitalopram, paroxetine, sertraline), SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), pregabalin
OCDObsessions and/or compulsions>1 hour/day, marked distress, interferenceCompulsions, including mental actsCBT with exposure and response prevention; equal or superior to drugsSSRIs (escitalopram, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine); second line clomipramine, venlafaxine XR
PTSDExposure to death, serious injury or sexual violenceIntrusion ≥1 of 5, avoidance ≥1 of 2, cognition/mood ≥2 of 7, arousal ≥2 of 6; >1 monthAvoidance of internal and external remindersTrauma-focused CBT; EMDR when TF-CBT is not an optionSSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline), venlafaxine XR
Acute stress disorderSame picture as PTSDWithin the first 30 days; most recoverAs PTSDTime is the only axis between the two
AgoraphobiaFear that escape is difficult or help unavailable≥2 of 5 situations: public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, lines or crowds, being out aloneAvoidance or need for a companionTested on the formative quiz; no module this week
Six months is the duration for specific phobia, social anxiety disorder and GAD. One month separates PTSD from acute stress disorder. One hour a day is OCD's criterion B. Only GAD carries a symptom count among the three anxiety disorders; PTSD carries four.

The drug map

Every first-line drug this week is an antidepressant or pregabalin. What changes is which names appear on which list.

DrugSpecific phobiaSocial anxietyGADOCDPTSD
Escitalopram—First lineFirst lineFirst line—
Sertraline—First lineFirst lineFirst lineFirst line
Paroxetine—First lineFirst lineFirst lineFirst line
Fluvoxamine—First line—First line—
Fluoxetine———First lineFirst line
Venlafaxine XR—First lineFirst lineSecond lineFirst line
Duloxetine——First line——
Pregabalin—First lineFirst line——
Propranolol PRN—Performance only———
Clomipramine———Second line—
  • Duloxetine is GAD only. Fluvoxamine is social anxiety and OCD, never GAD. Pregabalin is social anxiety and GAD.
  • Venlafaxine XR is first line in social anxiety, GAD and PTSD but second line in OCD, behind five SSRIs.
  • Sertraline and paroxetine are the two SSRIs on every list except specific phobia.
  • Benzodiazepines are on no first-line list. They are the trap option in GAD ("most evidence": antidepressant) and PTSD (wrong against antidepressant), and they are not first-line maintenance treatment because of tolerance, dependence, cognitive effects and falls.
  • SSRI side effects: GI symptoms, headaches, weight gain and sexual dysfunction. Sexual dysfunction is the common side effect of sertraline; tics and dystonia belong to antipsychotics, arrhythmia to tricyclics.
  • OCD dosing doctrine: start low, aim high; response at 6–12 weeks; adequate trial 12–15 weeks; continue at least a year; taper very slowly; the goal is improvement, not remission; relapse is high without behavioural strategies.

The therapy map and the two curves

DisorderTherapyWhat it does
Specific phobiaSystematic desensitizationRank fears 1–10, start at 1/10, graded exposure paired with relaxation, advance once desensitized
Social anxietyCBTCognitive restructuring of maladaptive thoughts plus exposures
GADCBT and MBCTPsychoeducation to prevent avoidance; exposure (extinction), relaxation, biofeedback, imagery also listed
OCDExposure and response prevention12–15 weekly sessions; hierarchy 0–100, start at the bottom, prevent rituals and avoidance
PTSDTrauma-focused CBT; EMDR; cognitive processing therapy; prolonged exposure; stress inoculationDBT is on the list only for self-harm in borderline personality disorder
Panic disorder (quiz)Interoceptive exposureInducing panic in a controlled setting with box-breathing; anxiety falls across exposures by habituation

The mechanism under all of it is the same pair of curves. Performing a compulsion or escaping gives an abrupt drop in anxiety straight back to baseline with the peak unchanged next time: negative reinforcement, and the disorder is maintained. Exposure with response prevention gives progressively lower peaks that resolve sooner, settling onto one low plateau: habituation, because the feared consequence does not occur and anxiety is learned to be time-limited. Avoidance is the behaviour common to every anxiety disorder, which is why exposure is the treatment everywhere. The CBT model is the thoughts, feelings, behaviours triangle with bidirectional arrows; in this course this is the cognitive triad, and any option containing "defenses" is psychodynamic and wrong.

Cognitive distortions

DistortionSignature move
Discounting the positiveExplaining away disconfirming positive evidence: "he only invited me to be nice"
CatastrophizationPredicting the worst outcome
OvergeneralizationOne event becomes an always or never rule
LabelingA global negative label on self or others

The numbers ladder

DisorderPrevalenceOnsetSexOther
Specific phobiaMost common mental disorder in women; second in men behind substance-relatedNot givenRanking differs by sexComorbid anxiety, mood, substance disorders
Social anxietySecond most common anxiety disorderMedian 13; 75% between 7 and 15More femalesMost common comorbidity MDD or other anxiety
GAD9% lifetimeMedian 30; the latest of the anxiety disorders2:1 femaleMDD comorbid up to 50%; European descent and developed countries
OCD2–3% lifetimeMean 19.5, earlier peak in males—~10% in first-degree relatives; WHO 10th leading cause of disability; chronic
PTSD9% (quiz band 6–9%)Mid-to-late 20s (band 25–30)2× femaleSuicide risk ×2–3; sexual and relationship violence the commonest source; higher in Aboriginal peoples, refugees, African-Americans

Two traps: 9% belongs to both GAD and PTSD, and 1–3% is OCD's number, planted as a distractor on the PTSD prevalence item. Social anxiety starts in early adolescence, OCD at the end of it, PTSD in the twenties, GAD at thirty.

Pairwise discriminators

  • Specific phobia vs social anxiety: is the feared thing the object or situation itself, or being judged?
  • Specific phobia vs panic disorder: cued and immediate on exposure, or recurrent and unexpected?
  • Agoraphobia vs the others: public transport, open or enclosed spaces, crowds, being out alone, feared because escape is hard. Public speaking is social anxiety; heights and flying are specific phobia.
  • Social anxiety vs GAD: worry confined to social and performance situations, or spread across many activities and uncontrollable?
  • GAD vs OCD: worry about real-life concerns versus recurrent obsessions or compulsions.
  • GAD vs MDD: anxious mood without recurrent low mood, remembering the 50% comorbidity.
  • GAD vs OCPD: episodic uncontrollable worry versus a pervasive early-adult pattern of orderliness, perfectionism and control.
  • GAD vs mania: "racing thoughts" with worry-driven insomnia, fatigue, no grandiosity and no uncharacteristic behaviour is GAD. Mania has decreased need for sleep with preserved energy, grandiosity and impulsive behaviour.
  • OCD vs hoarding, BDD, trichotillomania: hoarding driven by OCD obsessions is OCD; BDD is limited to appearance; trichotillomania is hair pulling without obsessions.
  • OCD vs OCPD: no intrusions and no response-driven rituals in OCPD; both can be diagnosed together.
  • OCD vs tics: compulsions follow obsessions; tics follow premonitory sensory urges.
  • PTSD vs acute stress disorder: more than one month versus the first 30 days.
  • Any of them vs a medical cause: hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, porphyria, CNS neoplasms, and substances including caffeine (moderate intake is 200–300 mg/day; four cups of coffee is about 540 mg). New panic at 70 is an atypical onset and a red flag.

The mood side

Four of the fifteen formative-quiz items reach into the depression and bipolar material from the pre-week videos and the mood teaching that follows. The rules:

TopicThe rule
Major depressive disorder≥5 of 9 symptoms in the same two-week period, at least one of which is depressed mood or anhedonia. The other seven (appetite, sleep, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, concentration, thoughts of death) are criteria but not core.
MDD across the lifespanAdolescents often present with irritability rather than sadness; MDD is common in adults; antidepressants are effective in adolescents; new-onset depression in the elderly may signal an emerging neurocognitive disorder.
Manic vs hypomanic episodeMania: ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized) of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy, plus ≥3 symptoms (≥4 if irritable only), with marked functional impairment. Hypomania: ≥4 days, no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalization. One week of irritability, less sleep, talkativeness, grandiosity and inability to complete assignments is a manic episode. Cyclothymia needs two years; mixed features need depressive symptoms.
LithiumCounsel about fine tremor (coarse tremor means toxicity), polyuria and polydipsia, weight gain, hypothyroidism, GI upset, acne. Dose is titrated to trough serum levels, drawn about 12 hours post-dose: not by weight, not by a loading protocol, and not by hepatic function, because lithium is renally cleared. Monitor levels, renal function, thyroid and calcium. Fatty liver belongs to valproate.
Preventing manic relapseA regular sleep cycle. Sleep loss is both a prodrome and a precipitant of mania; exercise is good general advice but not the best answer for manic recurrence.
Biopsychosocial sortingLow self-esteem is psychological; social isolation and belonging to a marginalized population are social; alcohol misuse sorts as biological. The question tests the domain, not whether the item is a risk factor.

The weekly formative quiz, walked through

QAskedAnswerWhy
1Common side effect of sertralineSexual dysfunctionSSRI class effect; tics and dystonia are antipsychotic effects, arrhythmia is tricyclic
2MDD over the lifespanNew-onset geriatric MDD may signal a neurocognitive disorderThe three distractors use "always", "rare" and "not effective", each false
3Lithium counsellingTremorVitiligo and osteoporosis are not lithium effects; fatty liver is valproate
4Initiating lithiumDose titrated to serum levelsNarrow therapeutic index; renal, not hepatic, clearance
529-year-old with three months of "racing thoughts", worry, insomnia, fatigue, irritability, tension, no grandiosityGADTired rather than energized, no grandiosity, no uncharacteristic behaviour; "racing thoughts" is the decoy. Three months sits below the six-month criterion, hence "at this time"
6The other core MDD criterion beside depressed moodAnhedoniaSuicidal ideation, psychomotor retardation and fatigue are criteria but not core
7Psychological risk factor for depressionLow self-esteemIsolation and marginalization are social; alcohol misuse is biological
8Anxiety decreasing across induced panic exposuresHabituationInteroceptive exposure; MBSR is a programme, attenuation is not the term, automatic thoughts are cognitive
9Three features of the cognitive triadThoughts, feelings, behaviours"Defenses" marks a psychodynamic distractor
10Lifestyle counselling after a manic episodeRegular sleep cycleSleep loss precipitates mania; the pre-week reflective question asked this
11One week of irritability, less sleep, talkativeness, feeling special, unable to complete assignments, medical causes excludedManic episodeOne week plus impairment; hypomania has no marked impairment; cyclothymia needs two years; no depressive symptoms for mixed features
12"He only invited me to be nice"Discounting the positivePositive evidence explained away; not catastrophizing, overgeneralizing or labeling
13Agoraphobia situationUsing public transportationPublic speaking is social anxiety; heights and flying are specific phobia
14Behaviour common to anxiety disordersAvoidanceSelf-harm, aggression and hypersomnolence point elsewhere
15Most effective treatment for GADCBT and an SSRIInterpersonal therapy is for depression; benzodiazepines are not first line
The formative quiz does not test OCD, PTSD, suicide risk assessment or disorders due to another medical condition. Four of the seven self-learning modules are absent from it, and four items reach into mood and bipolar material instead. It is not a blueprint for the Mastery Exercise; the seven self-learning modules are.

Threads that run through the week

  • Suicide risk is not confined to one topic: PTSD carries a two- to three-fold suicide risk, Canadian residents report 15% past-year suicidal ideation and medical students 11%, and a history of previous attempts is the most powerful predictor at any age. Asking does not increase risk.
  • Medical mimics appear in three modules: GAD's differential names pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism; the medical-condition module gives the full table and the pheochromocytoma remission case; the social anxiety case carries a past history of hyperthyroidism.
  • Substances appear in every case: lorazepam PRN for the flyer, whisky before presentations, four cups of coffee, and the HIV example's three-way split between virus, antiretroviral and drug use.
  • Comorbidity with depression is stated for social anxiety (most common comorbidity), GAD (up to 50%), OCD and PTSD; burnout sits upstream of depression on the wellness continuum.
  • Dehumanizing language about patients with mental illness, substance use or cognitive disability is the ethics module's everyday example, and it is the same population this week's clinical modules describe.

Discriminators and exam traps

  • Which drug is on which list: duloxetine GAD only; fluvoxamine social anxiety and OCD; pregabalin social anxiety and GAD; venlafaxine XR second line only in OCD; propranolol only for performance anxiety; nothing for specific phobia.
  • Which number is whose: 9% GAD and PTSD; 2–3% OCD; median 13 social anxiety; 19.5 OCD; 25–30 PTSD; 30 GAD; 2:1 GAD; 2× PTSD.
  • Which count is whose: 3 of 6 GAD; 1/1/2/2 PTSD; 5 of 9 MDD with one core; 2 of 5 situations agoraphobia; 3 symptoms mania (4 if irritable).
  • Which clock is whose: 6 months anxiety disorders; 1 month PTSD; 30 days acute stress; 1 week mania; 4 days hypomania; 2 years cyclothymia; 2 weeks MDD; 1 hour a day OCD.
  • Which therapy is whose: systematic desensitization, ERP, TF-CBT or EMDR, MBCT, interoceptive exposure; DBT is the distractor.
  • CBT plus medication beats medication alone but not CBT alone in OCD; in GAD the two are equivalent; in specific phobia only CBT has evidence.
The anxiety and related disorders differ in what is feared, how long it must last, what is counted, and which names sit on the first-line drug list. Treatment converges on CBT with exposure, whose mechanism is habituation, and on the SSRIs, with venlafaxine XR, duloxetine, pregabalin, propranolol and clomipramine each occupying a specific slot. The formative quiz tests those slots, the mood and lithium rules from the pre-week material, and the CBT vocabulary; the Mastery Exercise will also test the four modules it leaves out.

Night-Before High-Yield

Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders

Week 41 · Psych II — Mood & Anxiety Disorders
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Suicidal thoughts disclosed → four steps in order: plan and intent (passive vs active; which pills, access?) → intensity (frequency, practised or aborted attempts, note or will, chosen time or place) → SAD PERSONS → reasons for living. Asking does not increase risk.
Previous attempt → one of the most powerful predictors at every age. Always ask.
New panic at 70, or panic that remits after a pheochromocytoma is removed → anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: time course, atypical features, plausible mechanism. Hyperthyroidism and pheochromocytoma are the two named mimics.
Mood change two days after a stroke → depressive disorder due to another medical condition. Hopelessness four weeks after a cancer diagnosis → a reaction to the news; the tumour predated it.
One week of irritable mood, less sleep, grandiosity and unable to function → manic episode, not hypomania. Hypomania is ≥4 days without marked impairment.
'Racing thoughts' with fatigue, no grandiosity, no uncharacteristic behaviour → GAD, not bipolar disorder.
Benzodiazepines are on no first-line list; the answer for GAD and PTSD pharmacotherapy is an antidepressant. Specific phobia gets no drug at all.
PTSD-type symptoms in the first 30 days → acute stress disorder; most recover. Beyond one month → PTSD.
Depressed patient about to start an antidepressant → screen for a personal and family history of mania or hypomania first, with collateral; antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania.
Confusion, coarse tremor, ataxia or sudden vomiting on lithium → toxicity until a level in hospital says otherwise; NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, dehydration and summer sweating raise the level.
Psychosis or hospitalization during a 'hypomanic' episode → bipolar I regardless of duration; a full manic episode is bipolar I for good.
Frail elderly patient not eating or drinking with severe depression → fast-track to ECT: gold standard for psychotic depression, 3×/week, improvement by ~6.

Anxiety disorders side by side SLM01–03

Duration for phobia, SAD, GAD ≥6 months, all three
Only one with a symptom count GAD: ≥3 of 6 (restless, fatigued, concentration, irritable, tension, sleep)
